title: CS102 Unit 0a - Course Intro
summary: Title slide introducing the CS102 course introduction unit taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: CS102 Unit 0a - Course Intro. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. Opening title slide for the course introduction unit.
notes_text: First slide of the deck; establishes course and unit identity.

title: Introduction: How We Interact With Software
summary: Frames how pervasively people interact with software in daily life and asks what software really is.
main_text: This is how we often see and interact with software (through graphical interfaces on laptops, desktops, tablets, and phones). In truth we interact with software far more than we think. We are interacting with software when we drive, fly, turn on the lights, watch TV, go to the bank, or buy something with our credit card. So, what is software really?
notes_text: Sets up the motivating question of the unit: software is far more ubiquitous than the visible GUI suggests.

images.description: Collage of consumer devices (laptop, desktop macOS screen, tablet held in hand, smartphone) showing familiar graphical software interfaces, illustrating how users typically 'see' software.

title: Introduction: High-Level Languages, Compilers & Interpreters
summary: Contrasts the movie 'ones and zeros' view of software with reality: we write high-level code that compilers/interpreters translate to binary.
main_text: This is how the movies think computers 'see' software (streams of 1s and 0s). The far-right binary picture is reasonably accurate. While all programs eventually end up as 1s and 0s, we generally program using some form of 'high-level' or scripting language. We then use a 'magical' tool called the compiler or interpreter to translate that code. Because of how the hardware works, our software must be written using certain structures. This class is intended to teach you those programming structures.
notes_text: Introduces the translation pipeline: human-readable high-level code -> compiler/interpreter -> machine binary. Motivates why programming has required structures.

images.description: 'Matrix'-style green falling-character code image over a blue binary background, with a labeled 'Compilers / Interpreters' oval and arrows pointing from a high-level source-code snippet to the binary, teaching the source-to-binary translation flow.

title: And Now With AI
summary: Explains that generative AI is a new layer in software development, letting us create required code structures via natural-language prompts.
main_text: We are entering a new era of software development practice. While the computer still requires that our software be written using certain structures, generative AI is helping us evolve our ability to create those structures using more natural language instructions, prompts, and guidance. The prior compiler/interpreter pipeline still applies, but AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) can now generate source code from natural-language prompts.
notes_text: Positions AI as an additional authoring layer on top of the traditional compile/interpret pipeline, not a replacement for structured code.

images.description: Same compiler/interpreter pipeline diagram as prior slide, now extended with a generative-AI chatbot logo and a 'Write a program to do...' prompt box feeding source code, showing AI generating code that is then compiled.

title: AI and Software Development: Guidance for This Class
summary: Advises balanced AI use: AI can do early tasks, but over-reliance prevents building the skills employers value.
main_text: In approaching this class, consider: As you learn CS content, AI will be able to handle the simple tasks we ask of you in this early, introductory course. But if you overuse AI, you will NEVER learn the skills needed to handle tasks larger and more complex than AI could handle. Most companies wouldn't hire someone who can only produce what AI can; they need people with creativity, problem solving, and debugging skills. At the same time, using AI is becoming common practice (with some exceptions). You need to develop the critical thinking skills to formulate and decompose problems, debug code, and create portions of code.
notes_text: Frames the pedagogical stance on AI: use it, but not as a crutch. Emphasizes durable skills (decomposition, debugging, problem formulation).

title: AI and CS102 Homework Policy
summary: Details the two-version homework policy: a no-AI first version and an AI-allowed second version, graded on the maximum score.
main_text: Coding homeworks will be done twice (two versions). First version: NO use of AI or other resources besides course staff, textbooks, and C++ documentation/reference websites. You learn through muscle memory and by programming yourself (like playing an instrument); spend time (a week) struggling with the problem and getting help, since programming progress comes in bursts. Second version: you MAY use AI for the same problem and should ask AI tools to help improve the correctness, style, and efficiency of the code you wrote, with the goal of getting the program to work. Programs are graded by automated tests checking correct output in the desired format. Your MAXIMUM grade on either version is your score for that assignment, even if one of them is a 0. Violations of the first-version rules will be referred to the Office of Academic Integrity.
notes_text: Key logistics students ask about: no-AI first pass, AI-allowed second pass, max-of-two grading, automated testing, and academic-integrity enforcement.

title: This Class: A Long On-Ramp to Learning
summary: States the course goal: a long 'on-ramp' building programming basics and algorithmic thinking for future courses and careers.
main_text: The goal of this class is to be a LONG on-ramp to learning: the basics of programming, and (highlighted) the algorithmic thinking skills needed to excel in future courses and career paths.
notes_text: Uses a freeway on-ramp metaphor: a gradual, extended ramp into computing. Emphasis (highlighted) is on algorithmic thinking, not just syntax.

images.description: Photo of a freeway on-ramp with a stop sign, paired with an aerial photo of a diamond highway interchange, visually reinforcing the 'long on-ramp to learning' metaphor.

title: Course Structure: Four Units
summary: Describes the recurring components each unit contains and the four conceptual units of the course.
main_text: The course is broken into 4 units, each consisting of a repeating cycle of: Lectures; Lab (Tools + Practice + Teamwork); Portfolio (self-selected programming problems); and Homework (individual practice and programming assignments). The four units are: (1) Scalar Processing - Expressions & Conditionals; (2) Linear (1D) Processing - Loops; (3) Multidimensional Processing - Nested Loops; (4) Divide & Conquer - Functions and Abstraction.
notes_text: The four-unit arc mirrors increasing data dimensionality: scalars -> 1D -> multidimensional -> functional decomposition. Each unit repeats the lecture/lab/portfolio/homework cycle.

images.description: Cycle diagram showing the repeating unit components (Lectures, Lab, Portfolio, Homework) above four numbered circular-arrow icons representing the four units: Scalar Processing (Expressions & Conditionals), Linear 1D Processing (Loops), Multidimensional Processing (Nested Loops), and Divide & Conquer (Functions and Abstraction).

title: Exams and Grading: Level-Based Rubric
summary: Presents the level-based grading system where a starting grade is adjusted up or down by category to reach a final letter grade.
main_text: Grading uses a level scale mapped to letters: A=8, A-=7, B+=6, B=5, B-=4, C+=3, C=2 (start here), D=1, F=0. You begin at a Starting Grade of level 2 (C). Adjustments: Lab: +1 if you miss at most 3 labs, else +0. HW (late work max 75%, automated grading): +2 (75%+ on 2 and 100% on all others), +1 (75%+ on all but 1), +0 (less than 75% on 2 or more). Portfolio (TA graded): +1 if all complete and meets criteria, else +0. Written Midterm (WMT): +1 (85-100), +0 (70-84), -1 (50-69), -2 (35-49), -3 (<35), OR average of WMT+Final within those ranges. Programming Midterm (PMT): +1 (85-100), +0 (<85). Final: +1 (85-100), +0 (70-84), -1 (50-69), -2 (35-49), -3 (<35). Sample computation totals to level 7 = A-.
notes_text: Grading is additive on a discrete level scale rather than a weighted percentage. Note the WMT/Final averaging option that can rescue a weak midterm.

images.description: Vertical color-coded grade scale (A:8 down to F:0, with 'Start here' at C:2) beside a detailed grading rubric table listing Category, Criteria, and a worked Sample Grade column summing to Total 7 = A-.

title: Exams and Grading: Baseline and Exam Dates
summary: Explains that steady participation lands a B+, exams can raise (or lower) the grade, and lists the three exam dates.
main_text: By simply attending lab and completing assignments on time to basic levels of proficiency (see the HW policy before becoming anxious), you should land at a B+. From there, you have 3 exams to gain +2 levels to achieve an A - but beware, you can lose levels as well. Course exam dates: Exam 1 (Written) - Oct. 8 (in class); Exam 2 (Programming) - Nov. 5 (in Quiz section); Final (Written) - Dec. 13.
notes_text: Reassures that consistent effort yields a strong baseline (B+); exams are the upside (and downside) toward an A. Contains the concrete exam calendar.

title: Syllabus
summary: Section divider pointing students to the full course syllabus.
main_text: Syllabus. (Section slide directing students to review the complete course syllabus.)
notes_text: Transitional/section slide; the detailed syllabus is a separate document.

title: Expectations
summary: Lists instructor expectations: attend and engage in lectures, and 'catch the wave' by starting early and practicing weekly.
main_text: Attend lectures and be engaged: ask questions; we're a team and I need you; I'll give you my best, so try to give me yours. Catch the wave: start assignments early, schedule weekly practice time, and read and review other sources of input.
notes_text: Emphasizes engagement and consistent, early, well-scheduled practice (the 'catch the wave' surfing metaphor).

images.description: Photo of a surfer riding a wave, illustrating the 'Catch the wave!' expectation about momentum and starting assignments early.

title: 20-Second Timeout: About the Instructor
summary: Instructor introduction covering Mark Redekopp's background, education, work history, and interests.
main_text: Who Am I? Teaching faculty in EE and CS. Undergrad at USC in CECS. Grad at USC in Computer Engineering. Work(ed) at Raytheon. Enjoys learning other languages (Spanish, Mandarin, ...). Sports enthusiast: basketball, baseball, ultimate frisbee, pickleball.
notes_text: Personal introduction slide establishing instructor credibility and rapport.

images.description: Professional portrait photograph of the instructor (Mark Redekopp).

title: Programming Languages 1: Declarative Languages
summary: Defines declarative languages as describing the 'what' (data) but not the 'how', with HTML and CSS as examples.
main_text: Declarative Languages describe the WHAT (i.e., the data) but NOT the how. Examples: HTML and CSS. HTML markup declares document structure and content (headings, paragraphs, body), and CSS declares presentation rules (font-size, font-family, position, top/left) without specifying step-by-step procedures.
notes_text: Contrast target for the next slide (imperative). Declarative = specify desired result/structure, let the system determine execution.

images.description: HTML5 and CSS3 shield logos above a syntax-highlighted HTML source snippet (DOCTYPE, html, head, body, h1, p) and a CSS rule snippet (h4 and .number selectors with font-size, font-family, position properties), illustrating declarative code.

title: Programming Languages 2: Imperative / Structured Languages
summary: Defines imperative/structured languages as describing both the data and the step-by-step algorithm, using a recipe analogy.
main_text: Imperative/Structured Languages describe the WHAT (data) AND the HOW (instructions/algorithm). Examples: C/C++, Java, JavaScript, Python (used today). These are the focus of most programming courses. Programs are like a recipe for how to operate on data: the code lists ordered instructions (e.g., read a, b, c; compute the discriminant det = b*b - 4*a*c; if det >= 0 compute the two roots else print 'Imaginary roots'). The instructions are the recipe steps and the data are the ingredients; the computer reads the instructions and operates on the data.
notes_text: Core paradigm for the course. The recipe metaphor (instructions=steps, data=ingredients, computer=cook) recurs later in the deck.

images.description: Python 'Quadratic Equation Solver' code screenshot beside a recipe-card illustration with flour and eggs and a chef, mapping code instructions to recipe steps and data to ingredients, with the computer as the cook that reads instructions and operates on data.

title: High Level Languages: 'Mother Tongues' Timeline
summary: Displays a large historical chart tracing the genealogy and evolution of programming languages over the decades.
main_text: High Level Languages. A large 'Mother Tongues' poster/chart traces the roots and lineage of computer programming languages through the ages (roughly 1954-2001), showing how languages descend from and influence one another (e.g., Fortran, Cobol, Lisp, Algol, C, C++, Java, Python lineages). A 'Survival of the Fittest' sidebar notes reasons languages endure (wide audience, gets a job done, delivers new functionality, fills a niche, elegance, powerful backer, charismatic leader). Source: digibarn ComputerLanguagesChart.
notes_text: Illustrative/enrichment slide showing that today's languages evolved from a family tree of predecessors; not detailed exam material.

images.description: Large 'Mother Tongues' timeline poster charting the family tree of programming languages from the 1950s to ~2001, with a color-coded key and a 'Survival of the Fittest' sidebar listing why certain languages endure.

title: Why C++
summary: Justifies the choice of C++: widely used, close to hardware (fast, flexible, and dangerous), and foundational for learning other languages.
main_text: Why C++? C++ is used widely. C++ is 'close' to the hardware (HW), which makes it fast, makes it flexible (near-direct control of the hardware), and makes it dangerous (near-direct control of the hardware). In fact, many other languages are themselves written in C/C++. Because if you learn C++, you can likely learn most languages very quickly. And because that's what is used in CS 103.
notes_text: Motivates the language choice; 'close to hardware' is a double-edged sword (performance/control vs. footguns). Feeds into CS 103.

title: What Language Aspects Will We Learn?
summary: Enumerates the C/C++ skills and topics the course covers, overlapping the first portion of CS 103.
main_text: Programming skills in C/C++ (overlaps with the first 20% of CS 103): data representation; basics of discrete mathematics; expressions; conditional statements; iterative statements (loops); functions; and arrays. Also: problem solving using common programming 'idioms'.
notes_text: Roadmap of technical content. Maps directly to the four-unit structure (expressions/conditionals -> loops -> arrays/nested -> functions).

title: Section: Starting to Think Like a Computer
summary: Section divider transitioning into how computers internally represent and process information.
main_text: STARTING TO THINK LIKE A COMPUTER. (Section divider introducing the mindset shift toward how a computer represents and processes data.)
notes_text: Transitional slide; sets up the 'everything is a number' theme that follows.

title: It's a Numbers Game
summary: States two foundational facts: everything in a computer is a number, and computers process only one or two numbers at a time.
main_text: Fact 1: Everything in a computer is a NUMBER. Things like 102 and 3.9 are numbers, but so is text, images, and sound - everything. Fact 2: Computers can only work with or 'see' 1 or 2 numbers at a time (i.e., they can only do 1 thing at a time). Humans process information differently, and therein lies some of the difficulty of learning programming.
notes_text: Foundational mental model: (1) all data reduces to numbers; (2) computation is fundamentally sequential/local. Human vs. machine information processing mismatch is the core learning hurdle.

images.description: Python quadratic-solver code screenshot with a recipe card ('Combine 2c. Flour, Mix in 3 eggs'), reprising the recipe/instructions-and-data analogy for how a computer steps through numbers one at a time.

title: Example (1): Text as Numbers
summary: Shows that the character we read as 'a' is stored by the computer as the number 97.
main_text: What do you see? The letter 'a'. What does the computer see? A number - each text character is coded to a number. Example: the character 'a' corresponds to the code 97 (viewable via Character Map / Insert Symbol).
notes_text: Concrete instance of Fact 1: the glyph 'a' maps to numeric code 97 (its ASCII value). Bridges into the ASCII table on the next slide.

images.description: Large letter 'a' shown next to the number 97, illustrating that the character 'a' is stored as its numeric character code.

title: Text Representation: ASCII / UTF-8
summary: Introduces ASCII (UTF-8) as the common character encoding where every character maps to a decimal/hexadecimal number.
main_text: The most common character code is ASCII (UTF-8). Every character, even non-printing (control) characters, has a corresponding number, expressed in decimal (base 10) or hexadecimal (base 16). The ASCII chart lists codes such as: 'A' = 65 (0x41), 'a' = 97 (0x61), Space = 32, and control codes like NUL=0, Bell(BEL)=7, Line feed(LF)=10, Carriage return(CR)=13, DEL=127. Reference: commfront ASCII chart.
notes_text: Establishes ASCII/UTF-8 as the standard text encoding and reintroduces decimal vs. hexadecimal number bases (a recurring theme). Note 'A'=65 vs 'a'=97.

images.description: Full ASCII character-code chart with columns for Decimal, Hex, Name, and Char, listing printable and non-printing (control) characters from 0-127; the rows for 'A'=65 and 'a'=97 are highlighted with a red box.

title: Example (2): A Circle as Numbers
summary: Shows that a circle a human perceives is, to the computer, coordinate pairs of pixels or parameters (radius and origin) it must enumerate and color.
main_text: What do you see? A circle. What does the computer see? Coordinate pairs of each 'pixel' - or a parametric description such as r = 120 and origin = (10, 14). To draw it, the computer has to enumerate and visit each location and color it black. Example pixel coordinates along an edge: (x,y)=(60,100), (59,101), (57,102), (56,103).
notes_text: Second instance of 'everything is a number': geometry becomes coordinate/parameter data plus a per-pixel enumeration procedure. Foreshadows loops (visiting each location).

images.description: A hand-drawn black circle at top representing human perception, and a zoomed pixelated diagonal edge at bottom annotated with coordinate pairs like (56,103), (57,102), (59,101), (60,100), representing the computer's per-pixel view.

title: Example (3): An Image as Pixel Numbers
summary: Shows that a photographed face is, to the computer, a grid of many numbers (pixels) whose values correspond to color/brightness.
main_text: What do you see? A man's face. What does the computer see? Many numbers (aka pixels), where each value corresponds to a color (here, grayscale intensity). A zoomed region of the image resolves into a grid of numeric pixel values such as 0, 64, 128, 192. Image taken from the photo 'Robin Jeffers at Ton House' (1927) by Edward Weston.
notes_text: Third instance of 'everything is a number': a whole image is a 2D array of numeric pixel values. Grayscale values (0=black up to 255=white) map to brightness; sets up the brightness/contrast math next.

images.description: Grayscale photo of a man's face, with a callout zooming into a small region and expanding it into a 4x4 grid of numeric pixel values (0, 64, 128, 192) labeled 'Individual Pixels', showing value-to-color mapping.

title: The Connection With Mathematics: Brightness & Contrast
summary: Shows that image editing operations like brightness and contrast are simple arithmetic applied to every pixel value.
main_text: Because images are numbers, editing is math applied to every pixel. Brightness: each pixel value is increased/decreased by a constant amount, Pnew = Pold + B; B > 0 makes it brighter, B < 0 makes it less bright. Contrast: each pixel value is multiplied by a constant, Pnew = C*Pold + k; C > 1 gives more contrast, 0 < C < 1 gives less contrast. The same operation is performed on all pixels.
notes_text: Ties the 'everything is a number' theme to concrete arithmetic: addition -> brightness, multiplication -> contrast. Introduces uniform per-pixel operations (a precursor to loops over arrays).

images.description: Input-vs-output pixel transfer graph plus a grid of the same face rendered as -Brightness, Original, +Brightness, +Contrast, and -Contrast, visualizing how adding or multiplying pixel values changes the image.

title: Section: Working With Numbers in C++
summary: Section divider introducing numeric types and integer division/modulus in C++.
main_text: WORKING WITH NUMBERS IN C++ - Integers and floating-point types; Division and modulus operations. (Section divider for the C++ numeric-types portion.)
notes_text: Transition into hands-on C++ mechanics: types, division semantics, modulus.

title: Data Types: int and double
summary: Introduces C/C++ data types that tell the hardware how to interpret stored bits, focusing on int and double.
main_text: How should the bits (1s and 0s) the computer stores be interpreted - as a letter, an integer (an 'int'), or a number with decimals ('floating point' or 'double')? C/C++ types tell the hardware how to interpret the bits and which circuits to use to process them. First two C++ data types: int - integers only, no decimals (e.g., 4750, -18, 1908734); double - very large numbers down to very small fractions (e.g., 6.02E23, 1.5, -0.000248). Doubles still have limited precision (at some point they round off, which can cause BIG issues).
notes_text: Types are interpretation metadata over raw bits. int = exact whole numbers; double = wide range with fractions but finite precision (rounding caveat matters for correctness).

title: Division: Integer vs. Floating-Point
summary: Explains that division behaves differently depending on operand types: integer division truncates, while double or mixed division yields decimals.
main_text: Computers perform division differently based on the input types. Integer Division: dividing two integer values gives an integer result, with any remainder/fraction dropped (truncated): 10 / 4 = 2, 52 / 10 = 5, 6 / 7 = 0. Floating-point (double) and mixed division: 10.0 / 4.0 = 2.5, 52.0 / 10 = 5.2, 6 / 7.0 = 0.8571. Note: if one operand is a double, the other is temporarily promoted (implicitly 'cast') so the result is computed as a double.
notes_text: Critical gotcha: int/int truncates toward zero (no rounding). A single double operand promotes the whole expression to double. Common source of bugs.

title: Modulus (%) Operator
summary: Introduces the modulus operator, which returns the remainder of integer division, with worked and blank practice examples.
main_text: Dividing two integers yields an integer quotient. The modulus operator (%) divides two integers but yields the REMAINDER. Examples: 7 / 3 = 2 but 7 % 3 = 1; 75 / 10 = 7 but 75 % 10 = 5; 27 / 4 = __ but 27 % 4 = __ (practice); 59 / 12 = __ but 59 % 12 = __ (practice).
notes_text: Pairs integer division (quotient) with modulus (remainder). The blanks are in-class practice; answers are revealed on the SOLUTIONS slide.

title: Section: Solutions
summary: Section divider preceding the worked solutions to the modulus practice problems.
main_text: SOLUTIONS. (Section divider introducing the answers to the preceding practice problems.)
notes_text: Transitional slide before revealing modulus practice answers.

title: Modulus (%) Operator: Solutions
summary: Provides the completed answers for the modulus practice problems, showing both quotient and remainder.
main_text: Dividing two integers yields an integer quotient; the modulus operator (%) yields the remainder. Completed examples: 7 / 3 = 2 but 7 % 3 = 1; 75 / 10 = 7 but 75 % 10 = 5; 27 / 4 = 6 but 27 % 4 = 3; 59 / 12 = 4 but 59 % 12 = 11.
notes_text: Answer key for the practice slide: 27/4=6 r3, 59/12=4 r11. Reinforces quotient (/) vs remainder (%) on the same operands.

title: CS102 Unit 0 - Digital Representation and C++ Data Types and Constants
summary: Title slide for the unit covering how data is represented digitally and the fundamental C++ data types and constants.
main_text: CS102 Unit 0 - Digital Representation and C++ Data Types and Constants. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. Opening title slide for the digital-representation unit.
notes_text: Sets the scope: binary/digital representation of numbers, computer organization, and C++ types/literals.

title: Section: Range of Numbers
summary: Section divider introducing how a fixed number of digits or bits limits the range of representable numbers.
main_text: RANGE OF NUMBERS. (Section divider introducing the finite range of numbers representable with a fixed number of digits/bits.)
notes_text: Transition into the finite-range and overflow discussion.

title: Finite Range of Numbers
summary: Uses a hotel room-number analogy to show that a fixed digit count limits how many values can be represented, introducing overflow.
main_text: Recall: EVERYTHING in a computer is a number. Scenario: a hotel has 3-digit room numbers. How many rooms can it have? What if it uses 4-digit room numbers? What is the range for n-digit room numbers? Key Idea: a FIXED number of digits (or bits, for a computer) LIMITS the range of numbers we can represent. What is 999 + 1? 1000, obviously... right? Well, if we limit ourselves to 3-digit numbers, the answer is 000! We call this OVERFLOW, and it is a common issue programmers must account for. So, the number of digits available determines the range of numbers that can be represented.
notes_text: Overflow occurs when a result exceeds the fixed digit/bit width and wraps around (999+1 -> 000 in 3 digits). The hotel-room analogy maps digit count to representable value count.

images.description: Photos of a 3-digit room number ('610') and a 4-digit room number ('1337') illustrating how digit count bounds the number of rooms.
A number line marked 0 and a circular odometer-style wheel marked 0, illustrating how a fixed-width counter wraps back to 0 on overflow.

title: Bits, Bytes, Words
summary: Defines bits, bytes, and words as fixed-size memory units and gives the 0 to 2^n - 1 range formula for n-bit numbers.
main_text: Computers store data as bits (binary digits) in units of memory with a fixed number of bits. A single bit can only represent 1 and 0. To represent more than 2 values, we need a combination/sequence of many bits. Computer hardware (memory) defines common, easily accessible units of a fixed size: a BYTE is a group of 8 bits; a WORD varies in size but is usually 32 bits (4 bytes). For n-bit numbers, the range of values we can represent is 0 to 2^n - 1. For 8 bits, the range is 0 to 255. For 32 bits, the range is 0 to 4,294,967,295. Example encodings: a bit = 1; a byte such as 01000001 corresponds to a C++ char; a 4-byte word corresponds to a C++ int.
notes_text: Core definitions: bit (1 binary digit), byte (8 bits, ~ C++ char), word (usually 32 bits/4 bytes, ~ C++ int). Memorize the range formula 0..2^n-1 (8-bit -> 255, 32-bit -> ~4.29 billion).

images.description: Visual progression of storage units: a single bit ('1'), a byte ('01000001', labeled C++ char), and a 32-bit word of four bytes (labeled C++ int).
Memory-device table with Address column (0,1,2,3,...) and 8-bit Data values, highlighting one row as 'a byte' and a group of four rows as 'a word', showing memory is broken into bytes.

title: Finite Range of Binary
summary: Enumerates the binary combinations for 1, 2, and 3 bits to show that n bits yield exactly 2^n distinct values.
main_text: Computers represent binary numbers using a fixed number of bits. Given a fixed number of bits n, what is the range of numbers we can make? If n=1 bit: 0 = 0, 1 = 1 (2^1 = 2 values). If n=2 bits: 00 = 0, 01 = 1, 10 = 2, 11 = 3 (2^2 = 4 values). If n=3 bits: 000 = 0, 001 = 1, 010 = 2, 011 = 3, 100 = 4, 101 = 5, 110 = 6, 111 = 7 (2^3 = 8 values). Given n bits, 2^n numbers can be made.
notes_text: Concrete enumeration proving the 2^n rule: each added bit doubles the number of representable values. Values run 0 to 2^n - 1.

images.description: Three columns of binary-to-decimal enumeration tables for n=1, n=2, and n=3 bits, listing every bit pattern and its decimal value (0-1, 0-3, 0-7), annotated with 2^1=2, 2^2=4, 2^3=8 values.

title: Interlude: Basic Computer Organization
summary: Section divider introducing basic computer organization: the processor and memory.
main_text: INTERLUDE - Basic Computer Organization: Processor and Memory. (Section divider transitioning from number representation to how a computer is organized around a processor and memory.)
notes_text: Bridges from 'data is bits' to where and how those bits are processed and stored.

title: Digging Deeper: Transistors and Bits
summary: Explains that bits exist because transistors act as on/off switches producing two voltage levels, which we label 1 and 0.
main_text: Why do we have 'bits' (that can only be 2 values) and how do we process and store them? Modern computer chips are made from BILLIONS of tiny TRANSISTORS built on a chip of silicon (usually). A transistor is an electronic device that acts like a switch; it can be ON or OFF. This leads to only 2 values (high or low voltage) in computer hardware. 1s and 0s are arbitrary symbols representing high or low voltage. A single 1 or 0 is known as a BIT. The bit coming out of one transistor can control one or more other transistors, creating complex processing chains that can perform functions like arithmetic.
notes_text: Physical origin of binary: transistor as a switch -> two voltage levels (e.g., +5V/+12V = 1, 0V/-12V = 0). Chained transistors implement logic and arithmetic.

images.description: Photo of an Intel Core i7 processor package next to a magnified silicon die, showing where the billions of transistors live.
Diagram of a transistor acting as a switch: an on/off light switch branching to High Voltage (+5V/+12V) mapped to 1 and Low Voltage (0V/-12V) mapped to 0.

title: Computer Components: Processor and Memory
summary: Categorizes hardware into processor, memory, and I/O, defining the processor's role and RAM as volatile storage of program and data.
main_text: Computer hardware circuits can be categorized into PROCESSOR, MEMORY, and I/O circuits. If data is just bits that the processor manipulates with transistors, where do we store them when they are not being used? Processor: executes the program and performs all the operations. Main Memory (aka RAM): stores both data and program (instructions), and loses data when power is disconnected (it is volatile). The recipe analogy: the processor is the cook that reads instructions and operates on data. System flow: Input Devices feed into Memory, which holds the Program (instructions) and Data (operands); the Processor exchanges data with Memory and results go to Output Devices; the OS loads the software program upon starting the app.
notes_text: Three hardware categories: processor (compute), memory/RAM (volatile storage of code+data), I/O. RAM losing data on power-off is a key property (volatility). Reuses the recipe metaphor from Unit 0a.

images.description: Illustration of a chef reading a recipe card ('Combine 2c. Flour, Mix in 3 eggs') beside flour and eggs, mapping the processor to a cook that reads instructions and operates on data.

Block diagram: Input Devices -> Memory (RAM) holding Program (Instructions) and Data (Operands), with the Processor above exchanging data, and Output Devices on the right; labeled OS and Software Program.

title: Memory: Cells and Addresses
summary: Describes memory as addressable cells (usually 1 byte each) and uses the mailbox/safe-deposit analogy, noting bits carry no type meta-information.
main_text: Memory also uses transistors, but in a different way that allows the transistors to help 'remember' bits. It is broken into 'cells' that each store a group of bits (usually 1 byte = 8 bits) and is accessed via a unique number (aka an ADDRESS). The address is used to reference the value at a given location. Analogy: safe-deposit boxes or mailboxes - each has an identifying number and a value stored inside. The value can be an instruction, a number, a character, etc. You, the programmer, must know what to expect and how to interpret it - NO meta-information is present to tell you how to interpret the bits.
notes_text: Key model: memory = array of byte-sized cells, each with a numeric address. Critical point: raw bits carry no type tag; interpretation is the programmer's responsibility (motivates data types).

images.description: Address/Memory table listing addresses 0-5 and 1023 with 8-bit binary values, with address 2's value (10010000) highlighted, showing address-to-value referencing.
Photos of a RAM memory stick and its silicon die with an arrow to a bank of safe-deposit boxes, reinforcing the mailbox/address analogy for memory.

title: Memory Operations: Read, Write, and Buses
summary: Explains the two memory operations (read and write) and the address, data, and control buses used to perform them.
main_text: Memories perform 2 operations. READ: retrieves the data value in a particular location (specified using the address). WRITE: changes the data in a location to a new value. To perform these operations, a set of ADDRESS, DATA, and CONTROL inputs/outputs are used. Note: a group of wires/signals is referred to as a 'bus'. Thus, we say that memories have an address bus, a data bus, and a control bus. Example read: put address 2 on the address bus with control = Read, and the data 10010000 comes out on the data bus. Example write: put address 5 and data 00000110 in with control = Write to store the new value at location 5.
notes_text: Two operations (read/write) coordinated over three buses: address (which cell), data (the value), control (read vs write). 'Bus' = a group of signal wires.

images.description: Read-operation diagram: a processor drives Addr=2 and Control=Read into an Address/Memory table, and the value 10010000 is returned on the data lines (row 2 highlighted).
Write-operation diagram: a processor drives Addr=5, Data=00000110, and Control=Write into the Address/Memory table, updating location 5 (row 5 highlighted).

title: One At a Time
summary: Connects earlier ideas: numbers live as bits in memory accessed one value at a time, framing the core programming challenge of sequencing.
main_text: Recall that while we see the image of a man, the computer 'sees' a collection of numbers (aka pixels). Now we can understand why: every number is stored as bits in memory, and memory can only be accessed ONE data value at a time. This limitation of accessing one value at a time leads to a fundamental issue of programming: How do we break abstract tasks into a sequence of '1 at a time' operations?
notes_text: Ties memory addressing back to the 'everything is a number' theme. The one-value-at-a-time constraint motivates loops and algorithmic decomposition later in the course.

images.description: Grayscale photo of a man's face with a callout to a 4x4 grid of pixel values (0, 64, 128, 192) and an adjacent memory table (addresses 7420-7435) storing those values one per cell, showing pixels laid out sequentially in memory.

title: Section: C++ Data Types and Constants
summary: Section divider introducing C++ data types and constants (literals).
main_text: C++ DATA TYPES AND CONSTANTS. (Section divider transitioning into how C++ interprets stored bits via data types and how to write literal constants.)
notes_text: Marks the shift from hardware/representation to language-level types and literals.

title: Motivation for Data Types: Ambiguous Bytes
summary: Poses the problem that a block of raw bytes has no inherent boundaries or meaning, motivating why data types are needed.
main_text: Information is stored in groups of bits (bytes and words). Given a block of memory such as the bytes '61 39 0a 00 00 37 12 80' and 'bf fc 00 00 00 00 00 00', how many data values are stored (where does one value stop and another start) and what are their values? You cannot tell from the bits alone. Memory contents here are shown using HEXADECIMAL, which is a shorthand for binary: the 1s and 0s are converted to the symbols 0-9 and a-f to make them easier for humans to read.
notes_text: Sets up the need for types: identical raw bytes are ambiguous without boundaries and interpretation. Also introduces hex as human-readable shorthand for binary (each hex digit = 4 bits).

images.description: A block of computer memory shown as two rows of eight hexadecimal bytes (61 39 0a 00 00 37 12 80 / bf fc 00 ...), with the question of where one value ends and the next begins.

title: Motivation for Data Types: Same Bits, Different Meaning
summary: Shows that C/C++ types define both how many bytes a value occupies and how to interpret those bytes, using char/int/double over the same memory.
main_text: Information is stored in groups of bits (bytes and words). C/C++ TYPES indicate how many bits (bytes) of STORAGE (memory) are required AND how to INTERPRET the number being stored. Over the same raw bytes: interpreting one byte (61) as a char yields 'a'; interpreting four bytes (00 37 12 80) as an int yields 4750; interpreting eight bytes (bf fc 00 ...) as a double yields -3.75. The same bits mean different things depending on the type applied.
notes_text: The two jobs of a type: (1) size in bytes, (2) interpretation rule. Same bits -> different values under char vs int vs double. Hex is shown as human-readable binary shorthand.

images.description: The same hexadecimal memory block with three magnifying glasses labeling a 1-byte char ('a'), a 4-byte int (4750), and an 8-byte double (-3.75), showing how type determines size and interpretation.

title: C/C++ Data Types Overview
summary: Surveys the main C/C++ type categories: integer, floating point, string/text, and boolean.
main_text: C/C++ types indicate how many bits (bytes) of storage are required and how to interpret the number being stored. Integer types: int, unsigned int (and, technically, char - explained later). Floating point types (for very large numbers like 6.02E23 and very small numbers like 6.626E-34, i.e. an attempt to represent rational/real numbers): float or double (in general, prefer double over float because it has a greater range of expressivity). String/Text types: char, char arrays, and strings. Boolean type: bool (true/false). Next we look at how to write constants (aka 'literals') and declare variables of these types.
notes_text: Category map before diving into literals. Note the guidance to prefer double over float, and that char is technically an integer type.

title: Constants (aka Literals)
summary: Shows how to write literal constants for integers, doubles, characters, C-strings, and booleans, including escape sequences and NULL termination.
main_text: Integer literals: 496, 10005, -234. Double literals: 12.0, -16., 0.23, 6.02E23, 4e-2 (both very large and very small numbers, i.e. fractions/decimals). Characters (char type) are enclosed in SINGLE quotes ('): printing characters like 'a', '5', 'B', '!'; each quoted value is converted to its ASCII number (e.g., 'a' => 97). Non-printing special characters use ESCAPE sequences (preceded by a backslash): '\n' (newline/enter), '\t' (tab), '\\' (backslash), '\'' (apostrophe). C-Strings (there is also a C++ string type): 0 or more characters between DOUBLE quotes ("), e.g., "hi1\n", "12345", "b", "\tAns. is %d". A C-string ends with a '\0' = 0 (aka the NULL character) added as the last byte/character so code can delimit the end of the string. Boolean (C++ only): false, true; physically 0 = false and any non-zero value (1, -5, 300) = true. Note: C/C++ handling of single characters and strings differs from most other languages and is a major source of confusion.
notes_text: Key literal rules: single quotes = one char (-> ASCII code), double quotes = C-string (NULL-terminated with '\0'). Escape sequences \n \t \\ \'. Boolean truthiness: 0 is false, non-zero is true.

images.description: Warning banner with C/C++, Java, and Python icons noting that C/C++ handling of single characters and strings differs from most other languages and is a major source of confusion.
C-String memory layout table showing characters 'h','i','1','\n'(newline),'\0'(null),'#','d' stored one per byte at addresses 7420-7426 with decimal codes 104,105,49,10,00,35,100.

title: Exercise: Storing a String in Memory
summary: Practice exercise: store the C-string "cs 102" in memory using decimal ASCII byte values and terminate it with the NULL character.
main_text: Show how "cs 102" would be stored in the memory table below. Use decimal to represent each byte. How do we indicate the string is done ('terminated')? With the special NULL character (i.e., 0 or '\0'). Use the ASCII chart (control characters and printable characters) to convert each character to its decimal code, and remember to append the NULL terminator as the final byte.
notes_text: Solution using the ASCII chart: 'c'=99, 's'=115, space=32, '1'=49, '0'=48, '2'=50, then the NULL terminator 0. So the bytes stored starting at address 7420 are: 99, 115, 32, 49, 48, 50, 0. The trailing 0 marks the end of the C-string.

images.description: An empty Address/Memory table with addresses 7420-7427 for the student to fill in the byte values of the stored string.
Full ASCII reference chart split into control characters (0-31, 127) and printable characters (32-126) with decimal codes and glyphs, used to look up each character's decimal value.

title: Signed and Unsigned Integer Types
summary: Explains how the 2^n bit patterns are assigned to values: unsigned uses all patterns for non-negative numbers, signed splits them between positive and negative.
main_text: If we have a finite range of numbers (2^n) that we can make with n bits, what values should they correspond to? C++ defines both 'unsigned' and 'signed' integer types. UNSIGNED integer types use all bit combinations for POSITIVE (natural) numbers, from 0 to 2^n - 1. SIGNED integer types split the combinations, with half being positive numbers and half being negative. C++ also defines other intermediate sizes (1-, 2-, 4-, 8-byte integer types) that have more range but use more memory. For 8 bits, unsigned covers 0 to 255 while signed covers -128 to +127; as the counter passes the top it wraps (e.g., unsigned 255 -> 0; signed +127 -> -128).
notes_text: Same bit patterns, two interpretations: unsigned (0..2^n-1) vs signed (split, e.g. -128..+127 for 8 bits). The number-wheel shows wraparound at the boundary.

images.description: Two number-wheel diagrams: an UNSIGNED wheel running 0,1,...,254,255 back to 0, and a SIGNED wheel running 0,1,...,127 then -128,-129,...,-1 back to 0, showing how combinations map to values.

title: C/C++ Integer Data Types
summary: Reference table of C/C++ integer types with their signed/unsigned names, sizes in bytes/bits, and value ranges.
main_text: Integer variable types come in unsigned (positive-only, including 0) and signed (positive or negative) forms. Reference table: char / unsigned char = 1 byte, 8 bits; signed range -128 to +127, unsigned range 0 to 255. short / unsigned short = 2 bytes, 16 bits; signed -32768 to +32767, unsigned 0 to 65535. int / unsigned int = 4 bytes, 32 bits; signed about -2 billion to +2 billion, unsigned 0 to 4 billion. long long / unsigned long long (aka size_t) = 8 bytes, 64 bits; signed about -8x10^18 to +8x10^18, unsigned 0 to 16x10^18. Note: char, int, and long long are the three integer types we will use 99% of the time.
notes_text: Memorize sizes: char=1B, short=2B, int=4B, long long=8B. Larger types = more range but more memory. size_t is unsigned long long. Focus on char/int/long long.

title: C/C++ Floating Point Types
summary: Reference table for float and double types, with sizes and ranges, plus guidance to prefer double and avoid unnecessary floating point.
main_text: The float and double types allow decimal representation (e.g., 6.125) as well as very large integers (e.g., +6.023E23). Reference table: float = 4 bytes, 32 bits, about +/-7 significant digits x 10^(+/-38). double = 8 bytes, 64 bits, about +/-16 significant digits x 10^(+/-308). Prefer double over float - many compilers will upgrade floats to doubles anyway. Don't use floating-point if you don't need to: it suffers from rounding error and adds some time overhead to perform arithmetic operations.
notes_text: float (4B, ~7 sig digits) vs double (8B, ~16 sig digits). Default to double. Floating point trades exactness for range: watch for rounding error and slower arithmetic.

title: Additional Resources
summary: Points students to an external video for further explanation of binary representation.
main_text: Additional Resources: Understanding binary representation - a YouTube video is linked on the slide for further study of how binary works.
notes_text: Optional enrichment; external video link on binary representation.

title: Unit 0c Title: Programming Languages and C++ Program Structure
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 0c, covering programming languages and the structure of a C++ program, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: CS102 Unit 0c - Programming Languages and C++ Program Structure. Instructor: Mark Redekopp.

title: EdStem Questions
summary: A transition slide indicating that EdStem questions will be used during this lecture for interactive checks of understanding.
main_text: EdStem Questions
notes_text: Likely used to prompt in-class polling or interactive questions hosted on the EdStem platform.

title: Unit Objectives
summary: Lists the learning objectives for Unit 0c, including defining algorithm, syntax, and semantics, and understanding basic C++ program parts.
main_text: Unit Objectives: Define algorithm, syntax, and semantics. Know that statements in a program execute sequentially by default. Know the basic parts of a C++ program, including inclusion of library "headers", comments, code partitioned into functions, and the main() function as the starting point of execution.
notes_text: This slide frames the entire unit: definitions of algorithm/syntax/semantics, sequential execution as a default behavior, and the anatomy of a C++ program (headers, comments, functions, main()).

title: Section Divider: Algorithms & Programming Languages
summary: Section header slide dividing the lecture into the first major topic: algorithms and programming languages.
main_text: ALGORITHMS & PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES
notes_text: Marks the start of the algorithms and programming languages portion of the unit.

title: Humans and Computers
summary: Contrasts how humans tolerate ambiguity and use context to interpret language, while computers require precise, unambiguous, and discrete instructions.
main_text: Humans and Computers. Humans understand instructions differently than computers. Humans easily tolerate ambiguity and abstract concepts using context to help, e.g. "Steph Curry shot the lights out" or "I'm cooked." Computers must be precise, only executing well-defined instructions with no ambiguity, and operate on digital information which is finite and discrete (a fixed number of options).
notes_text: Sets up motivation for why algorithms/programs must be precise: computers cannot interpret figurative or ambiguous language the way humans do.

title: Algorithms: Definition and Examples
summary: Defines algorithms informally and formally as an ordered, unambiguous, executable, and terminating set of steps, and gives everyday examples, alongside images distinguishing hardware from software.
main_text: Algorithms. Algorithms are at the heart of computing! Informal definition: An algorithm is a precise way to accomplish a task or solve a problem. A more formal definition: An ordered set of unambiguous, executable steps that defines a terminating process. Examples: What is the algorithm for brushing your teeth? Calculating your GPA?
notes_text: The right side of the slide shows a code snippet labeled "Software" and a photo of a laptop with a CPU chip labeled "Hardware", illustrating that algorithms/software run on top of physical hardware.

images.description: A code editor snippet showing example software source code (JavaScript-like function), illustrating what 'software' looks like as written instructions.
A photo of a laptop computer next to an Intel Core i7 processor chip, illustrating the concept of 'hardware' as the physical machine that runs software.

title: Algorithm Representation
summary: Explains that an algorithm is not itself a program or language, and can be represented multiple ways (flow chart, pseudocode, specific program) with algorithmic thinking as the core skill.
main_text: Algorithm Representation. An algorithm is NOT a program or programming language. Just as a story may be represented as a book, movie, or spoken by a story-teller, an algorithm may be represented in many ways: flow chart, pseudocode (English-like syntax using primitives that most programming languages would have), or a specific program implementation in a given programming language. The skill we REALLY want to help you build is algorithmic thinking (i.e. developing algorithms).
notes_text: Emphasizes that the course's real goal is developing algorithmic thinking, independent of any one representation or language.

title: Section Divider: Code Organization and Sequence of Execution
summary: Section header slide introducing the topic of how code is organized and executed in sequence, using Scratch as a teaching tool.
main_text: CODE ORGANIZATION AND SEQUENCE OF EXECUTION
notes_text: Marks transition into using the Scratch visual programming language to teach sequential execution.

title: Sequence & Executability: Introducing Scratch
summary: Introduces the Scratch programming language (scratch.mit.edu) as a tool to explore program execution, with an exercise to make a sprite walk forward, turn right, and walk forward again.
main_text: Sequence & Executability. Let's learn a bit more about program execution by using another language named Scratch (http://scratch.mit.edu). Write a Scratch program to walk forward, turn right, then walk forward again. Remember computers need executable steps: How far forward? Turn right by how much?
notes_text: Introduces Scratch's cat sprite as the running example used throughout the following slides to demonstrate sequential and repeated execution.

images.description: A screenshot of the empty Scratch programming environment showing the orange cat sprite on a blank stage, before any blocks have been added.

title: Executability: Scratch Blocks
summary: Explains that Scratch handles syntax via a menu of predefined 'blocks' with configurable parameters, and walks students through creating a program with move/turn blocks.
main_text: Executability. Scratch handles the syntax by providing a menu of specific "blocks" that define what the language allows you to do. Anything you want to do that doesn't have a specific block requires you to compose/use multiple blocks. Some blocks have certain aspects you can set to control their behavior. Go to the Scratch website, click on Create, and close the tutorial. Write a Scratch program to walk forward, turn right, then walk forward again. Remember computers and algorithms need executable steps: How far forward? Turn right by how much?
notes_text: Highlights that Scratch's block categories (Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables) are analogous to a programming language's built-in syntax/vocabulary.

images.description: A screenshot of the Scratch editor's Motion block palette, showing blocks like 'move 10 steps', 'turn 15 degrees', 'go to x/y', and 'glide', highlighted with a pink box around the category menu on the left.

title: Sequence & Executability: Building and Running a Scratch Program
summary: Guides students to compose a Scratch program from the block menu, run it by clicking the green flag, and observe what happens when the flag is clicked a second time.
main_text: Sequence & Executability. You must compose a program from the "menu" of available blocks. Create the program shown to the right and then click the green flag to the left of the red stop sign. What happens? Click the green flag again. What happens?
notes_text: The referenced program uses 'when green flag clicked', 'move 100 steps', 'turn 90 degrees', 'move 100 steps' -- designed to make students notice the sprite's position does not reset between runs unless explicitly told to.

images.description: Screenshot of the blank Scratch stage with the cat sprite, and below it a Scratch script: 'when green flag clicked', 'move 100 steps', 'turn 90 degrees', 'move 100 steps', demonstrating a simple sequential program.

title: Explicit Content: Computers Do Only What You Tell Them
summary: Explains that computers execute exactly what is specified, no more and no less, and introduces the need for explicit starting position/direction and delays between steps.
main_text: Explicit Content. Computers do only what you tell them, no more, no less. What additional details might we want to instruct the computer? Where to start and what direction to face? To provide some delay between steps -- remember computers execute code very quickly compared to what a human can see.
notes_text: Introduces the 'go to x/y', 'point in direction', and 'wait N seconds' blocks as ways to make execution explicit and observable.

images.description: A Scratch script showing 'when green flag clicked', 'go to x:0 y:0', 'point in direction 90', 'move 100 steps', 'wait 1 seconds', 'turn 90 degrees', 'wait 1 seconds', 'move 100 steps', 'wait 1 seconds', demonstrating explicit setup and paced execution.

title: Big Idea: Sequential Execution
summary: Key concept slide (marked with a star) stating that programs execute one operation at a time in a definite, ordered sequence.
main_text: Big Idea: Sequential Execution. Notice: Program is executed 1 operation at a time in sequential fashion. Each operation is ordered (a definite first, second, third, ... operation).
notes_text: Marked with a star icon indicating this is a core takeaway ('Big Idea') of the unit. The accompanying Scratch script has numbered green circles (1, 2, 3) and a downward arrow tracing execution order through the first blocks.

images.description: A Scratch script with the first three blocks numbered 1, 2, 3 and a green downward arrow along the right side, visually tracing the top-to-bottom sequential execution order of the program.

title: Repetition 1: Introducing Loops
summary: Introduces the concept of a loop for repeating a set of actions multiple times, posing the question of how to make the sprite walk in a square.
main_text: Repetition 1. Computers are good at repeating tasks quickly. If we can find repeated structure, we can use a loop to repeat a set of actions multiple times. What actions can we repeat and how many times to have our cat friend walk in a square?
notes_text: Introduces the Scratch 'repeat 10 <actions>' block as the mechanism for looping, previewing the 'walk in a square' exercise.

images.description: A Scratch script showing the setup blocks (numbered 1-3) followed by a 'repeat 10' loop block containing a placeholder '<actions>' slot, with a green curved arrow indicating the loop repeats back to the top.

title: Repetition 2: A Complete Loop Example
summary: Shows a completed Scratch loop that repeats move/wait/turn/wait actions 4 times, demonstrating a loop with concrete repeated actions inside it.
main_text: Repetition 2. Computers are good at repeating tasks quickly. If we can find repeated structure, we can use a loop to repeat a set of actions multiple times.
notes_text: The accompanying diagram fills in the loop body from Repetition 1 with 'move 100 steps', 'wait 1 seconds', 'turn 90 degrees', 'wait 1 seconds' repeated 4 times, which draws a square path.

images.description: A completed Scratch script with setup blocks (1,2,3) followed by a 'repeat 4' loop containing 'move 100 steps', 'wait 1 seconds', 'turn 90 degrees', 'wait 1 seconds', with arrows showing the sequential flow into and around the loop -- this program draws a square.

title: Section Divider: Grouping Code in Functions (aka Blocks)
summary: Section header introducing functions (called 'Blocks' in Scratch), noted as optional content covered only if time allows.
main_text: GROUPING CODE IN FUNCTIONS (AKA BLOCKS). Only if time allows!
notes_text: Signals to students/instructor that this section on functions may be skipped depending on pacing.

title: Organizing Code - Functions: Creating a Block
summary: Introduces functions as a way to name and reuse sequences of code/actions, notes different languages call these functions/methods/procedures/subroutines, and has students create a Scratch block named WalkForwardAndTurn.
main_text: Organizing Code - Functions. Another way to allow reuse and easy modification is to give a name to a sequence of code/actions. Wherever we use the name, the associated sequence of code/actions will be executed. Most programming languages call these functions, methods, procedures, subroutines, etc. Scratch calls them "Blocks". Create a block named: WalkForwardAndTurn.
notes_text: This is the first step of a multi-slide exercise refactoring the repeated square-drawing actions into a reusable custom block.

images.description: Screenshot of the Scratch 'My Blocks' category with a 'Make a Block' button, and the 'Make a Block' dialog where a user types a block name and can add numeric/text inputs, boolean inputs, or labels.
labels: Add an input number or text

title: Organizing Code - Functions: Using the Custom Block
summary: Shows how to move the repeated actions into the WalkForwardAndTurn block definition, then drag the new block from 'My Blocks' into the repeat loop, replacing the inline actions.
main_text: Organizing Code - Functions. We can take the actions in our loop and drag them to the definition of WalkForwardAndTurn. Then click on "My Blocks", find your new block and drag it into the repeat loop.
notes_text: Before/after comparison: the left script has the loop body defined inline, while the right script replaces the inline actions with a single call to the WalkForwardAndTurn block, whose definition appears separately below.

images.description: Side-by-side Scratch scripts: the left shows the original script with actions inline inside a 'repeat 4' loop and a separate 'define WalkForwardAndTurn' block below it; the right shows the refactored script where 'repeat 4' now simply calls the WalkForwardAndTurn block, illustrating how extracting a function simplifies the main script.

title: Sequence of Execution With Functions
summary: Poses whether code with loops and functions still executes purely top-down, then explains that loops cause execution to repeat earlier code and functions cause execution to jump to a separate definition and return.
main_text: Sequence of Execution With Functions. We said we execute sequentially, but with loops and functions is our code still executed sequentially (top-down)? No. Loops cause execution to go back and repeat code, and functions may cause us to jump to a new set of actions, execute them, and then return back and resume the main program.
notes_text: The diagram's numbered steps (1-7, with sub-steps 5a-5d and 7a-7d) trace execution jumping from the main script into the WalkForwardAndTurn function definition and back, across two loop iterations, illustrating non-linear control flow despite the underlying sequential execution model.

images.description: A Scratch script annotated with numbered execution steps (1 through 7, with expanded sub-steps 5a-5d and 7a-7d for each function call) showing how control jumps from the main repeat loop into the separately defined WalkForwardAndTurn block and back again on each iteration.

title: Functions & Parameters/Arguments: Motivation
summary: Motivates the need for input parameters by asking how to generalize WalkForwardAndTurn to walk different lengths (e.g., for a rectangle), and begins adding 'distance' and 'delay' inputs to the block.
main_text: Functions & Parameters/Arguments. Our function "DelayedMove" is useful for the simple task we gave you to implement, but what if I wanted to walk in a rectangle? We now need to walk different lengths. Q: What might make it more useful and "general" so that we could reuse it in the future more easily? A: The ability to generalize how many steps to take and how long to wait might be helpful -- we call these "input parameters". Let's allow different values of steps and the delay to be input. Right click on the WalkForwardAndTurn and choose Edit. Click on "Add an Input (number or Text)" once and give the newly appearing box the name: distance, and click on "Add an Input" again and give the new box the name: delay.
notes_text: Note the slide references the function as "DelayedMove" in prose while the running example is actually named WalkForwardAndTurn; the concept being taught is generalizing functions via parameters.

images.description: Screenshot of the Scratch 'Make a Block' editor showing the WalkForwardAndTurn block definition with two new input parameters added, labeled 'distance' and 'delay', plus buttons to add more inputs or labels.
labels: Add an input number or text

title: Parameters/Arguments: Using Distance and Delay
summary: Shows dragging the new 'distance' and 'delay' parameter blocks into the function body in place of hardcoded constants, then filling in 100 and 1 as arguments in the main program, and poses a rectangle-walking exercise.
main_text: Parameters/Arguments. Back in the main window, two new entries "distance" and "delay". Drag these in place of the constants (100 or 1) in the move / wait blocks. Back in the main program, fill in the two text boxes with 100 and 1. How could you modify the main program only to make the cat walk in a rectangle of 200 wide and 100 long?
notes_text: Illustrates the distinction between a function's formal parameters (distance, delay) and the concrete arguments (100, 1) supplied at the call site.

images.description: Two Scratch diagrams: the top shows the WalkForwardAndTurn function definition with 'distance' and 'delay' parameter blocks dragged into the move/wait/turn blocks, replacing hardcoded numbers; the bottom shows the main script calling WalkForwardAndTurn with concrete argument values 100 and 1 highlighted in a blue box.

title: Section Divider: First C++ Programs
summary: Section header slide transitioning from Scratch examples to actual C++ program structure and syntax.
main_text: FIRST C++ PROGRAMS
notes_text: Marks the shift from the visual/block-based Scratch examples to real C++ code.

title: C/C++ Program Format/Structure
summary: Details the core building blocks of a C++ program: comments, #include directives, the main() function as the entry point, and other user-defined functions, illustrated with an annotated code example and its output.
main_text: C/C++ Program Format/Structure. Comments: anywhere in the code; multiline C-style => /* and */; single line C++ style => //. Include Libraries and Compiler Directives: #include's tell the compiler what other library functions you plan on using; using namespace std; -- just do it for now! main() function: starting point of execution for the program; all code/statements in C must be inside a function; statements execute sequentially (one after the next) and end with a semicolon (;); main() ends with a return 0; statement. Other functions: printName() is a function that can be "called"/"invoked" from main or any other function.
notes_text: The example program includes <iostream> and <cmath>, defines a printName(string name) function, and a main() that calls printName() twice and computes sin(M_PI/4), producing the output: Hello, Tommy Trojan, Tommy Trojan, 0.7071 (note the annotated slide shows a minor discrepancy where the output lists 'Tommy Trojan' twice though the code calls printName with both 'Tommy Trojan' and 'Tina Trojan').

images.description: An annotated, color-coded C++ source code listing demonstrating comments, #include directives, a user-defined printName() function, and the main() function calling printName() twice and computing a sine value, alongside a terminal window showing the program's console output.

title: Syntax and Semantics (Introductory Diagram)
summary: Introduces syntax as the grammatical rules of a language and semantics as the meaning expressed by code, illustrated with an if-statement flowchart and an assignment statement diagram.
main_text: Syntax and Semantics. Syntax: refers to the rules of a language for how it will be expressed and parsed (decomposed), similar to English grammar. Semantics: The meaning expressed by the code.
notes_text: The diagram shows the general form 'if (<condition>) { <statement> } <next_code>' as a flowchart branching on True/False, and an assignment statement '<var> = <expression>;' annotated with the semantic meaning: copy the resulting value of <expression> into the variable <var>.

images.description: A flowchart illustrating the syntax of an if-statement: a diamond-shaped condition check branching to True (executing <statement>) or False (skipping to <next_code>), paired with a diagram of an assignment statement '<var> = <expression>;' annotated to explain its semantics: the expression's value is copied into the variable.
labels: Copy the resulting value of <expression> into the variable <var>

title: Software Process (Edit -> Build -> Run)
summary: Illustrates the three-step software development process -- Edit, Build (compile), and Run -- showing how a C++ source file becomes an executable binary and produces output.
main_text: Software Process (Edit -> Build -> Run). Edit (write code) produces C++ file(s) (prog1.cpp). Build (compile and fix syntax errors) uses the compiler (g++) together with the Std C++ & Other Libraries to produce an Executable Binary Program ("prog1"). Run (fix logic / runtime errors) loads and executes the binary on hardware (e.g., an Intel Core i7) via a terminal/command line, producing output. Note: Codio and other web-based tools combine Build and Run together in 1 step.
notes_text: The example source declares int x = 5; and prints "Hello" and "x=5", matching the shown terminal output. This models the iterative edit-build-run development cycle (looped arrows show returning to Edit after fixing errors).

images.description: A pipeline diagram showing a C++ source file (prog1.cpp) flowing into a 'Build' box labeled g++/Compiler (drawing from a 'Std C++ & Other Libraries' cylinder), producing a binary '1110 0010...' executable file, which then flows into a 'Run' box on a CPU, ending in a terminal window showing 'Hello / x=5'. Three numbered stages (1 Edit, 2 Build, 3 Run) are labeled beneath with looping arrows showing developers cycling back to Edit.

title: Try It: Printing 'Hello!' Five Times
summary: A hands-on exercise having students write, run, and intentionally break a C++ for-loop program that prints 'Hello!' five times, to practice recognizing syntax versus semantic errors.
main_text: Try it. Go to Codechef or EdStem Lessons. Enter this program to print "Hello!" five times. Introduce some syntax errors. Introduce a semantic error. Program: #include <iostream>; using namespace std; int main() { for(int i=0; i < 5; i++) { cout << "Hello!" << endl; } return 0; }. C++ syntax requires statements to end with a semicolon (;) and be grouped by curly braces { }; removing one would lead to a syntax error. A semantic error is when you tell the computer to do the wrong thing but it still meets correct syntax -- changing "i=0" to "i=1" causes the program to print only 4 times instead of the desired 5.
notes_text: Directly contrasts a syntax error (missing semicolon or brace, caught by the compiler) with a semantic error (i=1 instead of i=0, which compiles fine but produces the wrong number of iterations) using the same for-loop example.

title: Formatting/Spacing and C++
summary: Demonstrates that the C++ compiler ignores whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) by showing two functionally identical programs with very different formatting, and references the IOCCC obfuscated code contest.
main_text: Formatting/Spacing and C++. The C++ compiler does NOT care about spaces, tabs, and newlines. The following two programs both compile and run equivalently. There is even an annual contest to see who can write the most obfuscated but legal C program: https://www.ioccc.org/years.html and https://www.ioccc.org/2020/yang/prog.c
notes_text: Both code panels implement the same 'print Hello! five times' for-loop as the previous slide, one cleanly formatted and one deliberately compressed/obfuscated onto irregular lines, to visually prove whitespace-insensitivity.

summary: An earlier version of the Edit-Build-Run diagram, using slightly different terminology such as 'Load & Execute' and showing a hard drive and RAM/CPU instead of a single 'Run' box.
main_text: Software Process. Edit & write code produces C++ file(s) (test.cpp). Compile & fix syntax (compile-time) errors uses the compiler (g++), drawing on Std C++ & Other Libraries, to produce an Executable Binary Image ("test") stored on disk. Load & run the executable program looking for and fixing semantic (runtime) errors loads the binary into memory and executes it on the CPU, producing output.

title: Syntax and Semantics (Expanded Explanation)
summary: A more detailed, older explanation of syntax versus semantics in programming languages, using an English-sentence analogy and a C++ if-statement example.
main_text: Syntax and Semantics. Programming languages have syntax and semantics. Syntax: refers to the rules of a language for how it will be expressed and parsed (decomposed); specific to the language; example: C++ statements should end with a semicolon (;). Semantics: refers to the meaning of what is written; often transcends the language (same concept in many languages). Example: A sentence -- the syntax refers to the proper grammatical rules for writing a sentence (capitalize the first word, have a subject and verb, end with a period, etc.); the semantics refer to the meaning conveyed by the sentence. C++ Code Example: 'if (<condition>) { <action> }' is the syntax; the semantics (meaning) is "the action will only be performed if condition is true".
notes_text: This older version expands on slide 24's brief definitions with the English-sentence analogy and an explicit statement of the if-statement's semantic meaning in prose rather than a diagram.

title: Unit 1a Title: Basic Output and Input (cout and cin)
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 1a, which covers basic C++ output and input using 'cout' and 'cin'.
main_text: Unit 1a - Basic Output and Input (with 'cout' and 'cin'). Instructor: Mark Redekopp.

title: Unit Objectives
summary: Lists the learning objectives for Unit 1a: C++ data types and constants, operators and precedence, cout/cin usage, whitespace handling in cin, and variable declaration/assignment.
main_text: Unit Objectives: List the various C++ data types. Identify what type a constant is. Know how to write constants in the appropriate C++ syntax. Know the C++ operators and their order of operations. Write basic output statements of text and constants using cout. Use cin statement to get keyboard input from the user. Predict how cin will treat input with whitespaces and extract data. Know how variables are declared and assigned. Trace the operation of assignment statements, expressions, and cin and cout commands.
notes_text: Frames the whole unit around data types/constants, operators/precedence, cout for output, and cin for input including whitespace handling and variable declaration.

title: Unit 1 Scalar Processing: Course Roadmap
summary: Positions Unit 1 (scalar/IPO processing) within the broader course roadmap, previewing later units on linear, multidimensional, and divide-and-conquer processing.
main_text: Unit 1 Scalar Processing. Unit 1: Scalar processing, aka IPO=Input-Process-Output Programs. Unit 2: Linear (1D) Processing. Unit 3: Multidimensional Processing. Unit 4: Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition).
notes_text: Unit 1 (highlighted, current unit) is grayed-out-contrasted against future units 2-4, each illustrated with an icon showing increasing data complexity (scalar values, 1D arrays, 2D grids, and function composition) flowing through a CPU chip.
