title: String or Array? Yes!
summary: Introduces the concept that a string is fundamentally an array of characters terminated by a null character.
main_text: String or Array? Yes! Now that we know about arrays, you might realize that a string looks CONSPICUOUSLY like an array of characters! A string constant is an array of chars that ends with a null char. The string "CS 102" is equivalent to a character array with indices [0] through [6] containing: 'C', 'S', ' ', '1', '0', '2', '\0'. The null character '\0' marks the end of the string.
notes_text: This is the key insight that connects prior array knowledge to string representation. The null terminator is critical for C-style strings.

images.description: Diagram showing the string "CS 102" mapped to a character array with index positions [0] through [6], where each cell contains one character: 'C', 'S', ' ', '1', '0', '2', '\0'. A double arrow connects the string literal to the array representation.

title: Initializing Character Arrays
summary: Shows how to initialize character arrays using comma-separated character lists or string literals, and explains that the compiler can infer array size from initialization.
main_text: Initializing Character Arrays. We can store a string in an array of chars. We can either use a comma separate list of chars or just a string in double quotes ("). If an initialization list is provided you need not specify the size in the square brackets (i.e. just use empty []) as the compiler can figure out what size the array must be by counting the initial values. Code examples: int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; double dec[4] = {0.25, 0.3}; (remaining elements initialized to 0). char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'}; For char arrays easier to use "". char str2[3] = "CS"; str2 initialization is same as str1. char str3[] = "CS"; allocates array of size 3. char str4[] = "How long is this string?!"; allocates array of size 26. Specifying sizes is not necessary when using initial values list.
notes_text: Note that the dec array shows partial initialization where unspecified elements default to 0. The str1 and str2 examples show two equivalent ways to initialize character arrays.

images.description: Two memory diagrams showing array contents: the data array with values 9,7,8,9,5 at indices [0]-[4], and the dec array with values 0.25, 0.3, 0, 0 at indices [0]-[3]. Also a small diagram showing str1 as an empty array.

title: Character Arrays and Strings (1)
summary: Explains how C/C++ string constants are character arrays ending with a null character, introduces the term C-String, and demonstrates printing and modifying character arrays.
main_text: Character Arrays and Strings (1). In C/C++, string constants (the text in between " ") are just character arrays. Each character consumes 1 element in the array. Ends with the null character (e.g. 0 decimal or '\0' ASCII). This approach of using an array of char's to store a string is referred to as a C-String because there was no string type in C (i.e. before C++). Code example: #include <string>. using namespace std; int main() { char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'}; char str2[7] = "CS 102"; cout << str1 << endl; // prints "CS". cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 102". str2[5] = '3'; cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 103". return 0; } Program Output: CS, CS 102, CS 103, hello. Memory diagram shows str2 at addresses 520-526 with indices [0]-[6] containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.
notes_text: The term C-String is important to distinguish from the C++ string type introduced later. Individual characters can be modified using array indexing.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str2 stored in computer memory at addresses 520-526, with indices [0]-[6], containing characters 'C', 'S', ' ', '1', '0', '2', '\0'.

title: Strings Before C++
summary: Contrasts how strings were handled in C (character arrays only) versus C++ which introduced the string type to solve character array issues.
main_text: Strings Before C++. Before there was C++, there was C! In C, the string type did NOT exist! Only character arrays. C++ introduced the string type to solve many of the issues that character arrays have. (Detailed in the next slides). C example: char s1[6]="CS102" with a 'no' symbol next to the word 'string' indicating no string type available. C++ example: char s1[6]="CS102" and also string s = "CS102" showing both options are available.
notes_text: This slide sets up the motivation for why C++ strings were created. The limitations of C-strings will be explored in the following slides.

images.description: Visual comparison showing the C language logo with only char array syntax available (with a prohibition symbol on the word 'string'), and the C++ logo showing both char array and string type syntax available.

title: Where Does It End?
summary: Uses an analogy of fans in a crowd to motivate the concept of string boundaries and the need for a termination marker.
main_text: Where Does It End? In this picture, look at a row of fans. Where does one friend group end and another group of friends start? The slide shows a photograph of USC football fans in a stadium crowd, wearing cardinal and gold colors, with letters spelling 'FIGHT ON USC' painted on their chests. The analogy illustrates the difficulty of determining boundaries without explicit markers, motivating why strings need a null terminator.
notes_text: This is a motivational slide using an analogy. Just as you cannot tell where one group of friends ends in a crowd without a marker, the computer needs the null character to know where a string ends in memory.

images.description: Photograph of USC football fans in a stadium, wearing cardinal and gold, with letters painted on their chests spelling 'FIGHT ON USC'. Used as an analogy for why strings need explicit end markers.

title: Character Arrays and Loops
summary: Demonstrates how to iterate through character arrays using loops, and explains that cout and cin have built-in loops for handling character arrays.
main_text: Character Arrays and Loops. How many things can a computer do at a time? To printout a string/character array, we'd have to print one character at a time! But C/C++ treats character arrays specially. cout has a loop inside its code to print strings/character arrays. How does it know when to stop? The null char! Though not shown, cin also has a loop inside to input a string. We say cout and cin have a special relationship with character arrays. Code example: char str1[7] = "CS 102"; for(int i=0; str1[i] != '\0'; i++) { cout << str1[i]; } cout << endl; // but cout has its own loop so you don't have to write the loop above but just what you see below. cout << str1 << endl; // prints "CS 102". Program Output: CS 102, CS 102. Memory diagram shows str1 at addresses 520-526 with contents 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.
notes_text: The loop condition str1[i] != '\0' is key to understanding how C-strings are processed. The null terminator serves as the loop's stopping condition.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str1 stored at addresses 520-526, indices [0]-[6], containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0' in computer memory.

title: cout's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Explains that cout automatically loops through character arrays to print them, unlike other array types which require manual loops.
main_text: cout's Special Relationship with Character Arrays. To print out all elements of any array type OTHER than a character array (i.e. int, double, bool, etc.) you must write your OWN loop (i.e. because computers can only do 1 thing at a time). But for character arrays, you can just give cout the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to print out all characters for you. So, internally it is actually looping over the characters so you don't have to. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to print out all the characters in the array. Thus, we say cout treats character arrays specially. Code example: int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; char str1[] = "Many chars"; for(int i=0; i < 5; i++){ cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; // doesn't work for an int, double or any other type of array. cout << data << endl; // cout treats char. arrays specially. cout << str1 << endl; Program Output: 9 7 8 9 5, 0x7fffce40, Many chars.
notes_text: Note that printing an int array name directly outputs its memory address (0x7fffce40), not its contents. This contrasts with character arrays where the name prints the string contents.

images.description: Two memory diagrams: one showing data array with values 9,7,9,9,5 at indices [0]-[4], and one showing str1 array with 'M','a',...,'s','\0' at indices [0]-[10].

title: cin's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Explains that cin automatically reads an entire string into a character array, stopping at the next space, unlike other array types which require element-by-element input.
main_text: cin's Special Relationship with Character Arrays. To get input for all elements of an array type OTHER than character arrays (i.e. int, double, etc.) you must write your OWN loop. But for character arrays, you can just give cin the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to receive all characters the user types and store them sequentially in the array. So, internally it is actually looping over the characters so you don't have to. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to get a full string (stopping at the next space). cin treats character arrays specially. Code example: int data[5]; char str1[8]; int sum = 0; cin >> data; // won't even compile. // right way to get int array contents: for(int i=0; i<5; i++){ cin >> data[i]; } cin >> str1; Memory diagrams show str1 before input with garbage values ('?') and sum=0, then after user types 'CS102', str1 contains 'C','S','1','0','2','\0' with remaining positions as garbage.
notes_text: cin stops reading at whitespace. This is an important limitation - it cannot read strings with spaces using the >> operator.

images.description: Two memory state diagrams showing str1 before and after cin input. Before: all positions contain '?' (garbage) with sum=0. After user types 'CS102': positions [0]-[4] contain 'C','S','1','0','2', position [5] has '\0', remaining positions still garbage.

title: A Problem with cin and Character Arrays
summary: Demonstrates the buffer overflow danger when cin reads more characters than a character array can hold, and introduces C++ strings as the solution.
main_text: A Problem with cin and Character Arrays. What if the user types in TOO much (more characters than our array has room to store)? cin will not stop! It will keep storing the characters the user types, overwriting whatever data and variables came after the array. Warning: cin does not CHECK that the string typed by the user will fit in the array; instead it simply overwrites memory leading to undefined (bad) behavior! C++ strings fix this issue, allocating more space based on what is typed. Code example: int main() { char str1[4]; int sum = 0; cin >> str1; cout << sum << endl; // won't see 0 because sum was modified when cin received the string that was too long! string s2; cin >> s2; // works regardless of user input length. } Memory diagrams show str1 with 4 slots and sum, then after user types 'CS102', str1 overflows into sum's memory: 'C','S','1','0','2','\0'...
notes_text: This is a critical security and correctness issue known as buffer overflow. C++ strings dynamically resize to avoid this problem.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing buffer overflow: str1 has only 4 bytes at addresses 520-523, with sum at address 524. When user types 'CS102' (5 chars + null), the string overflows past str1 into sum's memory location, corrupting the sum variable.

title: What About Other Operations
summary: Shows that comparing character arrays with == does not work, requiring manual element-by-element loops, and motivates the introduction of the C++ string type.
main_text: What About Other Operations. How would you check whether two strings (character arrays) are equal (i.e. have the same character sequence)? Since we can only do 1 thing at a time, we'd have to use a loop. Does '==' have a special relationship with character arrays? NO!!! Most operations on strings require a loop since we can only do 1 thing at a time. cin and cout are exceptions. Every other operation requires the programmer to write a loop! So, when C++ came along they said, let's fix this. Let's provide code to deal with strings. Enter the C++ string type. Code example: char str1[7] = "CS 102"; char str2[7] = "CS 103"; if(str1 == str2) { ... } // Doesn't work. // Instead you'd need some kind of loop: bool same = true; for(int i=0; /* some condition */; i++) { if(str1[i] != str2[i]) { same = false; } } Memory shows str1 and str2 side by side at addresses 520-526, both containing similar characters but differing at index [5]: '2' vs '3'.
notes_text: The == operator on character arrays compares memory addresses, not string contents. This is a common source of bugs for beginners.

images.description: Memory diagram showing two character arrays str1 and str2 stored in computer memory at addresses 520-526, each containing 'C','S',' ','1','0' but differing at index [5]: str1 has '2' and str2 has '3', both ending with '\0'.

title: C-Strings != C++ strings
summary: Comparison table contrasting C-Strings (character arrays) with C++ strings across constants, variables, includes, I/O, and available operations.
main_text: C-Strings != C++ strings. Comparison table: As constants (same): C-String uses "hi", C++ String uses "hi". As variables (different): C-String uses char str1[3] = "hi"; char str2[4] = "bye";. C++ String uses string str1 = "hi"; string str2 = "bye";. To use: C-String requires No special #include. C++ String requires #include <string>. Works with cout: C-String Yes!, C++ String Yes!. Works with cin: C-String Yes, but potentially dangerous. C++ String Yes!. Other ops: C-String None. C++ String supports Reassignment, Comparison (==, <, >, etc.), Substrings. Why are strings messy? Because they are variable length, where as other variable types are a fixed size! Any int can fit in the memory of another int variable. But for strings what if we want to store a new, longer string in the memory of a shorter string? We don't have room?
notes_text: This is a key reference slide. The fundamental issue is that strings are variable-length data, unlike fixed-size types like int or double.

title: Character Arrays and Strings (2)
summary: Demonstrates that C++ strings can do everything character arrays can do, with code showing both types used side by side for output, modification, and input.
main_text: Character Arrays and Strings (2). C++ strings can do everything that character arrays can do. Code example: int main() { char str2[7] = "CS 102"; string str3 = "CS 102"; cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 102". cout << str3 << endl; // prints "CS 102". str2[5] = '3'; str3[5] = '3'; cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 103". cout << str3 << endl; // prints "CS 103". cin >> str2; // get a new string from the user (suppose user types "hello"). cin >> str3; cout << str2; cout << str3; return 0; } Program Output: CS 102, CS 102, CS 103, CS 103, hello, hello. Memory diagram shows str2 at addresses 520-526 containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.
notes_text: This slide proves that switching from char arrays to C++ strings requires minimal code changes while gaining significant benefits.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str2 character array at addresses 520-526, indices [0]-[6], containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.

metadata.topic: C++ string compatibility with char arrays

title: C++ Strings
summary: Introduces the C++ string type with its do's and don'ts, including #include <string>, no size declaration needed, array-style indexing, and safe cin input.
main_text: C++ Strings. In C++, the library adds a new object type named string (C++) and provides an easier alternative to working with plain-old character arrays (C-language). Do's and Don'ts: Do #include <string>. Don't need to declare the size (i.e. [7]), just assign. Do still use it like an array by using [index] to get individual characters. Do still use cin/cout with strings. Don't worry about how many characters the user types when inputting to a C++ string. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { char str1[7] = "CS 102"; string str2 = "CS 102"; str1[5] = '3'; // now str1 = "CS 103". str2[5] = '4'; // now str2 = "CS 104". cout << str1 << endl; // prints "CS 103". cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 104". cin >> str1; // If the user types more than 6 chars..uh oh! cin >> str2; // str2 will adjust to hold whatever the user types. }
notes_text: The key advantage is that C++ strings handle memory management automatically, eliminating buffer overflow risks present with character arrays.

title: What Do Strings Do
summary: Explains that C++ strings abstract character arrays behind the scenes and demonstrates string concatenation using the + operator.
main_text: What Do Strings Do. strings simply abstract character arrays. Behind the scenes strings are just creating and manipulating character arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Can concatenate (append) to a string with the + operator. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { string str2 = "CS 102"; // str2 stores 6 chars. = "CS 102". str2 = "Computer Science"; // now str2 stores 16 characters. // Can append using '+' or '+=' operator. str2 = str2 + " is cool"; // now str2 stores 24 characters. } The diagram shows str2 as an object containing a pointer (value 24 for size) that points to successive plain-old character arrays: first "CS 102", then "Computer Science", then "Computer Science is cool". Each time the string is reassigned or appended, a new character array is allocated.
notes_text: The + operator for strings is an example of operator overloading in C++. The string object manages memory allocation and deallocation automatically.

images.description: Diagram showing how the str2 string object works internally. The str2 box contains a pointer (showing value 24) that points to successive character arrays. Three states shown: 'CS 102' (crossed out), 'Computer Science' (crossed out), and 'Computer Science is cool' (current). Each is labeled as 'Plain-old character array'.

title: String Size
summary: Introduces the .size() member function for C++ strings, which returns the number of real characters excluding the null terminator.
main_text: String Size. Strings track how many characters they are storing. Call the <stringname>.size() function to get the string's size. Returns the actual number of real characters (and does not count overhead like the null character). Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { string str2 = "CS 102"; cout << str2.size() << endl; // 6. str2 = "Computer Science"; cout << str2.size() << endl; // 16. str2 = str2 + " is cool"; cout << str2.size() << endl; // 24. }
notes_text: The .size() function is essential for loops that process strings character by character. It returns the count of visible characters, not including the internal null terminator.

title: String Comparison
summary: Explains that comparison operators do not work with C-Strings but do work with C++ strings, performing lexicographic (dictionary-order) comparison.
main_text: String Comparison. Comparison operators do not work with plain old character arrays (C-Strings). C++ strings do perform lexicographic (alphabetical/dictionary-order) comparison when comparison operators (<, >, ==, etc.) are applied. Examples: "a" < "z" ? T/F. "a" > "aa" ? T/F. "ab" < "ba" ? T/F. "aab" < "aac" ? T/F. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { char str1[4] = "abc"; string str2 = "abc"; if( str1 == "abc" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 == "abc" ) // works..true {...} if( str1 < "aac" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 < "aac" ) // works..false {...} string str3 = "acb"; if( str3 > str2 ) // works..true {...} }
notes_text: Lexicographic comparison compares character by character using ASCII values. This slide presents quiz-style T/F questions without revealing answers, saving those for the solutions section.

title: Substrings
summary: Introduces the .substr() function for extracting portions of C++ strings, with two overloaded versions: one-argument and two-argument forms.
main_text: Substrings. C++ strings allow you to produce a new string from a substring of a current string. Call either of the 2 versions: .substr(start_index) or .substr(start_index, length) function on the string. 1st version generates substring from starting index location all the way to the end of the string. 2nd version generates substring from the starting index and includes the next 'length' characters. Note: when a function has the same name but different options for parameters we say the function is overloaded. Returns a new string. Even if length is 1 (i.e. if length is 1 you might think you just get a char, but you still get a string). Code example: int main() { string str1 = "CS102"; string str2 = str1.substr(2); // str2 = "102". str1 = "Hello World"; str2 = str1.substr(6,2); // str2 = "Wo". str2 = str1.substr(0,1); // str2 = "H". }
notes_text: The substr function is one of the most commonly used string operations. Note that the second parameter is length, not an end index.

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the solutions section for the string comparison exercises.
main_text: SOLUTIONS.
notes_text: This is a divider slide separating the lecture content from the answers to the T/F exercises on slide 18.

title: String Comparison Solutions
summary: Provides the answers to the lexicographic string comparison exercises: reveals that all four comparisons evaluate to TRUE or FALSE.
main_text: String Comparison (Solutions). Comparison operators do not work with plain old character arrays (C-Strings). C++ strings do perform lexicographic (alphabetical/dictionary-order) comparison when comparison operators (<, >, ==, etc.) are applied. Answers: "a" < "z" ? TRUE. "a" > "aa" ? FALSE. "ab" < "ba" ? TRUE. "aab" < "aac" ? TRUE. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { char str1[4] = "abc"; string str2 = "abc"; if( str1 == "abc" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 == "abc" ) // works..true {...} if( str1 < "aac" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 < "aac" ) // works..false {...} string str3 = "acb"; if( str3 > str2 ) // works..true {...} }
notes_text: Explanations: "a" < "z" is TRUE because 'a' has a lower ASCII value than 'z'. "a" > "aa" is FALSE because "a" is a prefix of "aa" and shorter strings come first. "ab" < "ba" is TRUE because 'a' < 'b' at index 0. "aab" < "aac" is TRUE because at index 2, 'b' < 'c'.

title: Unit 3a - Nested Loops Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 3a on Nested Loops for CS 102, authored by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 3a - Nested Loops. Mark Redekopp.

title: Unit 3 Overview
summary: Overview of the four units in the course, positioning Unit 3 as covering multidimensional processing with nested loops.
main_text: Unit 3. Unit 1: Scalar processing, aka IPO=Input-Process-Output Programs. Unit 2: Linear (1D) Processing. Unit 3: Multidimensional Processing. Unit 4: Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition). Unit 1 covers scalar input-process-output programs. Unit 2 covers linear or one-dimensional processing using simple loops. Unit 3 introduces multidimensional processing using nested loops. Unit 4 covers functional decomposition and divide-and-conquer approaches.
notes_text: This slide contextualizes where nested loops fit in the course progression, building from scalar to linear to multidimensional processing.

images.description: Diagram showing Unit 1 scalar processing: a single input flows through a CPU processor to a single output, enclosed in curly braces.
Diagram showing Unit 2 linear processing: a row of multiple inputs flows through a CPU processor to a row of multiple outputs, enclosed in curly braces.
Diagram showing Unit 3 multidimensional processing: a 2D grid of inputs flows through a CPU processor to a 2D grid of outputs, enclosed in brackets.
Diagram showing Unit 4 functional decomposition: two function boxes labeled f(x) and g(y) connected in sequence.

title: Multidimensional Processing
summary: Introduces the concept of multidimensional processing using nested loops, with two example programs: factoring numbers and drawing rectangles.
main_text: Multidimensional Processing. Most non-trivial programs require "multidimensional" processing. The distinguishing feature is the use of NESTED loops. Each nested loop represents one dimension. A representative example might be an outer loop to get multiple inputs and an inner loop to process each input. We will likely still keep our general structure but repeat a subset in each nested loop: Prompt, Input, Process, Output. Two example programs are shown. First example: 'Enter numbers to factor (end with -1)'. User enters 9, program outputs 1 3 9. User enters 12, program outputs 1 2 3 4 6 12. User enters -1 to end. Second example: 'Enter rectangle's height & width'. User enters 3 5, program outputs three rows of five asterisks (*****) each. The numbered step indicators show the flow through prompt, input, inner loop processing, and output stages for each example.
notes_text: The numbered step indicators (1-4) on each example show the PIPO pattern: 1=Prompt, 2=Input, 3=Process (inner loop), 4=Output/next iteration.

images.description: Diagram showing multidimensional processing: a 2D grid of inputs flowing through a CPU to a 2D grid of outputs, illustrating how nested loops handle multi-dimensional data.

Two terminal/console output examples showing nested loop programs. The first shows a factoring program that repeatedly reads numbers and prints their factors. The second shows a rectangle-drawing program that prints rows of asterisks. Numbered step indicators (1-4) mark the prompt, input, processing, and output phases.

title: Loops Inside Loops
summary: Explains that any code can be placed inside a loop body, including another loop, with flowchart illustrations for both while and for loop structures.
main_text: Loops Inside Loops. What kind of code can we put in the body of a loop? ANYTHING...even other loops. While loop syntax: while (condition) { // What can go here? }. For loop syntax: for(init; condition; update) { // What can go here? }. The answer is: What code can we put in the body of a loop? Another loop! The while loop flowchart shows: check condition, if True execute while block statements then loop back to condition, if False proceed to following statements. The for loop flowchart shows: init, check condition, if True execute for block statements then update then loop back to condition, if False proceed to following statements.
notes_text: This slide establishes the fundamental concept that loop bodies can contain any valid code, including other loops, which is the basis for nested loops.

images.description: Flowchart for a while loop showing a diamond-shaped condition node with True path leading to 'while Block Statements' box that loops back, and False path leading to 'Following statements'. A text box in the middle asks 'What code can we put in the body of a loop? Another loop!'
labels: What code can we put in the body of a loop?

images.description: Flowchart for a for loop showing init box, diamond-shaped condition node, True path to 'For Block Statements' then 'Update' looping back to condition, and False path to 'Following' statements.

title: Nested Loop Sequencing
summary: Explains the key idea that the inner loop runs completely for each iteration of the outer loop, with a code trace and flowchart showing execution order.
main_text: Nested Loop Sequencing. Key Idea: The inner loop runs in its entirety for each iteration of the outer loop. Code example: while (cond1) { // code1; while(cond2) { // code 2; } // code3; }. The execution sequence is traced with numbered steps 1 through 16. Cond1 is evaluated as T, T, F across iterations. Cond2 is evaluated as T, T, F during the first outer iteration and T, F during the second. The numbered execution order shows: 1(cond1=T), 2(code1), 3(cond2=T), 4(code2), 5(cond2=T), 6(code2), 7(cond2=F), 8(code3), 9(cond1=T), 10(code1), 11(cond2=T), 12(code2), 13(cond2=F), 14(code3), 15(cond1=F), 16(exit). The flowchart shows cond1 decision leading to code1, then cond2 inner loop with code2, then code3, looping back to cond1.
notes_text: The numbered step trace is critical for understanding nested loop execution order. Notice how the inner loop resets and runs completely each time the outer loop iterates.

images.description: Flowchart showing nested while loop execution: cond1 diamond leads to code1 box, then cond2 diamond with True path to code2 (inner loop) and False path to code3, which loops back to cond1. False from cond1 leads to Following statements.

title: Nested Loops Example 1
summary: Presents a C++ nested for loop example that prints pairs of i and j values, emphasizing that the inner loop completes fully before the outer loop advances.
main_text: Nested Loops Example 1. Key idea: Perform all iterations of the inner loop before starting the next iteration of the outer loop. Said another way: The inner loop executes completely for each single iteration of the outer loop. Code: int main() { for(int i=0; i < 2; i++){ for(int j=0; j < 3; j++){ cout << i << " " << j << endl; } } }. Trace through the execution of this code and show what will be printed. Exercise: rectangle. A trace table shows columns for i and j values.
notes_text: The solution to this trace is shown on slide 14. Students should work through this exercise before looking at the answer.

title: Visualizing Nested Loops
summary: Shows how nested loops map to multidimensional data structures, with 2 loops for 2D grids (rows/columns) and 3 loops for 3D structures (rows/columns/planes).
main_text: Visualizing Nested Loops. Nested loops often help us represent and process multi-dimensional data. 2 loops allow us to process data that corresponds to 2 dimensions (i.e. rows/columns). 3 loops allow us to process data that corresponds to 3 dimensions (i.e. rows/columns/planes). A 5x5 grid is shown with row indices 0-4 and column indices 0-4. The cell at position (2,3) is highlighted and labeled '2,3' to show how two loop variables (row, column) address a specific cell.
notes_text: This visualization helps students understand why nested loops are needed: each loop variable controls one dimension of the data.

images.description: A 5x5 grid table with row indices 0-4 on the left and column indices 0-4 on top. The cell at row 2, column 3 is highlighted and labeled '2,3', demonstrating how two nested loop indices address a specific position in a 2D structure.
A 3D cube made of smaller unit cubes, representing a three-dimensional data structure that would require three nested loops to process (rows, columns, and planes/depth).

title: Nested Loops Example 2 - Guessing Game
summary: Demonstrates a nested loop guessing game where the outer loop represents one game and the inner loop represents individual turns within each game.
main_text: Nested Loops Example 2. When you write loops consider what the body of each loop means in an abstract sense. The body of the outer loop represents 1 game (and we repeat that over and over). The body of the inner loop represents 1 turn (and we repeat turn after turn). Code: int main() { int secret, guess; char again = 'y'; // outer loop while(again == 'y') { // Choose secret num. 0-19 secret = rand() % 20; guess = -1; // inner loop while(guess != secret) { cout << "Enter guess: "; cin >> guess; } cout << "Win!" << endl; cout << "Play again (y/n): "; cin >> again; } return 0; }. Brackets on the right side of the code annotate '1 game' spanning the outer loop body and '1 turn' spanning the inner loop body.
notes_text: This example illustrates how to think about nested loops at an abstract level: each loop level has a meaningful semantic role (game vs. turn).

title: Sequential vs. Nested Loops
summary: Contrasts sequential loops (running one after another) with nested loops (inner loop runs fully per outer iteration), with code and partially blank output for the nested case.
main_text: Sequential vs. Nested Loops. Sequential loops are run one after the other. Each loop runs to completion before the next starts. Nested loops runs the inner loop to completion for each iteration of the outer loop. Code: int main() { // Sequential Loops for(int i=0; i < 4; i++){ cout << i << " "; } cout << endl; for(int k=3; k >= 0; k--){ cout << k << " "; } cout << endl << endl; // Nested Loops for(int i=0; i < 4; i++){ cout << i << " "; for(int k=3; k >= 0; k--){ cout << k << " "; } cout << endl; } return 0; }. Program Output for Sequential Loops: 0 1 2 3 then 3 2 1 0. The Nested Loops output section has blank lines for students to fill in as an exercise.
notes_text: The solution is provided on slide 15. The sequential loops produce two separate lines, while nested loops produce four lines where each line starts with i followed by the countdown 3 2 1 0.

title: break Statement with Nested Loops
summary: Explains that break only exits the innermost loop, and to exit all loops you must modify a variable to fail the outer loop condition.
main_text: break Statement with Nested Loops. break will only exit the inner-most loop, not all the nested loops. This can be exactly what you want in some cases. In other cases, you may want to break out of all loops, but realize a single 'break' statement cannot do that. Instead, must change a variable so that the outer loop condition will fail. Code: int main() { char again = 'y'; while(again == 'y') { /* Give the user 10 turns but stop if guess right */ int i, guess, secretNum = /*..*/; for(i=0; i < 10; i++) { cin >> guess; if(guess == secretNum){ break; } } if( i == 10 ) cout << "You lose!" << endl; else cout << "You win!" << endl; cin >> again; } return 0; }. An arrow points from the break statement to the closing brace of the for loop, showing that break exits only the for loop, not the while loop.
notes_text: The check 'if(i == 10)' after the for loop determines whether the loop ended because the user ran out of turns or because they guessed correctly via break.

title: Nested Loops Example 3 - Factoring Program
summary: Complete C++ program using nested loops to find and print all factors of user-entered numbers until -1 is entered as a sentinel value.
main_text: Nested Loops Example 3. Code: int main() { int num; cout << "Enter numbers to factor (end with -1)" << endl; cin >> num; // get first num while(num != -1){ // find all factors of num, one at a time for(int factor = 1; factor <= num; factor++){ if(num % factor == 0) { cout << factor << " "; } } cout << endl; cin >> num; // get next num } return 0; }. Program Output: Enter numbers to factor (end with -1). User enters 9, output: 1 3 9. User enters 12, output: 1 2 3 4 6 12. User enters -1, program ends.
notes_text: This is the factoring example previewed on slide 3. The outer while loop handles multiple numbers (sentinel-controlled), and the inner for loop finds all factors of each number using the modulo operator.

title: Nested Loops Example 4 - Trace Exercise
summary: Presents a tracing exercise with a while/for nested loop that processes even numbers from user input, with blank output for students to complete.
main_text: Nested Loops Example 4. Trace through the execution of this code and show what will be printed if the user types in: 8 4 7 6. Code: int main() { int x = 0; cin >> x; while( x%2 == 0 ){ for(int i=x; i >= 0; i -= 2){ cout << i << " "; } cout << endl; cin >> x; } cout << "Done" << endl; return 0; }. Program Output: (blank area for students to fill in). The outer while loop continues as long as x is even (x%2 == 0). The inner for loop counts down from x to 0 by 2s. With input 8 4 7 6: x=8 is even so print 8 6 4 2 0, x=4 is even so print 4 2 0, x=7 is odd so the while loop exits and prints Done. The value 6 is never read.
notes_text: The solution is on slide 16. Key insight: the while loop condition checks evenness, so 7 causes termination before 6 is ever read.

title: Nested Loops Example 1 - Solution
summary: Solution to the nested for loop tracing exercise, showing the complete output and a trace table of i and j values.
main_text: Nested Loops Example 2 (Solution). Trace through the execution of this code and show what will be printed. Code: int main() { for(int i=0; i < 2; i++){ for(int j=0; j < 3; j++){ cout << i << " " << j << endl; } } }. Program Output: 0 0, 0 1, 0 2, 1 0, 1 1, 1 2. Trace table: When i=0, j takes values 0, 1, 2. When i=1, j takes values 0, 1, 2. The inner loop (j=0 to 2) completes entirely for each value of the outer loop variable i.
notes_text: This is the solution to the exercise from slide 6. The output confirms the key principle: the inner loop runs all its iterations before the outer loop advances.

title: Sequential vs. Nested Loops - Solution
summary: Solution showing the output difference between sequential and nested loops, with sequential producing two lines and nested producing four lines.
main_text: Nested vs. Sequential Loops (Solution). Sequential loops are run one after the other. Each loop runs to completion before the next starts. Nested loops runs the inner loop to completion for each iteration of the outer loop. Code: int main() { // Sequential Loops for(int i=0; i < 4; i++){ cout << i << " "; } cout << endl; for(int k=3; k >= 0; k--){ cout << k << " "; } cout << endl << endl; // Nested Loops for(int i=0; i < 4; i++){ cout << i << " "; for(int k=3; k >= 0; k--){ cout << k << " "; } cout << endl; } return 0; }. Program Output: Sequential: 0 1 2 3 then 3 2 1 0. Nested: 0 3 2 1 0, 1 3 2 1 0, 2 3 2 1 0, 3 3 2 1 0. Each nested output line starts with the current i value followed by the full countdown 3 2 1 0.
notes_text: This is the solution to slide 9. The key difference: sequential loops produce independent output sequences, while nested loops combine the outer variable with the full inner loop output on each line.

title: Nested Loops Example 4 - Solution
summary: Solution to the tracing exercise showing output when user inputs 8 4 7 6, demonstrating how the even-number check controls the outer while loop.
main_text: Nested Loops Example 4 (Solution). Trace through the execution of this code and show what will be printed if the user types in: 8 4 7 6. Code: int main() { int x = 0; cin >> x; while(x%2 == 0){ for(int i=x; i >= 0; i -= 2){ cout << i << " "; } cout << endl; cin >> x; } cout << "Done" << endl; return 0; }. Program Output: 8 6 4 2 0, then 4 2 0, then Done. Explanation: x=8 is even, inner loop prints 8 6 4 2 0. x=4 is even, inner loop prints 4 2 0. x=7 is odd, while condition fails, prints Done. The input value 6 is never read because the program exits the while loop when it encounters 7.
notes_text: This is the solution to slide 12. The value 6 is never consumed from input because 7 causes the while loop to terminate.

title: Task 2 - All Pairs Trace

J=0,K=4: (4,12). J=1,K=2: (1,7). J=1,K=3: (1,8). J=1,K=4: (1,12). J=2,K=3: (7,8). J=2,K=4: (7,12). J=3,K=4: (8,12). Each step shows the array with only the two elements being paired highlighted.

title: Task 2 - Programming Mechanics

Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: The key insight is that the inner loop index K depends on the outer loop index J (K starts at J+1), making this a dependent nested loop.

title: Task 3 - Check Array Uniqueness Problem
summary: Introduces Task 3: checking if all numbers in an array are unique, showing both a non-unique and unique example array.

Array: [4, 1, 7, 8, 12, 7, 6] - the two 7s at indices [2] and [5] are highlighted in red showing the duplicate. Example 2 - Check if all numbers are unique: YES. Array: [4, 1, 10, 8, 12, 7, 6] - all values are distinct. What if we can only see 1 or 2 numbers at a time - shown with a blank array of 7 elements to illustrate the computer's limited view.
notes_text: This motivates the need for nested loops - a human can scan all values at once, but a computer can only compare two at a time.

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness with Large Data
summary: Shows that checking uniqueness becomes harder for humans with larger datasets, motivating the need for a systematic algorithmic approach.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all the numbers in an array are unique. It may not be as easy even for a human when we increase the amount of numbers? Questions: What process would you use as a human? Can we do this in 1 pass? If we can only see 1 thing or perform 1 operation at a time, what other variables do we need? Do we always have to do the same amount of work, or might we find an answer 'early'? Sample Data: 6 40 3 96 44 94 74 9 23 22 56 64 12 7 51 31 24 80 88 10 91 27 38 30 78 60 37 69 26 11 39 50 68 21 41 48 66 46 20 25 82 98 76 34 55 70 4 54 90 28 14 71 73 85 81 65 77 59 57 43 33 49 87 19 17 16 1 2 15 72 45 93 86 92 36

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness Check Trace (First Element)
summary: Traces comparing element at index 0 (value 5) against all subsequent elements using indices J=0 and K=1 through 6.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all numbers are unique. The trace shows comparing the first element (5) against all others: J=0, K=1: compare data[0]=5 with data[1]=2. J=0, K=2: compare 5 with data[2]=8. J=0, K=3: compare 5 with data[3]=1. J=0, K=4: compare 5 with data[4]=7. J=0, K=5: compare 5 with data[5]=9. J=0, K=6: compare 5 with data[6]=3. We've seen all the numbers now? Can we state they are all unique? What are you 'remembering' to answer that question? Can the computer do that?
notes_text: After comparing element 0 against all others, we only know that 5 has no duplicate - we still need to check all other pairs.

title: Task 3 - Why K Should Not Start at 0
summary: Explains why the inner loop index K must not start at 0 to avoid comparing an element with itself, which would always yield a false duplicate.
main_text: Task 3. Why not start k at 0 as well? We never want to compare an element with itself. The diagram shows J=0, K=0 with a prohibition symbol, and the comparison data[j] == data[k] would be data[0] == data[0], which is always true and would incorrectly indicate a duplicate.
notes_text: This is a common mistake when implementing the uniqueness check. Starting K at J+1 avoids self-comparison and also avoids redundant pair checks.

images.description: Array diagram with J=0, K=0 both pointing to the same element, with a red prohibition/no symbol indicating this is wrong. A box shows data[j] == data[k] to illustrate the self-comparison problem.

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness Check Trace (Second Element)
summary: Continues the uniqueness trace with J=1, comparing element at index 1 (value 2) against elements at indices 2 through 6.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all numbers are unique. Trace continues with J=1: J=1, K=2: compare data[1]=2 with data[2]=8. J=1, K=3: compare 2 with data[3]=1. J=1, K=4: compare 2 with data[4]=7. J=1, K=5: compare 2 with data[5]=9. J=1, K=6: compare 2 with data[6]=3. No duplicates found for element at index 1.
notes_text: The pattern continues: for each J, K starts at J+1 and goes to the end. This ensures each pair is checked exactly once.

images.description: Five array state diagrams showing J=1 fixed while K goes from 2 to 6, highlighting the two compared elements each time.

title: Task 3 - Final Pair in Uniqueness Check
summary: Shows the last comparison in the uniqueness check with J=5, K=6 comparing the final pair of elements.
main_text: Task 3. Check if all numbers are unique. Final comparison: J=5, K=6: compare data[5]=9 with data[6]=3. These are the last two elements to compare, completing all pairwise checks.
notes_text: This shows the end of the nested loop execution. All pairs have been checked with no duplicates found.

images.description: Single array state diagram showing J=5, K=6 as the final pair comparison.

title: Task 3 - Uniqueness Programming Mechanics
summary: Presents the key programming questions for implementing the uniqueness check: index dependency, output timing, and stopping conditions.
main_text: Task 3. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? How and when are we ready to print our answer? How do we stop (one or both loops)? Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: Key decisions: use a bool flag (allUnique), break out of inner loop when duplicate found, break out of outer loop too. Answer is printed after both loops complete or after early termination.

title: Task 4 - Reverse Array Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 4: reversing an array of integers, questioning whether it needs a nested loop or can be done in one pass.
main_text: Task 4. Reverse an array of integers. Question: Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Example: Reverse an array's contents. Before: data = [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10, 9] at indices [0] through [8]. After: data = [9, -10, 17, 6, -5, 12, -3, 8, 4]. A red downward arrow indicates the transformation from original to reversed array.
notes_text: This task can be done in a single pass with two pointers moving toward each other, not requiring nested loops.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing the before and after states of reversing the array, connected by a red downward arrow.

title: Task 4 - Array Reversal Trace (Swapping)
summary: Traces the array reversal process showing swaps between elements at positions J and K moving inward from both ends.
main_text: Task 4. Reverse an array's contents. Trace with J (left pointer) and K (right pointer) and n=9: J=0, K=8: swap data[0]=4 with data[8]=9. J=1, K=7: swap data[1]=8 with data[7]=-10. J=2, K=6: swap data[2]=-3 with data[6]=17. J=3, K=5: swap data[3]=12 with data[5]=6. J=4, K=4: J meets K at the middle element -5. A question mark indicates: should we keep going? Pink double-headed arrows show each swap operation.
notes_text: When J equals K (or J > K), we have reached the middle and should stop. The middle element does not need to be swapped.

images.description: Five array state diagrams showing the progressive swapping from both ends toward the middle, with pink double-headed arrows indicating each swap. Variables J, K, and n are tracked on the right.

title: Task 4 - Why Stop at Halfway
summary: Demonstrates that continuing swaps past the halfway point undoes the reversal, so the loop must stop at n/2.
main_text: Task 4. Should we keep going? The trace continues past the middle showing what happens if we don't stop: J=2, K=6: swap -3 and 17 (correct). J=3, K=5: swap 12 and 6 (correct). J=4, K=4: middle element -5 (stop here). J=5, K=3: swap 6 and 12 - this UNDOES the earlier swap! J=6, K=2: swap 17 and -3 - this UNDOES another earlier swap! No! We must stop at the halfway point to avoid 'undoing' the swaps we've just done.
notes_text: This is a crucial insight: the loop condition must be j < n/2 (or equivalently j < k). Going past the middle reverses the reversal.

images.description: Array state diagrams showing swaps continuing past the midpoint, with the last two swaps undoing previous work. A warning box at the bottom explains why stopping at halfway is necessary.

title: Task 4 - Reversal Programming Mechanics
summary: Discusses implementation considerations for array reversal including even/odd length handling and index dependency.
main_text: Task 4. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Does an even or odd length array need to be handled separately? Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Are the indexes we need to generate independent or is one dependent on another? Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: Even and odd length arrays are handled the same way with j < n/2. For odd arrays, the middle element stays in place. The two indexes are dependent: k = n-1-j.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted C++ code template for array setup.

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives to Front
summary: Introduces Task 5: moving all negative numbers to the front of an array while preserving the order of negative numbers.
main_text: Task 5. Move all negative numbers to the front of the array, preserving order of negative numbers (but not necessarily positive numbers). Question: Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Can we identify the items to move as we perform 1 pass? If we need to move it, would we know where to place it? When we move it, do we risk overwriting something we should not? Move all negative numbers to the front of the array: Before: data = [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10, 9, 1, 2, -7]. After: data = [-3, -5, -10, -7, 8, 6, 17, 4, 9, 1, 2, 12].
notes_text: This uses a leading/trailing pointer technique. Negative numbers maintain their relative order but positive numbers may be reordered.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing the before and after states. Before: mixed positive and negative values. After: all negatives moved to front. Connected by a red downward arrow.
labels: Move all negative numbers to the front of the array:

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives Trace Part 1
summary: Traces the first part of moving negatives to front using leading and trailing pointers, showing swaps when negatives are found.
main_text: Task 5. Move all negative numbers to the front of the array. Trace with leading and trailing pointers on array [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10]: leading=0, trailing=0: data[0]=4 (positive, no swap). leading=1, trailing=0: data[1]=8 (positive, no swap). leading=2, trailing=0: data[2]=-3 (negative! swap with trailing). After swap: [-3, 8, 4, ...]. leading=2, trailing=0: then swap data[leading] with data[trailing]. leading=3, trailing=1: data[3]=12 (positive). leading=4, trailing=1: data[4]=-5 (negative! swap). After swap: [-3, -5, 4, 8, ...]. leading=4, trailing=1: [-3, -5, ...then 8 swapped to position].
notes_text: The trailing pointer marks where the next negative should go. Leading pointer scans through the array. When a negative is found at leading, swap it to the trailing position.

images.description: Eight array state diagrams showing the leading and trailing pointer positions and array contents at each step, with swap arrows shown when negatives are found and moved.

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives Trace Part 2
summary: Continues the trace showing the remaining swaps and the final state of the array with all negatives at the front.
main_text: Task 5. Move all negative numbers to the front of the array. Continuing the trace: leading=5, trailing=2: data[5]=4 (in the swapped position). leading=6, trailing=2: data[6]=17 (positive). leading=7, trailing=2: data[7]=-10 (negative! swap with trailing position 2). After swap: [-3, -5, -10, ...]. The bottom section shows a second example with array [4, 8, -3, 12, -5, 6, 17, -10]: leading=8, trailing=3: final result is [-3, -5, -10, 12, 8, 6, 17, 4].
notes_text: The final array shows all negatives (-3, -5, -10) at the front in their original relative order, while positives may be reordered.

images.description: Multiple array state diagrams continuing the trace from the previous slide, showing the final swaps and resulting array state.

title: Task 5 - Move Negatives Programming Mechanics
summary: Discusses when to increment leading vs trailing pointers and states the loop invariants for the partition algorithm.
main_text: Task 5. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? When do we increment leading? When do we increment trailing? Invariants: All values behind trailing are negative. All values between leading and trailing are positive. Code template: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task ... return 0; }
notes_text: Loop invariants are a formal way to reason about correctness. Leading always increments; trailing only increments when a swap occurs.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted C++ code template for array setup.

title: Task 6 - Insert at Location Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 6: inserting a new value at a specific index in an array, shifting existing elements to make room.
main_text: Task 6. Assuming an array of size max, but only n occupied elements, insert a new value, v, at location, loc, shifting others back. Question: Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Do we insert then shift? Or shift then insert? In what order should we shift the needed values? Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. Before: data = [4, 8, 7, 3, 12, 1, 9, ?, ?], n=7, max=9. After: data = [4, 8, 5, 7, 3, 12, 1, 9, ?], n=8, max=9.
notes_text: Must shift right before inserting to avoid overwriting. Shift from end toward insertion point, not the other way.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing before and after insertion of value 5 at index 2, with a red downward arrow between them. Variables n and max shown beside the arrays.

title: Task 6 - Wrong Way to Shift (Left to Right)
summary: Shows why shifting from left to right (low index to high) is incorrect - it overwrites values before they can be moved.
main_text: Task 6. Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. Wrong approach - shifting left to right: k=2: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 7 to position 3, but overwrites 3. k=3: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 7 (the already-copied value) to position 4. k=4: copies 7 again. Result: [4, 8, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, ?, ?] - all positions from 2 onward become 7. A prohibition symbol indicates this approach is wrong.
notes_text: This demonstrates the classic pitfall of shifting in the wrong direction. Each shift overwrites the next element before it can be saved.

images.description: Four array state diagrams showing the incorrect left-to-right shift, with data[k+1]=data[k] labels on the right. The value 7 propagates through all positions. A red prohibition symbol at the bottom indicates this is wrong.

title: Task 6 - Correct Way to Shift (Right to Left)
summary: Shows the correct approach to shifting elements from right to left (high index to low) before inserting.
main_text: Task 6. Insert 5 at location 2 into the array of 7 elements and 9 locations. Correct approach - shifting right to left: k=6: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 9 to position 7. k=5: data[k+1] = data[k] copies 1 to position 6. k=4: copies 12 to position 5. k=3: copies 3 to position 4. k=2: copies 7 to position 3. Now position 2 is free to insert the new value. Each step shows data[k+1] = data[k] on the right side.
notes_text: By starting from the rightmost element and working left, each element is safely moved to the right before its position is needed.

summary: Shows the final step of inserting the value 5 at the now-empty location 2 and incrementing n.

title: Task 7 - Find Unique Number Problem Statement
summary: Introduces Task 7: finding the one number in an array that has no duplicate pair, using nested loop comparison.
main_text: Task 7. Given there is 1 number that does NOT have a duplicate (pair), find and output that unique number. Questions: Is this generating all pairs again? Might we be able to answer 'early'? Find the unique number: Array data = [4, 7, 4, 12, 7, 3, 12] with empty gray cells below. Sample Data: 33 13 23 72 20 6 61 66 46 54 33 1 17 47 29 73 18 1 50 73 89 46 5 98 13 32 70 32 10 10 87 53 99 12 5 61 12 18 76 96 87 60 96 82 47 52 29 76 93 70 71 6 7 39 48 48 17 99 36 82 72 60 71 89 36 98 54 93 7 66 39 52 53 50 20
notes_text: Every number appears exactly twice except for one unique number. The approach requires checking each element against all others.

images.description: Array diagram showing data=[4,7,4,12,7,3,12] and a large sample dataset in a box below.

title: Task 7 - Finding Unique with One-Way Pairs (Fails)
summary: Shows that checking only one ordering of pairs (j,k where k>j) fails to correctly identify the unique number because the match for the second occurrence is missed.
main_text: Task 7. Find the unique number finding all pairs (with only one ordering rather than both for each pair). Array: [8, 3, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5]. Trace: J=0, K=1 through K=6: checking 8 against all others, finds match at K=4 (8). J=1, K=2 through K=6: checking 3, finds match at K=5 (3). J=2, K=3 through K=6: checking 5, finds match at K=6 (5). But for J=2, K=6 with value 3 - we didn't find a match for the 2nd item in a pair that DID exist! The problem: when we find a pair (3,3) at J=1,K=5, the second 3 at index 5 is never checked as a 'first' element against later elements.
notes_text: This approach of only checking (j,k) where k>j fails because the second occurrence of a paired number might appear to be unique when checked as j.

images.description: Array trace diagrams in two columns showing J and K positions with highlighted matching pairs. A prohibition symbol and note at bottom indicates the approach fails.

title: Task 7 - Finding Unique with Both Orderings
summary: Shows the correct approach using all pairs in both orderings (k starts at 0, not j+1), checking each element against every other element.
main_text: Task 7. Find the unique number with all pairs (in both orders). Array: [8, 3, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5]. Trace for J=0: K=0 (skip self), K=1: 8 vs 3, K=2: 8 vs 5, K=3: 8 vs 6, K=4: 8 vs 8 (match found! 8 has a pair). J=1: K=0: 3 vs 8, K=1 (skip self), K=2: 3 vs 5, K=3: 3 vs 6, K=4: 3 vs 8, K=5: 3 vs 3 (match found!). For J=2: checking element 8 at index 0, finds match at K=4. And so on for each element.
notes_text: By letting K range from 0 to n (skipping when k==j), each element is fully checked against all others. This correctly identifies unmatched elements.

images.description: Array trace diagrams in two columns showing J and K positions, checking both orderings. Green/yellow highlighted cells show matches found.

title: Task 7 - Complete Trace Finding 6 as Unique
summary: Complete trace showing all elements being checked, concluding that 6 is the unique number because it has no match in the array.
main_text: Task 7. Find the unique number. Array: [8, 3, 5, 6, 8, 3, 5]. Continuing the trace for later J values: J=3: checking 8 at index 0 vs 5 at index 2, then 5 vs 6, 3 vs 6, 5 vs 6, etc. J=4: K=0 through K=6 checking element 6 against all others. 6 vs 8, 6 vs 3, 6 vs 5, 6 vs 6... but wait, there is no other 6 in the array! After checking all K values, no match is found for data[4]=6. 6 is the unique number! The value 6 is highlighted in pink/magenta at the bottom.
notes_text: The inner loop completes without finding a match, so the boolean 'unique' flag remains true, identifying 6 as the answer.

images.description: Array trace diagrams showing the final checks, with element 6 highlighted in pink/magenta as the unique number. A box at bottom declares '6 is the unique number!'

Phase 2 - Shift left: loc=3: data[3]=data[4], copies 12 to index 3 (data[loc]=data[loc+1]). loc=4: data[4]=data[5], copies 9 to index 4. loc=5: data[5]=data[6], copies 10 to index 5.

summary: Traces the single-pass removal of all occurrences of 11 using leading and trailing pointer technique.
main_text: Task 11. Remove all occurrences of val=11 from the array [8, 11, 2, 11, 12, 9, 11]. Trace with lead and trail pointers: lead=0, trail=0: data[0]=8 != 11, so data[trail]=data[lead], trail++, lead++. Action: data[trail]=data[lead]; trail++; lead++. lead=1, trail=1: data[1]=11 == val, so just lead++. Action: lead++; lead=2, trail=1: data[2]=2 != 11, data[1]=2, trail++. Action: data[trail]=data[lead]; trail++; lead++. lead=3, trail=2: data[3]=11 == val, lead++. lead=4, trail=2: data[4]=12, data[2]=12, trail++. Action: data[trail]=data[lead]; trail++; lead++. lead=5, trail=3: data[5]=9, data[3]=9, trail++. lead=6, trail=4: data[6]=11 == val, lead++. Action: lead++;
notes_text: When the value is not 11, copy from lead to trail and advance both. When it is 11, only advance lead. Trail ends up as the new n.

So the result is: out = [8, 2, 12, 9] with n=4 (n = trail). The trailing pointer's final value becomes the new n.
notes_text: The key insight: n = trail at the end. Elements beyond index trail-1 are logically removed even though they may still contain old values in memory.

title: Sequential vs. Random Access
summary: Explains the two main array access patterns: sequential access (looping through all elements) and random access (computing a specific index directly).
main_text: Sequential vs. Random Access. Most array-based tasks fall into either a sequential-access pattern or random-access pattern. Sequential access iterates (loops) through all elements. Used for tasks that require looking at all elements in the worst case. Random access computes the ONE index to access. Used for tasks that only require accessing one specific element. Sequential example: int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < 20; i++){ total += scores[i]; } Array scores at addresses 520-1076 with indices [0]-[19] containing values 96, 84, 93, ..., 90. Random access example: int stuID; cout << 'Enter ID\n'; cin >> stuID; cout << 'Your score: '; cout << scores[stuID]; cout << endl; A stuID value of 2 directly accesses scores[2]=93.
notes_text: Sequential access is O(n) while random access is O(1). Many array algorithms combine both patterns.

images.description: Two diagrams: Left shows sequential access with an arrow sweeping across all array elements with a loop summing them. Right shows random access where stuID=2 directly indexes into scores[2]=93.

title: Arrays as Look-Up Tables
summary: Explains how to use one array's values as indices into another array, creating a look-up table pattern for precomputed results.
main_text: Arrays as Look-Up Tables. Use the value of one array as the index of another. Suppose you are given some integers as data [in the range of 0 to 5]. Suppose computing squares of integers was difficult (no built-in function for it). Could compute them yourself, record answer in another array and use data to 'look-up' the square. Code example 1 (two-step): // the data int data[8] = {3, 2, 0, 5, 1, 4, 5, 3}; // The LUT int squares[6] = {0,1,4,9,16,25}; for(int i=0; i < 8; i++){ int x = data[i]; int x_sq = squares[x]; cout << i << ',' << x_sq << endl; } Code example 2 (combined): for(int i=0; i < 8; i++){ int x_sq = squares[data[i]]; cout << i << ',' << x_sq << endl; }
notes_text: The LUT pattern is a form of random access. The value from data[] is used as an index into squares[], avoiding recomputation. This is a common optimization technique.

title: Approach to Priority Problem
summary: Demonstrates the priority scheduling problem using look-up tables with pri and req arrays to select requestors in priority order.
main_text: Approach to 'Priority' Problem. Find the 2D structure. Consider when sequential loops are necessary vs. nesting loops. In this program the values of the priority array can be used to check the requests array in order from most to least priority. Example trace with pri=[0,1,2,3] and req=[0,1,0,1]: Selected=1 (pri[1]=1 is highest priority requestor). pri updates to [0,2,3,1]. req=[0,1,1,1]: Selected=2. pri=[0,3,1,2]. req=[0,0,1,0]: Selected=2. pri=[0,3,1,2]. req=[1,1,1,1]: Selected=0. pri=[3,1,2,0]. req=[1,1,1,1]: Selected=3. pri=[1,2,0,3]. req=[0,0,0,0]: Quit.
notes_text: The priority array acts as a look-up table that determines the order in which requestors are checked. After each selection, priorities are updated.

images.description: Multiple state diagrams showing pri and req arrays at each step, with the selected requestor highlighted in green. Shows 'Highest priority' and 'Lowest priority' labels above the pri array.

title: Connecting to Priority Homework
summary: Discusses how the priority array can serve as a look-up table for the request array and how remove-first applies to this problem.
main_text: Connecting To 'Priority' Homework. Can the pri array be used as a look-up table for the req array ..OR.. vice versa. How can remove-first be relevant here once we find the given requestor. The same trace from the previous slide is shown with pri and req arrays being updated at each step as requestors are selected in priority order: selected values are 1, 2, 2, 0, 3, then Quit when all requests are 0.
notes_text: After selecting a requestor, we need to update the priority array - this is where the remove-first operation from Task 10 becomes relevant.

images.description: Same priority scheduling trace as previous slide, re-shown to emphasize the connection between LUT usage and the remove-first operation.

title: Task 1 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for linear search using a for loop with break and a boolean found flag.
main_text: Task 1 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? How would you generate the appropriate indexes? When can you stop? When would you be ready to return -1? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task cin >> val; bool found = false; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { if(val == data[i]){ cout << i << endl; found = true; break; } } if(!found) { cout << -1 << endl; } return 0; }
notes_text: Key elements: bool found flag initialized false, break when match found, check found after loop to output -1 if needed.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 1 linear search.

title: Task 2 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for generating all unique pairs using nested for loops with k starting at j+1.
main_text: Task 2 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? How would you generate the appropriate indexes? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task for(int j=0; j < n; j++) { for(int k=j+1; k < n; k++) { cout << data[j] << ',' << data[k] << ' '; } } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: The inner loop starts at k=j+1, making the inner variable dependent on the outer. This generates n*(n-1)/2 unique pairs.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 2 all pairs generation with nested loops.

title: Task 3 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for checking array uniqueness using nested loops with a boolean flag and break statements.
main_text: Task 3 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? How and when are we ready to print our answer? How do we stop (one or both loops)? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task bool allUnique = true; for(int j=0; j < n; j++) { for(int k=j+1; k < n; k++) { if(data[j] == data[k]){ allUnique = false; break; } } if(!allUnique) break; } if(allUnique) { cout << 'All unique' << endl; } else { cout << 'Not all unique' << endl; } return 0; }
notes_text: Two break statements are needed: one for inner loop, one for outer loop, both triggered by the allUnique flag becoming false. The k=j+1 start avoids self-comparison.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 3 uniqueness check.

title: Task 4 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for array reversal using a single for loop iterating to n/2 with swap operations.
main_text: Task 4 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Does an even or odd length array need to be handled separately? Can we do this in 1 pass or do we need a nested loop where we examine 'pairs'? Are the indexes we need to generate independent or is one dependent on another? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task for(int j=0; j < n/2; j++) { // swap data[j] and data[k] (k=n-j-1) int temp = data[j]; data[j] = data[n-j-1]; data[n-j-1] = temp; } return 0; }
notes_text: The loop runs to n/2 (integer division handles both even and odd cases). The paired index is k=n-j-1. Uses standard three-variable swap with temp.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 4 array reversal.

title: Task 5 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for moving negatives to front using leading/trailing pointer technique with single-pass swap.
main_text: Task 5 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? When do we increment leading? When do we increment trailing? Invariants: All values behind trailing are negative. All values between leading and trailing are positive. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int lead, trail = 0; for(lead=0; lead < n; lead++) { if(data[lead] < 0) { // swap leading and trailing int temp = data[lead]; data[lead] = data[trail]; data[trail] = temp; // only increment if we move trail++; } } return 0; }
notes_text: Leading always advances (via for loop). Trailing only advances when a negative is found and swapped. The invariants guarantee correctness.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 5 move negatives to front.

title: Task 6 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for inserting a value at a specific location with bounds checking, right-to-left shift, and n increment.
main_text: Task 6 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we want to move from k to k+1 OR k-1 to k? Based on the above where should we start and stop our loop? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[20]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int loc, val; cin >> loc >> val; if(n < 20 && loc >= 0 && loc <= n){ for(int k=n-1; k >= loc; k--) { data[k+1] = data[k]; } data[loc] = val; n++; } else { cout << 'Invalid' << endl; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: Bounds checking ensures n < max (20) and loc is valid. The loop goes from n-1 down to loc, shifting each element right. Then insert and increment n.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 6 array insertion with bounds checking.

title: Task 7 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for finding the unique number using nested loops with j!=k check and boolean unique flag.
main_text: Task 7 - Solution. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? How do we avoid matching ourself? How do we know we've found a unique item? When and how can we stop early? Variations: Allow 0 or more unique values and output the unique values OR output 'All have a pair' if each number has a pair. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task for(int j=0; j < n; j++) { bool unique = true; for(int k=0; k < n; k++) { if(j != k){ if(data[j] == data[k]){ unique = false; break; } } } if(unique){ cout << data[j] << endl; break; } } return 0; }
notes_text: The if(j != k) check prevents self-comparison. The inner break exits when a match is found. The outer break exits when the unique element is identified.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 7 finding the unique number.

title: Task 8 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for merging two sorted arrays using three while loops for the three phases of merge.
main_text: Task 8 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? What cases or 'phases' exist for the merge process? What two elements should be compared and what element should be placed in the output? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n1=0, n2=0, in1[20], in2[20], out[40]; int num; // Read array 1 cin >> num; while(num != -1){ in1[n1++] = num; cin >> num; } // Read array 2 cin >> num; while(num != -1){ in2[n2++] = num; cin >> num; } // now perform the given task int r1 = 0, r2 = 0, w = 0; while(r1 < n1 && r2 < n2) { if(in1[r1] < in2[r2]) { out[w++] = in1[r1++]; } else { out[w++] = in2[r2++]; } } while(r1 < n1) { // place remaining in1 out[w++] = in1[r1++]; } while(r2 < n2) { // place remaining in2 out[w++] = in2[r2++]; } // Output the results return 0; }
notes_text: Three phases: (1) compare and place smaller while both arrays have elements, (2) copy remaining from in1, (3) copy remaining from in2. Uses post-increment on indices.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 8 merge sorted arrays, split across two columns.

title: Task 9 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for inserting into a sorted array using while loop to find location, then for loop to shift, with capacity check.
main_text: Task 9 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Are the indexes independent or is one dependent on another? How and when are we ready to print our answer? How do we stop (one or both loops)? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, loc = -1, curr = 0; cin >> val; if(n < 100){ while(curr < n && val > data[curr] ) { curr++; } loc = curr; for(int curr = n-1; curr >= loc; curr--) { data[curr+1] = data[curr]; } data[loc] = val; n++; } else { cout << 'No room' << endl; } // Output the results return 0; }
notes_text: Two sequential operations: (1) while loop to find insertion location by scanning until data[curr] >= val, (2) for loop to shift right from n-1 down to loc. Then insert and increment n.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 9 sorted array insertion.

title: Task 10 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for removing the first occurrence of a value: find with break, then shift left, then decrement n.
main_text: Task 10 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? In what order should you shift? Will you shift from k to k-1 or k+1 to k? And where would you stop? Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, loc; cin >> val; // find first occurrence of val for(loc = 0; loc < n; loc++) { if(data[loc] == val) { break; } } if(loc < n) { // shift items up from loc to n // invariant: data[loc] is always safe to overwrite for( ; loc < n-1; loc++) { data[loc] = data[loc+1]; } n--; } // Output the results ... return 0; }
notes_text: The find loop uses break when found. If loc < n after the loop, the value was found and we shift left. The invariant notes that data[loc] is always safe to overwrite.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 10 remove first occurrence.

title: Task 11 - Solution Code
summary: Complete C++ solution for removing all occurrences using leading/trailing pointer single-pass technique.
main_text: Task 11 - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we just need to track the maximum VALUE or the INDEX of the maximum value? Given that you can move the maximum number to the end of the array, how could this be used to SORT the entire array? Repeat the process for the first n-1 elements, then repeat for the first n-2 elements, etc. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, lead, trail; cin >> val; trail = 0; for(lead = 0; lead < n; lead++) { if(data[lead] != val) { data[trail] = data[lead]; trail++; } } n = trail; // Output the results for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << data[i] << ' '; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: When data[lead] != val, copy to trail position and advance trail. When equal to val, only advance lead (skip). n = trail gives the new size.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 11 remove all occurrences.

title: Task 12a - Selection Sort Step Solution
summary: Complete C++ solution for finding the max and swapping it to the end using index tracking (selection sort step).
main_text: Task 12a - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we just need to track the maximum VALUE or the INDEX of the maximum value? Given that you can move the maximum number to the end of the array, how could this be used to SORT the entire array? Repeat the process for the first n-1 elements, then repeat for the first n-2 elements, etc. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int cmax = 0; for(int i=1; i < n; i++) { if(data[i] > data[cmax]){ cmax = i; } } // swap the max and end element int temp = data[n-1]; data[n-1] = data[cmax]; data[cmax] = temp; // Print out results for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << data[i] << ' '; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: cmax starts at 0 and updates whenever a larger element is found. After the loop, one swap places the max at the end. This is one step of selection sort.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 12a selection approach.

title: Task 12b - Bubble Sort Step Solution
summary: Complete C++ solution for bubbling the maximum to the end using adjacent comparisons and swaps.
main_text: Task 12b - Sol. What programming issues (mechanics) should you think about? Do we just need to track the maximum VALUE or the INDEX of the maximum value? Given that you can move the maximum number to the end of the array, how could this be used to SORT the entire array? Repeat the process for the first n-1 elements, then repeat for the first n-2 elements, etc. Solution code: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task for(int i=0; i < n-1; i++) { if(data[i] > data[i+1]){ int temp = data[i]; data[i] = data[i+1]; data[i+1] = temp; } } // Print out results for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << data[i] << ' '; } cout << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: Compares adjacent elements data[i] and data[i+1], swapping when left > right. Loop runs to n-1 since we access i+1. This is one pass of bubble sort.

images.description: Yellow-highlighted complete C++ solution code for Task 12b bubble approach.
