title: Multidimensional Processing
summary: Introduces multidimensional processing as the key concept of Unit 3, characterized by nested loops where each loop represents one dimension.
main_text: Multidimensional Processing. Most non-trivial programs require 'multidimensional' processing. The distinguishing feature is the use of NESTED loops. Each nested loop represents one dimension. A representative example might be an outer loop to get multiple inputs and an inner loop to process each input. We will likely still keep our general structure but repeat a subset in each nested loop: Prompt, Input, Process, Output. Two examples shown: Example 1 - Enter numbers to factor (end with -1): Input 9, output 1 3 9. Input 12, output 1 2 3 4 6 12. Input -1 to quit. Example 2 - Enter rectangle's base & height: Input 3 5, output three rows of five asterisks (*****).
notes_text: This slide provides a forward look at what multidimensional processing means in practice - nested loops for processing multiple inputs, each of which requires its own loop-based processing.

images.description: Top: diagram showing 2D grid data flowing through a processor to produce 2D output (same as slide 2). Bottom left: terminal showing factoring example with numbers 9 and 12. Bottom right: terminal showing rectangle drawing with asterisks. Both demonstrate nested loop applications.

main_text: Unit 3c - Debugging Strategies/Tips. Presented by Mark Redekopp.

main_text: Debugging - Part 1. (Part 2 in a few weeks).

title: Bugs
summary: Introduces the origin of the term 'bug' in computing, showing the famous first computer bug found in a relay of the Harvard Mark II.
main_text: Bugs. The original 'bug'. The slide shows a photograph of a logbook page from September 9, 1947, documenting the first actual case of a bug being found. A moth was found trapped in Relay #70, Panel F of the Harvard Mark II computer. The handwritten log entry reads: 'First actual case of bug being found.' This incident is widely cited as the origin of the term 'bug' in computing, though the term was used informally before this event.
notes_text: Grace Hopper's team is often credited with this discovery. The logbook page with the moth taped to it is preserved at the Smithsonian.

images.description: Photograph of a historical logbook page from September 9, 1947, showing handwritten entries and a moth taped to the page. The entry documents the first actual case of a computer bug being found in Relay #70, Panel F of the Harvard Mark II.
labels: First actual case of bug being found

title: Step 1: Review your Own Code
summary: Introduces rubber duck debugging as the first debugging strategy: explain your code line by line to yourself or an inanimate object to find errors.
main_text: Step 1: Review your Own Code. Rubber Duck Debugging: Reference from an anecdote from a book, 'The Pragmatic Programmer', that has become popular. Idea: Explain your code line by line to yourself or some other 'object'. Note: Commenting your code is a way to do this. The concept is that by forcing yourself to articulate what each line of code does, you will naturally discover logical errors and misunderstandings in your own code. Walking through your code can help you find the bug.
notes_text: Rubber duck debugging is a well-known technique from 'The Pragmatic Programmer' by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas. The idea is that explaining code out loud forces you to think more carefully about each step.

images.description: Meme image of a rubber duck with text reading 'Explain your code to an inanimate object' and 'Walking through your code can help you find the bug', illustrating the rubber duck debugging concept.
labels: EXPLAIN YOUR CODE TO AN INANIMATE OBJECT
WALKING THROUGH YOUR CODE CAN HELP YOU FIND THE BUG

title: Step 2: Test Cases and Expected Outputs
summary: Explains the importance of creating test cases that cover different code paths and determining expected output before debugging.
main_text: Step 2: Test Cases & Expected Outputs. Determine input test case(s) that will exercise various parts of your code. Each if/else block. When the loop executes 0, 1, or more times. Determine the expected output. You cannot effectively debug without an expectation of the right output so you know when the program is working. Before you can identify what is wrong, you need to know what the correct behavior should be. Test cases should cover edge cases and different branches of your program.
notes_text: This step is critical because many students try to debug without knowing what the correct output should be, making it impossible to verify fixes.

title: Step 3: Tracing
summary: Demonstrates hand-tracing code execution using a variable table to walk through code line by line with a failing input scenario.
main_text: Step 3: Tracing. Use one of your input scenarios that is not working and trace the execution of your code by hand. Make a table of variables and walk the code line by line. The slide shows a C++ program that checks if a number is prime. The code includes: #include <iostream>, #include <cmath>, using namespace std; int main() { int n; cout << "Enter an integer:" endl; cin >> n; bool isPrime; isPrime = true; for(int i=2; i < sqrt(n); i++) { if(n % i == 0) { isPrime = false; break; } } if(isPrime) { cout << "Prime" << endl; } else { cout << "Not prime" << endl; } return 0; }. A variable tracking table with columns for i, n, and isPr(ime) is shown alongside the code for recording values during manual tracing.
notes_text: Note the bug in this code: the loop condition uses i < sqrt(n) instead of i <= sqrt(n), which would fail for perfect squares like 9 (since sqrt(9)=3 and the loop stops before checking i=3).

images.description: A code listing showing a C++ prime-checking program in a yellow/tan code box, alongside an empty variable tracking table with columns labeled i, n, and isPr. The table is meant for students to fill in values as they trace through the code manually.

title: Step 4: Print Statements / Narration
summary: Explains using print statements to narrate program execution, placing them in control structures to verify flow and variable values.
main_text: Step 4: Print Statements / Narration. Let the computer 'trace' for you by using print statements. Now that you know what to expect, the most common and easy way to find the error is to add print statements that will 'narrate' where you are and what the variable values are. Be a detective by narrowing down where the error is. Put a print statement in each 'for', 'while', 'if' or 'else' block...this will make sure you are getting to the expected areas of your code. Then print variable values so you can see what data your program is producing.
notes_text: Print statement debugging (also called printf debugging) is one of the most widely used debugging techniques at all skill levels. The key insight is to use print statements strategically in control flow blocks to verify both the path of execution and the data being processed.

images.description: Cartoon illustration of a detective character with a magnifying glass, representing the idea of being a detective when debugging code by narrowing down where errors occur.

title: Tips
summary: Provides practical advice for writing and debugging programs incrementally: write small portions, compile, test, then add more.
main_text: Tips. Don't write the entire program all at once. Write a small portion, compile and test it. Write the code to get the input values, add some couts to print out what you got from the user, and make sure it is what you expect. Write a single loop and test it before doing nested loops. Once one part works, add another part and test it. The key principle is incremental development: build and verify your program in small, testable pieces rather than writing everything and then trying to debug a large, complex program all at once.
notes_text: Incremental development is especially important for beginners who may struggle to debug large programs. Testing input handling first is a practical starting point.

title: Codio Debugger
summary: Section divider slide introducing the Codio Debugger tool, transitioning from general debugging strategies to using a specific debugger tool.
main_text: Codio Debugger. This section introduces the Codio debugger, a built-in debugging tool available in the Codio online IDE used in the course.
notes_text: Codio is the online development environment used in CS102. The following slides cover how to use its built-in debugger.

title: Debuggers
summary: Describes the core capabilities of debugger tools: setting breakpoints, stepping through code line by line, and viewing variable values.
main_text: Debuggers. Allows you to: Set a breakpoint (the code will run and then stop when it reaches the certain line of code). Step through your code line by line so that you can see where the flow of the program goes. Show variable values when you have stopped at a certain line of code. Debuggers automate the manual tracing process by letting the computer pause execution at specified points, allowing you to inspect the program state at each step.
notes_text: This slide summarizes the three fundamental features common to all debuggers, not just Codio's. These same capabilities exist in VS Code, GDB, LLDB, and other debugging tools.

title: Starting the Debugger
summary: Explains how to launch the Codio debugger using the 'Debug Current File' button and what happens when the program encounters an error.
main_text: Starting the Debugger. In Codio, use the 'Debug Current File' on the far right of the top menu bar to launch the debugger targeting the file your cursor is in. When you run the program, it highlights the exact line where the code breaks. Thus, whenever the code does not run as you expect or want, one of your first steps should be: Run the debugger.
notes_text: The 'Debug Current File' button is specific to Codio's interface. The debugger will compile with debug symbols automatically.

images.description: Screenshot of the Codio 'Debug Current File' button, shown as a dark blue button with a bug icon and dropdown arrow on the right side of the menu bar.

title: Breakpoints
summary: Explains how to set breakpoints in Codio by clicking the code margin, causing execution to pause at specified lines for variable inspection.
main_text: Breakpoints. Allows you to specify lines of code where you want the flow to stop and analyse the values of the variables/function calls/etc. In Codio, you can set it up by clicking on the margin of the code and see a red dot appear at the line of the code. The slide shows a code example with line numbers 35-41, where line 36 shows 'int main() {' highlighted in red/pink, and line 37 has a red breakpoint dot set on 'int vals[10] = {9, 7, 14, 20, 2, 8,...'. Other visible lines include: line 38 'cout << "Enter a number: ";', line 39 'int num;', line 40 'cin >> num;'.
notes_text: Breakpoints are non-destructive and do not modify your source code, unlike print statements. You can add and remove them freely during a debugging session.

images.description: Screenshot of Codio code editor showing a C++ program with line numbers 35-41. Line 36 (int main) is highlighted in pink/red. Line 37 has a red breakpoint dot in the margin next to an array initialization. The code includes variable declarations and cin/cout statements.

title: Debugger Commands
summary: Describes the four main debugger commands: Run, Step Over (Next), Step Out, and Step Into, along with the debugger panel showing call stack, variables, watches, and breakpoints.
main_text: Commands. Run: Runs the program (until breakpoint). Note: it will pause temporarily when at a cin statement and wait for you to type the input. Step Over (Next): Run the current line and pause at the next line of code. Step Out: Finishes (step out of) the current function's code (or hit the breakpoint), and then pause at the next line of the previous function on the stack. Step Into: If current line is a function, it steps into the function pausing at the first line of the function body. If current line is not a function, it executes the line (like step over). The debugger panel on the right side shows: Program is paused status, Call Stack showing reverse.cpp(36)main(), Local variables displaying vals, num, and loc values, Watches section with no watch expressions, Breakpoints section, and Console.
notes_text: Step Over is the most commonly used command for basic debugging. Step Into is essential when you suspect a bug is inside a function call. Step Out is useful when you have stepped into a function and want to return to the caller quickly.

images.description: Screenshot of the Codio debugger panel on the right side of the IDE showing the program paused state. The panel displays sections for Call Stack (showing reverse.cpp(36)main()), Local variables (showing vals array values, num: 1431653565, loc: 21845), Watches (no watch expressions), Breakpoints, and Console. Debugger control buttons (Run, Step Over, Step Into, Step Out, Stop) are visible at the top.

title: Showing Values
summary: Demonstrates how the debugger displays local variable values that update in real-time as you step through program execution.
main_text: Showing Values. We can view the value of local variables which will update as we step through the program. The Local variables panel shows the current values: vals: (-136422928, 32767, 0, 0, 1431653488, 21845, 143...), num: 1431653565, loc: 21845. These values represent uninitialized variable states before the program has assigned meaningful values to them. As you step through code, these values will change to reflect the actual computations being performed.
notes_text: The garbage values shown (like 1431653565 for num) are typical of uninitialized variables in C++. This is a good demonstration of why variables should always be initialized before use.

title: Unit 4 Overview
summary: Reviews the course unit progression from scalar processing through multidimensional processing to Unit 4's focus on divide and conquer via functional decomposition.
main_text: Unit 1: Scalar processing, aka IPO=Input-Process-Output Programs. Unit 2: Linear (1D) Processing. Unit 3: Multidimensional Processing. Unit 4: Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition). Each unit builds on the previous, progressing from simple single-value processing to arrays, to multidimensional data, and now to breaking programs into reusable function units.
notes_text: This slide provides context for where functions fit in the overall course structure. The visual diagrams show increasing complexity of data flow from scalar inputs/outputs to array-based and matrix-based processing, culminating in modular function blocks.

images.description: Four diagrams showing data flow patterns for each unit: Unit 1 shows single input through a processor to single output; Unit 2 shows an array input through a processor to array output; Unit 3 shows a 2D matrix input through a processor to 2D matrix output; Unit 4 shows modular function blocks f(x) and g(y) inside a dashed container representing functional decomposition.

title: Functional Decomposition Overview - Before
summary: Introduces the concept of functional decomposition by showing a monolithic main function with duplicated search code that could be extracted into a reusable function.
main_text: Idea: Extract common (small) code sequences into separate blocks (aka functions, procedures, subroutines, or methods) that we can 'call' from anywhere in our code. By decomposing our software into functions, we can: Reduce coding effort. Reuse code. Increase maintainability. Increase readability (the name of a function is often a 'comment' about what that function's code does). Build up large solutions from smaller pieces. Example code (before decomposition): int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } bool found100 = false, found0 = false; // Find 100 for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { if(100 == data[i]){ found100 = true; break; } } // Find 0 for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { if(0 == data[i]){ found0 = true; break; } } cout << "found 100: " << found100 << endl; cout << "found   0: " << found0 << endl; return 0; }. The two highlighted search loops contain nearly identical code that differs only in the value being searched for, making them candidates for extraction into a function.
notes_text: The red-outlined sections in the code highlight the duplicated search patterns that will be refactored into a single reusable function on the next slide.

images.description: Small diagram showing two function blocks f(x) and g(y) inside a dashed container, representing how code can be organized into separate callable units.

title: Functional Decomposition Overview - After
summary: Shows the refactored version of the previous slide's code where the duplicated search logic has been extracted into a reusable 'find' function.
main_text: Idea: Extract common (small) code sequences into separate blocks (aka functions, procedures, subroutines, or methods) that we can 'call' from anywhere in our code. By decomposing our software into functions, we can: Reduce coding effort. Reuse code. Increase maintainability. Increase readability (the name of a function is often a 'comment' about what that function's code does). Build up large solutions from smaller pieces. Example code (after decomposition): The extracted function: bool find(int d[], int len, int v) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { if(v == d[i]){ return true; } } return false; } The simplified main: int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } bool found100 = false, found0 = false; // Find 100 found100 = find(data, n, 100); // Find 0 found0 = find(data, n, 0); cout << "found 100: " << found100 << endl; cout << "found   0: " << found0 << endl; return 0; }. The duplicated loops are replaced by two simple function calls to find(), dramatically reducing code and improving readability.
notes_text: Compare with the previous slide to see how the two nearly-identical search loops were replaced by calls to the single find() function. The function takes the array, its length, and the value to search for as parameters.

images.description: Small diagram showing two function blocks f(x) and g(y) inside a dashed container, representing modular function organization.

title: Functions Overview
summary: Defines functions as the unit of code decomposition and abstraction, explaining both concepts with a map service example.
main_text: Functions (aka procedures, procedures, or methods) are the unit of code decomposition and abstraction. Decomposition: Breaking programs into smaller units of code. Abstraction: Generalizing an action or concept without specifying how the details are implemented. A Map Service example shows how a complex application is decomposed into separate functions: ValidateInputs(), RetrieveMap(), GetOverlayData(), Render(), and Publish(). Each function handles one specific responsibility, and the overall service is built by composing these functions together. The map image of Los Angeles illustrates the end result of such a map service, showing that users interact with the final product without needing to know how each function works internally.
notes_text: The map service example demonstrates both decomposition (breaking the service into five distinct functions) and abstraction (each function name describes what it does without revealing implementation details).

images.description: A vertical stack of five labeled function boxes forming a 'Map Service' pipeline, with a vertical label 'Function Decomposition' on the right side. Below the stack is a map image of Los Angeles showing traffic overlay data, illustrating the output of such a decomposed service.

title: Recall: Walking a Square in Scratch
summary: Demonstrates function definition and calling using Scratch block programming, showing progression from inline code to a parameterized custom function block.
main_text: We can define a function (i.e. block of code) once and then 'call' it any time we want to execute that block of code. Can provide different input values (aka 'arguments' / 'parameters') and even get an output (aka 'return' value). Three versions of a Scratch program that walks a square are shown: Version 1 (left): Inline code with a repeat loop containing move 100 steps, wait 1 seconds, turn 90 degrees, wait 1 seconds blocks directly in the main script. Version 2 (middle): The repeated block is extracted into a custom 'WalkForwardAndTurn' block definition (define WalkForwardAndTurn) containing: move 100 steps, wait 1 seconds, turn 90 degrees, wait 1 seconds. The main script calls WalkForwardAndTurn in the repeat loop. Version 3 (right): The custom block is parameterized with 'distance' and 'delay' inputs: WalkForwardAndTurn(100, 1). The definition uses these parameters (move distance steps, wait delay seconds, turn 90 degrees, wait delay seconds), making the function reusable with different values.
notes_text: This Scratch example bridges the gap from visual block-based programming to the concept of functions in C++. The three stages show the evolution from hardcoded inline code to a reusable parameterized function.

images.description: Three Scratch program screenshots showing the evolution of a square-walking program: first with inline code in a repeat loop, second with the code extracted into a custom WalkForwardAndTurn block, and third with the block parameterized to accept distance and delay as inputs. Red boxes highlight the inline code being extracted, and pink boxes highlight the parameters being added.

title: Function Signatures/Prototypes
summary: Explains how functions are treated as blackboxes with a name, input parameters, and return value, and introduces the concept of function signatures/prototypes in C/C++.
main_text: We think of a function as a blackbox (don't know or care how it does the task internally) of code where we can provide inputs and get back a value. Or think of it as a web-app (or form) where you supply data to 'named' inputs and get back a value. In C/C++, a function has: A name. Zero or more input parameters. 0 or 1 return (output) values. We only specify the type. 0 return values is indicated with void type. The signature (or prototype) of a function specifies these aspects so others know how to 'call' the function. Example: int max(int a, int b); This is the Function Signature/Prototype for a max function that takes two integer inputs and returns an integer.
notes_text: The web form analogy (shown as a 'Max' form with fields a and b and a Submit button) helps students understand that functions take named inputs and produce output, similar to submitting a form.

images.description: A web form mockup labeled 'Max' with two input fields 'a:' and 'b:' and a Submit button, illustrating the analogy between a function and a web form that takes named inputs.

A 3D blackbox diagram showing a box labeled 'max' with two blue input spheres labeled 'a' and 'b' entering from the top and a green output triangle emerging from the right side, representing the function as a blackbox that takes inputs and produces output.

title: Common Functions: pow and rand
summary: Introduces two common C/C++ library functions: pow (raise to power from cmath) and rand (generate random number from cstdlib), with their signatures and blackbox diagrams.
main_text: pow function: Signature: double pow(double base, double exponent); From the cmath library. Raise to power: Returns base raised to the power exponent, i.e. base^exponent. Available since C90, C99, C++98, C++11. rand function: Signature: int rand(void); From the <cstdlib> library. Generate random number: Returns a pseudo-random integral number in the range between 0 and RAND_MAX. This number is generated by an algorithm that returns a sequence of apparently non-related numbers each time it is called. This algorithm uses a seed to generate the series, which should be initialized to some distinctive value using function srand. Both functions are shown with blackbox diagrams: pow takes two inputs (base and exp) and produces base^exp as output. rand takes no inputs and produces a random integer as output.
notes_text: These are among the first library functions students will use. The pow function requires #include <cmath> and rand requires #include <cstdlib>. The srand function is used to seed the random number generator.

images.description: Two blackbox diagrams side by side. Left: a box labeled 'pow' with two blue input spheres labeled 'base' and 'exp' on top and a green output sphere labeled 'base^exp' on the right. Right: a box labeled 'rand' with no inputs and a green output triangle labeled 'Random integer' on the right.

title: Functional Programming Exercises
summary: Practice converting arithmetic expressions into nested function calls using fictitious add, sub, mul, and div functions to build understanding of function call evaluation order.
main_text: While we can write arithmetic expressions directly in C++, let's practice using functions to perform the same operations. Suppose you are given: int add(int p, int q); // returns p+q. int sub(int p, int q); // returns p-q. int mul(int p, int q); // returns p*q. int div(int p, int q); // returns p/q. Convert the following expressions to use functions and no operators (+, -, *, /). Example: // Add 3 numbers: a = x + y + z; // which upholds the order of ops: a = add(add(x,y),z); or a = add(x,add(y,z));. Exercise 1: a = x / y + y * z - x; Answer: a = _____ (blank for student to fill in). Exercise 2: a = x * (y - z) / z; Answer: a = _____ (blank for student to fill in). Key Ideas: Execution works from inside to outside (i.e. f(g(x)) invokes g(x) first). The return value of a function is substituted and used in the larger expression. Disclaimer: These functions (add, sub, etc.) are fictitious and in C++ we just use the +, -, etc. operators, but this is to practice using functions.
notes_text: This exercise helps students understand nested function calls and evaluation order. The key insight is that inner function calls are evaluated first, and their return values replace the function call in the expression.

title: Function Call Statements
summary: Demonstrates how to call functions in C++ code, emphasizing that return values must be saved or used immediately or they are lost.
main_text: Reminder that you can call a function anywhere. Result is replaced into bigger expression. Take care to 'save' the result. If you don't save the return value into a variable or use it immediately, the result is lost. Example code: #include <iostream> #include <cmath> #include <algorithm> using namespace std; int main() { // can call functions // in an assignment double res = cos(0); // res = 1.0 // can call functions in an // expression X sqrt(2) / 2; // forgot to save result (marked with X as an error) res = sqrt(2) / 2; // save 1.414/2 in res cout << max(34, 56) << endl; // outputs 56 return 0; } Reference: http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/
notes_text: The red X on 'sqrt(2) / 2;' highlights a common beginner mistake: calling a function and performing computation without assigning the result to a variable. The value is computed but immediately discarded.

title: Reading Documentation
summary: Emphasizes the importance of reading library function documentation and provides links to key C++ reference pages for cmath, cctype, and cstdlib.
main_text: Much of programming is calling other library functions which do small pieces of work in an effort to accomplish the overall application. Learn to read documentation. Documentation at: http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/ (math functions like pow, sqrt, cos, sin, etc.). http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cctype/ (character type functions like isalpha, isdigit, toupper, tolower, etc.). http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cstdlib/ (general purpose functions like rand, srand, abs, atoi, etc.).
notes_text: Students should bookmark these reference pages. Being able to look up function signatures, parameters, and return types from documentation is a critical programming skill.

title: Solutions Section Divider

main_text: SOLUTIONS

title: Functional Programming Exercises - Solutions
summary: Provides the solutions to the functional programming exercises, showing how to convert arithmetic expressions into nested function calls.
main_text: While we can write arithmetic expressions directly in C++, let's practice using functions to perform the same operations. Suppose you are given: add(p, q) // returns p+q. sub(p, q) // returns p-q. mul(p, q) // returns p*q. div(p, q) // returns p/q. Convert the following expressions to use functions and no operators (+, -, *, /). Example: // Add 3 numbers: a = x + y + z; a = add(add(x,y),z); a = add(x,add(y,z));. Exercise 1 Solution: a = x / y + y * z - x; a = sub(add(div(x,y),mul(y,z)),x);. Exercise 2 Solution: a = x * (y - z) / z; a = div(mul(x, sub(y,z)), z);. Key Ideas: Execution works from inside to outside (i.e. f(g(x)) invokes g(x) first). The return value of a function is substituted and used in the larger expression. Disclaimer: These functions (add, sub, etc.) are fictitious and in C++ we just use the +, -, etc. operators, but this is to practice using functions.
notes_text: Exercise 1 breakdown: x/y becomes div(x,y), y*z becomes mul(y,z), those are added with add(), then x is subtracted with sub(). Exercise 2 breakdown: y-z becomes sub(y,z), x*(y-z) becomes mul(x,sub(y,z)), then divided by z with div().

title: Functions Overview
summary: Introduces functions as the unit of code decomposition and abstraction, with definitions of both concepts.
main_text: Functions (aka procedures, procedures, or methods) are the unit of code decomposition and abstraction. Decomposition: Breaking programs into smaller units of code. Abstraction: Generalizing an action or concept without specifying how the details are implemented. A Map Service example demonstrates function decomposition: ValidateInputs(), RetrieveMap(), GetOverlayData(), Render(), Publish(). Each function handles one part of the overall task. The map of Los Angeles illustrates the end result of abstraction where users interact with a high-level interface without knowing the implementation details.
notes_text: The Map Service example shows how a complex program is broken into discrete, named steps.

images.description: A diagram showing a Map Service broken into five sequential functions: ValidateInputs(), RetrieveMap(), GetOverlayData(), Render(), and Publish(), labeled as Function Decomposition. Below is a map of Los Angeles showing traffic overlay as an example of the final abstracted output.

title: Function Signatures/Prototypes
summary: Explains functions as black boxes with a name, parameters, and return value, and introduces the concept of a function signature or prototype.
main_text: We think of a function as a blackbox (don't know how it does the task internally) where we can provide inputs and get back a value. A function has: A name. Zero or more input parameters. 0 or 1 return (output) values - We only specify the type. The signature (or prototype) of a function specifies these aspects so others know how to 'call' the function. Example: int max(int a, int b); This is the Function Signature/Prototype showing the return type (int), function name (max), and two parameters (int a, int b).
notes_text: The black box analogy is key: callers only need to know the signature, not the implementation.

images.description: A 3D black box diagram representing the max function. Two inputs labeled 'a' and 'b' enter from the top, the box is labeled 'max', and one output exits to the right, illustrating the function as a black box with inputs and an output.

title: User Defined Functions
summary: Describes the three steps to create user-defined functions: declare (prototype), define (implementation), and call.
main_text: We can define our own functions in 3 steps. Step 1: 'Declare' your function by placing the prototype (signature) at the top of your code. Step 2: 'Define' the function (actual code implementation) anywhere (above or below main()) by placing the code in { }. Step 3: 'Call' the function from main() or another function passing in desired inputs and using the return value (output). Example code: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int max(int a, int b); // prototype. int main() { int x, y, mx; cin >> x >> y; /* Code for main */ } int max(int a, int b) { if(a > b) return a; // immediately stops max. else return b; // immediately stops max. }
notes_text: The return statement immediately exits the function, returning the specified value to the caller.

images.description: A 3D black box diagram of the max function with inputs a and b and one output, alongside the function signature int max(int a, int b);

title: Calling a Function (1)
summary: Explains how to correctly call a function, including argument mapping and common mistakes to avoid.
main_text: We 'call' or 'invoke' the function by: Using its name and place variables or constants that the current function has declared in the order that we want them to map to the parameter/argument list. First variable listed (x) will map to the first parameter (a) in the function's argument list, the second variable (y) to the second parameter (b), etc. Don't: Relist the return type in the call. Relist the type of the arguments. Use variable names that don't exist in the current function. Forget to save the returned value. Correct call: mx = max(x, y); Bad examples (marked with X): mx = int max(x, y); mx = max(int x, int y); mx = max(a, b); max(x, y); The function definition: int max(int a, int b) { if(a > b) return a; else return b; }
notes_text: Common beginner mistakes include re-specifying types in the call or using parameter names from the function definition instead of local variables.

title: Calling a Function (2)
summary: Demonstrates that functions can be called multiple times from anywhere in code, and explains the semantics of a function call.
main_text: We can 'call' (activate/invoke) our function from any other location in our code as many times as we like. Semantics of a function call: Pause the caller code (i.e. main). Pass copies of the arguments to the function (i.e. pass a copy of x and y to a and b). Let the function execute. When the function completes we return back to the caller (i.e. main) and resume execution. Any return value is substituted in place of the function call. Example with user input -5 7: int mx = 1 + max(x, y); // call max. cout << mx << endl; cout << max(0, x) << endl; // call max. Program Output (if user types -5 7): 8 and 0.
notes_text: The expression 1 + max(x,y) shows that a function call can appear inside a larger expression; the return value replaces the call.

title: Execution Timeline
summary: Traces the step-by-step execution timeline of a program with function calls, showing how control flows between main and the called function.
main_text: We always start at main() and execute sequentially until a function call or the end of main(). When we hit a function call, execution of main pauses and execution of max begins. Max will compare the arguments and return the bigger. Upon return we go back to where we left off in the previous function and replace the function call with the return value. We continue to evaluate the expression in which the function call was made (i.e. 1 + max). We assign the result to mx. We continue sequentially until another function call or until the end of main(). Another function call again causes main to pause and max begins execution anew. Max compares arguments. It then returns to the caller (main) and substitutes its return value in the larger expression. Numbered execution steps shown in code: 1-int x,y,mx; 2-cout<<max(0,x); 3-if(a>b) first call; 4-return value; 5-7 value assigned; 6-int mx=1+max(x,y); 7-cout<<mx; 8-end; 9-if(a>b) second call; 10-return. Program Output: 8 and 0.
notes_text: The numbered annotations on the code trace show the non-linear execution order when functions are called.

images.description: The code listing has numbered circles (1 through 10) and arrows showing the order of execution jumping from main into the max function and back, illustrating how control flow transfers during function calls.

title: Why Functions? (1)
summary: Motivates the need for functions by showing duplicated code that prints triangles of different sizes.
main_text: Desired Program Output: /// // / ///// //// /// // /. The code without functions has duplicated logic: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int main() { // Print a triangle of 3 rows for(int i=0; i < 3; i++){ for(int k=0; k < 3-i; k++){ cout << '/'; } cout << endl; } // Print a triangle of 5 rows for(int i=0; i < 5; i++){ for(int k=0; k < 5-i; k++){ cout << '/'; } cout << endl; } return 0; }. Functions are best use to perform code that would otherwise have to be duplicated. By 'factoring' common code into its own function and possibly parameterizing it we can make flexible, reusable blocks of code.
notes_text: This slide sets up the motivation for the refactored version on the next slide.

title: Why Functions? (2)
summary: Shows the refactored version of the triangle-printing code using a parameterized printTri function to eliminate duplication.
main_text: Desired Program Output: /// // / ///// //// /// // /. Refactored code using a function: #include <iostream> using namespace std; void printTri(int rows); int main() { printTri(3); printTri(5); return 0; } void printTri(int rows) { for(int i=0; i < rows; i++){ for(int k=0; k < rows-i; k++){ cout << '/'; } cout << endl; } }. Here we have factored the common code into its own function parameterized based on how many rows are desired.
notes_text: Compare with the previous slide to see how duplication was eliminated by extracting a function with a parameter.

title: Functions Calling Functions (1)
summary: Demonstrates how one user-defined function can call another, with printTri calling printRow.
main_text: We could create 1 or 2 functions to do this job (probably could all be done in printTri but we want you to see how one function can call another). Anytime a function calls another, the caller pauses and the called function begins. When a function ends it returns to the previous function (the one that called it). Code example: #include <iostream> using namespace std; void printRow(int n); // prototype. void printTri(int rows); // prototype. int main() { printTri(3); printTri(5); return 0; } void printTri(int rows) { for(int i=0; i < rows; i++){ printRow(rows-i); } } void printRow(int n) { for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << '/'; } cout << endl; }. Program Output: /// // / ///// //// /// // /.
notes_text: Red arrows in the code show the call chain: main calls printTri, which calls printRow, which returns to printTri, which returns to main.

images.description: Red arrows in the code trace the call flow from main to printTri to printRow and back, showing how functions can call other functions in a chain.

title: Functions Calling Functions (2)
summary: Extends the example by adding a printRect function and generalizing printRow with a fill character parameter.
main_text: We could create 1 or 2 functions to do this job (probably could all be done in printTri but we want you to see how one function can call another). Anytime a function calls another, the caller pauses and the called function begins. When a function ends it returns to the previous function (the one that called it). Extended code with printRect: #include <iostream> using namespace std; void printRow(int n); // prototype. void printTri(int rows); // prototype. void printRect(int r, int c); // prototype. int main() { printTri(3); printRect(5); return 0; } void printTri(int rows) { for(int i=0; i < rows; i++){ printRow(rows-i, '/'); } } void printRect(int r, int c) { for(int i=0; i < r; i++){ printRow(c, '/'); } } void printRow(int n, char fill) { for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cout << fill; } cout << endl; }. Program Output: /// // / ///// //// /// // /.
notes_text: printRow is now more general, accepting a fill character, showing how parameterization increases reuse across printTri and printRect.

title: Two Sets of Argument Names
summary: Section divider introducing the concept of formal and actual parameters in function calls.
main_text: Formal and Actual Parameters. Two Sets of Argument Names. This section covers the distinction between the names used inside a function definition (formal parameters) and the names used when calling the function (actual arguments).

title: Argument Names
summary: Uses a play/movie casting analogy to explain the difference between character names (formal parameters) and actor names (actual arguments).
main_text: A script (play or movie) could be produced in many different places each with different casts (actual actors and actresses). Thus, the script is written in terms of character names but when the cast is chosen, actual people's names are mapped/substituted. In the play, everything is setup to use the character names (the audience wouldn't know what's going on if they use the actresses real name). Before or after the play, people's actual (real) names are used to refer to people. The same thing happens with arguments passed to a function. A Julius Caesar cast list is shown with two columns: character names (like Casca/Octavius' Soldier, Julius Caesar, Portia/Octavius' Soldier, etc.) and real actor names (like Alexis Lagon, Alec Mallmann, Maddie Baylor, etc.).
notes_text: This analogy helps explain why function parameters have their own names independent of the caller's variable names.

images.description: A cast list table for Julius Caesar showing character names in the left column (Casca/Octavius' Soldier, Julius Caesar, etc.) mapped to actor names in the right column (Alexis Lagon, Alec Mallmann, etc.), illustrating the analogy between character names (formal parameters) and real names (actual arguments).

title: Formal and Actual Argument Names
summary: Defines formal and actual argument names precisely, using the play analogy and a mypow function example.
main_text: In the analogy, the play is a function. Formal argument name (character names): The names used INSIDE the function code which act as a placeholder to know which input is which. When taking the power would pow(x,y) give the same result as pow(y,x)? No! So we need to know which input is the base and which is the exponent...formal argument names help us know that. Actual argument names (names of the actors): The actual values and variables in the calling function that they want to pass or map to the functions formal arguments. Example: // prototype double mypow(double base, int exp); int main() { double x=2, y=3; // actual args double result1 = mypow(x,y); double result2 = mypow(y,2); ... } // formal args double mypow(double base, int exp) { . . . }. Formal Arguments (character names) vs Actual Arguments (real names).
notes_text: The pow(x,y) vs pow(y,x) example demonstrates why parameter order and naming matter.

images.description: A partial cast list from Julius Caesar reused to reinforce the analogy between character names (formal parameters) and actor names (actual arguments), with labels Formal Arguments (character names) and Actual Arguments (real names).

title: Mapping Formals to Actuals
summary: Explains how actual arguments are mapped to formal parameters by position when a function is called.
main_text: When we call a function, the ACTUAL arguments are assigned into the FORMAL arguments. Ex: formal = actual; The mapping is just based on the ORDER we list the formals in the function signature and the ORDER we list the actuals when we call the function. The first formal is assigned the first actual. The second formal is assigned the second actual. The third formal is assigned the third actual. And so on. Each time we call the function we can use a different set of 'actresses' (i.e. different actuals for each call). Code example: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototype double mypow(double base, int exp); int main() { double x; int y; cin >> x >> y; // actual args double result1 = mypow(x,y); double result2 = mypow(y,2); ... } // Playbill for 1st call: base = x; exp = y; // Playbill for 2nd call: base = y; exp = 2; // formal args double mypow(double base, int exp) { int result = 1; for( ; exp != 0; exp--){ result *= base; } return result; }
notes_text: The 'Playbill' annotations show the concrete assignment of actuals to formals for each separate function call.

title: Variable Scope
summary: Introduces variable scope concepts including global and local variables, their visibility and lifetime.
main_text: 'Scope' of a variable refers to the Visibility (who can access it) and Lifetime of a variable (how long is the memory reserved). For now, there are 2 scopes we will learn. Global: Variables are declared outside of any function and are visible to all the code/functions in the program. For various reasons, it is 'bad' practice to use global variables. You MAY NOT use them in CS 102. Local: Variables are declared inside the { } in a function and are only visible in those { } and die when the end brace } is reached. Code example: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // Global Variable int x=1; int add_x() { int n; // n is a 'local' variable cin >> n; // y and z NOT visible (in scope) here // but x is since it is global return (n + x); } // n dies here int main() { // y and z are 'local' variables int y=0, z; z = add_x(); y += z / x; // n is NOT visible cout << x << ' ' << y << endl; return 0; } // y and z die here
notes_text: Global variables are discouraged and prohibited in CS102. Local variables exist only within their enclosing braces.

title: Exercises
summary: Section divider slide indicating that exercises follow for practicing the concepts covered.
main_text: Exercises. This section contains practice exercises for writing and using functions.

title: Example Functions 1 - calcInterest
summary: Demonstrates a calcInterest function with three parameters (amount, years, rate) that returns a double, showing prototype, black box diagram, and full code.
main_text: Function Signature/Prototype: double calcInterest(double amt, int yrs, double rate); A black box diagram shows main passing three actual arguments (amount, 30, r) into the calcInterest function which has formal parameters amt, yrs, and rate, and produces an output called interest. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <cmath> using namespace std; // prototype double calcInterest(double amt, int yrs, double rate); int main() { double amount, r; cin >> amount >> r; double interest = calcInterest(amount, 30, r); cout << "Interest: " << interest << endl; return 0; } double calcInterest(double amt, int yrs, double rate) { return amt * pow(rate/12, 12*yrs); }
notes_text: This example shows mixing variables and literal constants as actual arguments in a function call.

images.description: A 3D black box diagram showing three inputs (amount, 30, r) from main flowing into the calcInterest box with formal parameters amt, yrs, rate, and one output labeled interest flowing out.

title: Example Functions 2 - getAndCheckLogin
summary: Shows a bool-returning function that takes a string parameter, prompts for a password, and returns whether it matches.
main_text: Function Signature/Prototype: bool getAndCheckLogin(string exp_pwd); A black box diagram shows main passing 'pass' (which holds "Open123!") into the getAndCheckLogin function with formal parameter exp_pwd, and the function outputs a bool value called valid. Code example: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototype bool getAndCheckLogin(string exp_pwd); int main() { string pass = "Open123!"; // secret password bool valid; valid = getAndCheckLogin(pass); if(valid == true) { cout << "Success!" << endl; } else { cout << "Password mismatch!" << endl; } return 0; } bool getAndCheckLogin(string exp_pwd) { string pwd; cout << "Enter your password: " << endl; cin >> pwd; return pwd == exp_pwd; }
notes_text: The function encapsulates both user input and comparison logic, returning a boolean result to the caller.

images.description: A 3D black box diagram showing main passing the variable 'pass' (containing Open123!) into the getAndCheckLogin function with formal parameter exp_pwd, outputting a diamond-shaped bool value labeled valid.

title: Example Functions 3 - printLoginResult
summary: Demonstrates a void function that takes a bool parameter and prints a success or failure message without returning a value.
main_text: Function Signature/Prototype: void printLoginResult(bool correct); A black box diagram shows main passing 'valid' into the printLoginResult function with formal parameter correct. The function has no output (void return type). Code example: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototype void printLoginResult(bool correct); int main() { string pass = "Open123!"; // secret password bool valid; valid = getAndCheckLogin(pass); printLoginResult(valid); return 0; } void printLoginResult(bool correct) { if(correct == true) { cout << "Success!" << endl; } else { cout << "Password mismatch!" << endl; } }
notes_text: This void function demonstrates that not all functions need to return a value; some just perform an action like printing output.

images.description: A 3D black box diagram showing main passing the variable 'valid' into the printLoginResult function with formal parameter correct. No output arrow exits the box, illustrating a void function.

title: Example Functions 4 - genCoinFlip
summary: Shows a function with no parameters that returns a bool, demonstrating a zero-input function using random number generation.
main_text: Function Signature/Prototype: bool genCoinFlip(); A black box diagram shows main calling genCoinFlip with no inputs. The function outputs a diamond-shaped bool value labeled heads. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <cstdlib> using namespace std; // prototype bool genCoinFlip(); int main() { bool heads; heads = genCoinFlip(); if(heads == true) { cout << "Heads!" << endl; } else { cout << "Tails!" << endl; } return 0; } bool genCoinFlip() { int r = rand(); // Generate random integer return (r%2) == 1; }
notes_text: This example shows that functions can have zero parameters. The rand() function from cstdlib is used internally.

images.description: A 3D black box diagram showing main calling genCoinFlip with no inputs entering the box, and one diamond-shaped bool output labeled heads exiting the box.

title: Predicate Functions
summary: Introduces predicate functions that return bool to assert or confirm something about input, usable in if-conditions and loops.
main_text: We can write functions that return a bool (true or false) to assert or confirm something about the input. These functions can then be called in the condition of an if statement or a loop. Examples: bool isNegative(double x) { return x < 0; } bool isDigit(char c) { return (c >= '0' && c <= '9'); } bool _________(int s1, int s2, int s3, int s4) { return (s1 == s2) && (s2 == s3) && (s3 == s4); } int main() { int a; char b; int f, g, y, z; cin >> a >> b >> f >> g >> y >> z; if( isNegative(a) ) { cout << "Error..neg. #" << endl; } if( isDigit(b) ) { cout << "digit character" << endl; } if( (f==g) && (g == y) && (y == z) ) { cout << "Yes..._________" << endl; } return 0; }
notes_text: The blank function name is likely an exercise for students to fill in. Predicate functions improve readability by giving meaningful names to boolean conditions.

title: Unit 4c - Argument Passing
summary: Title slide introducing the Argument Passing lecture for CS 102 Unit 4c, authored by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 4c - Argument Passing. Mark Redekopp.

title: Unit 4 Overview
summary: Overview of the four course units, positioning Unit 4 (Divide and Conquer / Functional Decomposition) in context of earlier units.
main_text: Unit 1: Scalar processing, aka IPO=Input-Process-Output Programs. Unit 2: Linear (1D) Processing. Unit 3: Multidimensional Processing. Unit 4: Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition). Each unit is illustrated with a diagram showing inputs flowing through a processor to outputs, with increasing complexity from scalar to multidimensional data. Unit 4 shows functions f(x) and g(y) as modular components.
notes_text: This slide provides course roadmap context; Unit 4 focuses on breaking programs into smaller function-based components.

images.description: Four diagrams showing data flow from inputs through a processor to outputs, progressing from single scalar values, to 1D arrays, to 2D arrays, to modular function blocks f(x) and g(y).

title: Argument Passing (Pass-by-Value)
summary: Introduces the pass-by-value concept using the analogy of emailing an attached document, emphasizing that communication is one-way.
main_text: Passing an argument to a function makes a copy of the argument. It is like e-mailing an attached document. You still have the original on your computer. The recipient has a copy which she can modify but it will not be reflected in your version. Communication is essentially one-way. Caller communicates arguments to callee, but callee cannot communicate back because she is working on copies. The only communication back to the caller is via a return value.
notes_text: The email attachment analogy is a key conceptual model: sending an attachment creates an independent copy, just like pass-by-value creates a copy of the argument for the called function.

images.description: Clip art of an email envelope with a paperclip attachment, illustrating the analogy of emailing an attached document.

title: Pass by Value (1)
summary: Demonstrates that function parameters are local copies using a dec() function example, showing the copy mechanism with a visual diagram.
main_text: Fact: Function arguments/parameters act like local variables to that function. They only live as long as the function is executing and then get deallocated. When arguments are passed a copy of the actual argument value (e.g. 3) is given to the function's input argument. So, the function is operating on a copy and that copy only lives as long as the function. Code example: void dec(int); int main() { int y = 3; dec(y); cout << y << endl; return 0; } void dec(int y) { y--; } The output is 3 because dec() modifies its own local copy of y, not main's y. A diagram shows main's y with value 3 being copied to dec's y, which then becomes 2, but main's y remains 3.
notes_text: The key insight is that y in main and y in dec are separate variables. Decrementing y in dec does not affect y in main.

images.description: Diagram showing two platforms representing main() and dec() scopes. Main's y holds value 3, an arrow shows the value being copied to dec's y. Inside dec, y becomes 2, but main's y stays at 3.

title: Pass by Value (2)
summary: Explores the problem that same-named variables in different functions are separate entities and the only way to communicate back is via return.
main_text: Wait! But they have the same name, 'y'. What's in a name...Each function is a separate entity and so two 'y' variables exist (one in main and one in dec to decrement it). The only way to communicate back to main is via return. Try to change the code appropriately. Main Point: Each function is a completely separate 'sandbox' (i.e. is isolated from other functions and their data) and copies of data are passed and returned between them. The code on the right shows blanks to fill in for fixing the dec function to use a return type and for main to capture the return value.
notes_text: This is a fill-in-the-blank exercise slide where students must fix the code to use return values instead of relying on pass-by-value side effects.

title: Pass by Value Solution
summary: Shows the corrected solution where dec() returns the decremented value and main captures it with y = dec(y).
main_text: Wait! But they have the same name, 'y'. What's in a name...Each function is a separate entity and so two 'y' variables exist (one in main and one in dec to decrement it). The only way to communicate back to main is via return. Try to change the code appropriately. Main Point: Each function is a completely separate 'sandbox' (i.e. is isolated from other functions and their data) and copies of data are passed and returned between them. Solution code: int dec(int); int main() { int y = 3; y = dec(y); cout << y << endl; return 0; } int dec(int y) { y--; return y; } Now dec returns int and main captures it with y = dec(y).
notes_text: The solution changes void dec to int dec, adds return y, and main captures the result with y = dec(y). This is the standard pattern for communicating results back from pass-by-value functions.

title: Reminders: Common Mistakes
summary: Lists common mistakes when calling functions: not listing return type in calls, re-listing argument types, and not saving return values.
main_text: Problem 1: Don't list return type when you call a function. It will substitute the return value in place of call. Problem 1: Don't relist the type of the argument when you make the call. Problem 2: Need to save return value. Problem 2: Need to pass a variable that exists in the calling function. Incorrect code: int dec(int val); // prototype int main() { int y = 3; int dec(y); // y = dec(y); cout << y << endl; return 0; } int dec(int val) { val--; return val; } Correct code: int dec(int val); // prototype int main() { int y = 3; y = dec(int val); // y = dec(y); cout << y << endl; return 0; } int dec(int val) { val--; return val; }
notes_text: Two side-by-side code examples show incorrect vs correct function call syntax. The left example incorrectly writes 'int dec(y)' instead of 'y = dec(y)'. The right incorrectly writes 'y = dec(int val)' instead of 'y = dec(y)'.

title: Passing Arrays As Arguments
summary: Explains the syntax for passing arrays to functions: empty brackets in prototype/signature and just the array name when calling.
main_text: Can we pass an array to another function? YES!! Syntax: Step 1: In the prototype/signature: Put empty square brackets after the parameter name if it is an array (e.g. int data[]). Step 2: When you call the function, just provide the name of the array. Code example: // Function that takes an array int sum(int data[], int size); int sum(int data[], int size) { int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { total += data[i]; } return total; } int main() { int vals[100]; /* some code to initialize vals */ int mysum = sum(vals, 100); cout << mysum << endl; // prints sum of all numbers return 0; } Step 1 is annotated at the prototype and definition showing int data[]. Step 2 is annotated at the call showing sum(vals, 100).
notes_text: The two key steps are marked with circled numbers on the code: (1) empty brackets in the parameter declaration, (2) just the array name at the call site.

title: Pass-by-Value & Pass-by-Reference
summary: Compares pass-by-value (emailing an attachment) with pass-by-reference (emailing a link to the original document).
main_text: What are the pros and cons of emailing a document by: Attaching it to the email. Sending a link (URL) to the document on some cloud service (etc. Google Docs). Pass-by-value is like emailing an attachment. A copy is made and sent. Pass-by-reference means emailing a link to the original. No copy is made and any modifications by the other party are seen by the originator.
notes_text: This analogy helps students understand the fundamental difference: attachments are independent copies (pass-by-value), while links provide shared access to the same data (pass-by-reference).

images.description: Email envelope with paperclip icon representing pass-by-value (attachment), and a Google Docs icon representing pass-by-reference (link to original).

title: Arrays And Pass-by-Reference
summary: Explains that scalar variables are passed by value (copies) while arrays are passed by reference (links), so changes to arrays inside functions affect the original.
main_text: Single (scalar) variables are passed-by-value in C/C++. Copies are passed. Arrays are passed-by-reference. Links are passed. This means any change to the array by the function is visible upon return to the caller. Single variables (aka scalars) are passed-by-value but arrays are passed-by-reference. Scalar example: void dec(int); int main() { int y = 3; dec(y); cout << y << endl; return 0; } void dec(int y) { y--; } Array example: void init(int x[], int size); int main() { int data[10]; init(data, 10); cout << data[9] << endl; // prints 0 return 0; } void init(int x[], int size) { // x is really a link to data for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { x[i] = 0; // changing data[i] } }
notes_text: This is a critical distinction in C/C++: scalars get copied, arrays get linked. The init function modifies the original data array through x[].

title: But Why? (Arrays Pass-by-Reference Rationale)
summary: Explains that arrays are passed by reference to avoid copying potentially huge amounts of data, using a warehouse analogy diagram.
main_text: If we used pass-by-value then we'd have to make a copy of a potentially HUGE amount of data (what if the array had a million elements). To avoid copying vast amounts of data, we pass a link. Code example shows int sum(int data[], int size) function that sums array elements and main calling it with sum(vals, 100). A diagram shows main() with a large warehouse labeled vals containing elements [0] through [99], and sum() receiving a reference to the same warehouse through data, plus a return value.
notes_text: The warehouse diagram visually shows that if we copied the warehouse (pass-by-value), it would be extremely wasteful. Instead, we just share the address.

images.description: Diagram showing main() with a large warehouse representing the vals array (addresses 520 to 916, indices [0] to [99]). The sum() function has its own platform with a data reference pointing to the same warehouse, and a return value going back.

title: So What Is Actually Passed?
summary: Reveals that when passing an array, the starting memory address (e.g. 520) is what gets passed, allowing the function to access the original array.
main_text: The 'link' that is passed is just the starting address (e.g. 520) of the array in memory. The called function can now use 520 to access the original array (read it or write new values to it). Code shows sum(int data[], int size) function. Diagram shows main() with vals warehouse at addresses 520-916, and an arrow passing the address 520 to sum()'s data parameter, shown as a small disk holding the value 520. The function uses this address to access the original array.
notes_text: This reveals the underlying mechanism: array names decay to pointers (addresses). The starting address is the actual value passed by value, but it enables pass-by-reference semantics for the array contents.

images.description: Diagram showing main() with the vals array warehouse, and an arrow pointing to sum()'s data parameter which holds address value 520 in a small disk/cylinder, representing the starting address of the array.

title: Analogy (Address Without Size)
summary: Uses house addresses and hotel rooms to illustrate that knowing a starting address does not tell you the size of the block.
main_text: The first house on a certain block of Catalina Ave. has the address 3600. How many houses are on that block? There is no way to know!! We would have to count that separately. Suppose a large family reunion reserves a block of hotel rooms. The first room is number 428. How many rooms are in the reserved block? There is no way to know!! We would have to count that separately.
notes_text: This analogy motivates why array size must be passed as a separate parameter: knowing the starting address alone is insufficient to determine how many elements exist.

metadata.topic: Why Array Size Must Be Passed Separately

title: Arrays in C/C++ vs. Other Languages
summary: Explains that C/C++ requires passing array size separately unlike Java or Python, and shows the size being passed alongside the array address.
main_text: Notice that if sum() only has the start address it would not know how big the array is. Unlike Java, Python or other languages where you can call some function to find the size of an array, C/C++ requires you to track the size yourself in a separate variable and pass it as a secondary argument. Code shows sum(int data[], int size) with size parameter. Diagram shows main() passing both the address 520 and the value 100 (size) to sum(), which receives them as data and size parameters respectively, alongside the return value.
notes_text: This is a key difference between C/C++ and higher-level languages. Students coming from Python or Java need to adjust to manually tracking array sizes.

images.description: Diagram showing main() passing both the array starting address (520) and size (100) as two separate values to sum()'s data and size parameters.

title: Why Don't We Return Arrays from Functions
summary: Explains that arrays do not need to be returned from functions because pass-by-reference means the original array is already modified in place.
main_text: In C++, we generally do NOT return arrays from a function...because we do NOT need to! WHY? Because we modified the original array in the function. Code example shows a fill function that initializes array elements: int[] fill(int data[], int size); is crossed out and replaced with void fill(int data[], int size); The function void fill(int data[], int size) { for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { data[i] = i; } } modifies the original array. int main() { int vals[100]; /* some code to initialize vals */ fill(vals, 100); cout << vals[0] << endl; // prints sum of all numbers return 0; } Diagram shows main() passing address 520 and size 100 to fill(), which modifies the original array directly.
notes_text: Since arrays are passed by reference, the fill function writes directly to the original array in main. No return is needed because the changes are already visible to the caller.

images.description: Diagram showing main() passing array address (520) and size (100) to fill(), which modifies the original array data directly without needing to return it.

title: Array Passing Summary
summary: Summarizes array passing syntax, the need to pass size separately, and notes that C++ std::vector is an alternative learned later.
main_text: Syntax: In the prototype/signature: Put empty square brackets after the parameter name if it is an array (e.g. void f1(int data[])). When you call the function, just provide the name of the array (e.g. f1(data);). Functions only know what you pass them. You must pass the size of the array as an additional parameter in addition to the link to the array. Arrays are passed-by-reference meaning no copy is made and changes by a function are actually being made to the original. The C++ std:: library provides some alternatives to 'plain-old arrays' (like vectors), but you will learn about these in CS 103/104 and should not use them in CS 102.
notes_text: This is a key summary slide. Students should memorize: empty brackets in declaration, array name only in call, always pass size, changes affect original.

title: Tips for Coding Functions (Section Divider)
summary: Section divider slide introducing tips for coding functions as modular units.
main_text: Functions as modular units. TIPS FOR CODING FUNCTIONS.

title: Tips for Coding Functions
summary: Advises looking for repeated code to factor into functions, turning differing values into parameters, and passing needed variables as arguments.
main_text: Look for common, repeated code and factor it out as a function. Find differences in data values or constants that are used and turn those into parameters. Any variables the code uses must be passed in as arguments. A value used after the code must be returned as the return value. If you can carve out several lines of code that perform one logical task, consider pulling those lines out as a function.
notes_text: This is practical advice for identifying when and how to extract functions from existing code.

title: Finding Functions (Example)
summary: Shows a before/after example of extracting a printFlag function from duplicated nested loop code that prints triangular flag patterns.
main_text: Before (without function): #include <iostream> using namespace std; int main() { // Print flag of 3 rows for(int i=0; i < 3; i++) { for(int k=0; k < 3-i; k++) { cout << '/'; } cout << endl; } // Print flag of 5 rows for(int i=0; i < 5; i++) { for(int k=0; k < 5-i; k++) { cout << '/'; } cout << endl; } return 0; } After (with function): #include <iostream> using namespace std; void printFlag(int rows); int main() { printFlag(3); printFlag(5); return 0; } void printFlag(int rows) { for(int i=0; i < rows; i++) { for(int k=0; k < rows-i; k++) { cout << '/'; } cout << endl; } } The constant 3 and 5 become the parameter rows.
notes_text: This example demonstrates the process: identify duplicate code, find what differs (the number 3 vs 5), make that difference a parameter, and extract the common code into a function.

title: Functions As Independent Units (1)
summary: Emphasizes that functions should be self-contained, using generic parameter names and returning values rather than accessing external variables.
main_text: Functions should be self contained units. Cannot access variables from other functions. Should implement a general 'recipe' for how to do a task given generic inputs (parameter names). Consider the arguments/parameters as generic names that represent specific inputs when the function is invoked. Remember: Functions can only access: The input arguments. The local variables they declare. Functions can only return one value. All other values (local variables & input arguments) 'die' at the end of the function. Incorrect code (doesn't work): void getInput(); // prototype void getInput() { cout << "Enter an int: "; cin >> x; // Can't access x from main } int main() { int x; // get from user getInput(); cout << x << endl; return 0; } Correct code (does work): int getInput(); // prototype int getInput() { int num; cout << "Enter an int: "; cin >> num; return num; } int main() { int x; // get from user x = getInput(); cout << x << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: The incorrect version tries to access main's x variable from getInput, which is impossible. The correct version declares its own local variable, returns it, and main captures the return value.

title: Functions As Independent Units (2)
summary: Shows a well-designed max function that takes inputs and returns output, easily composable for finding max of 3 numbers.
main_text: Generally, don't do input/output in a function (unless the function specifically indicates it should)...just process values and return something. Example: Take the maximum of 2 numbers and print them out. Easy to extend to other tasks: take max of 3 numbers. Good function decomposition; generic, easy to reuse: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int max(int a, int b); int main() { int x, y, mx; cin >> x >> y; cout << max(x,y) << endl; return 0; } int max(int a, int b) { if(a > b) return a; else return b; } Extended to take max of 3 numbers: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int max(int a, int b); int main() { int x, y, z, mx; cin >> x >> y >> z; cout << max(max(x,y), z) << endl; return 0; } int max(int a, int b) { if(a > b) return a; else return b; } Challenge: Could you extend to take the max of 4?
notes_text: Good decomposition separates I/O from processing. The max function is composable: max(max(x,y),z) finds the max of 3 numbers by nesting calls.

title: A Question (Modularity Analogy)
summary: Uses an interlocking brick (LEGO) analogy to ask which set of pieces is more useful: one large specialized piece or several smaller reusable ones.
main_text: Which is a more useful set of interlocking brick (you know the name) pieces? The slide shows two options: on the left, one large L-shaped LEGO piece; on the right, several smaller standard LEGO pieces of various sizes. The smaller, modular pieces are more versatile and can be combined in many ways.
notes_text: This analogy reinforces the principle that smaller, reusable functions (like smaller LEGO bricks) are more versatile than large, monolithic ones.

images.description: Two sets of yellow LEGO bricks: left side shows one large L-shaped specialized piece, right side shows several smaller standard bricks of varying sizes that can be combined in multiple ways.

title: Functions As Independent Units (3) - Bad Decomposition
summary: Shows examples of bad function decomposition where I/O is embedded inside the function, making it non-reusable and non-composable.
main_text: Generally, don't do input/output in a function (unless the function specifically indicates it will)...just process values and return something. Example: Take the maximum of 2 numbers and print them out. Easy to extend to other tasks: take max of 3 numbers. Bad function decomposition -- performs I/O (version 1): int max(); int main() { int mx; mx = max(); cout << mx << endl; return 0; } int max() { int x, y; cin >> x >> y; if(x > y) return x; else return y; } This code works for the stated task (output max of 2 inputs) but cannot easily be reused for 3 or more numbers! Can't do: max(max()); Would cin 4 numbers, doesn't take in an input. Bad function decomposition -- performs I/O (version 2): void max(int a, int b); int main() { cin >> x >> y; max(x, y); return 0; } void max(int a, int b) { if(a > b) cout << a << endl; else cout << b << endl; } This code works for the stated task (output max of 2 inputs) but cannot easily be reused for 3 or more numbers! Can't do: max(max(x,y),z); Would cout 2 values.
notes_text: Both bad examples embed I/O into the function, preventing reuse. The LEGO brick analogy from the previous slide applies: these are large specialized pieces that cannot be recombined.

images.description: Small LEGO brick icons showing the metaphor of large specialized pieces (bad) vs small reusable pieces (good), reinforcing the modularity message.

title: Exercises (Section Divider)
summary: Section divider slide introducing the exercises section of the lecture.
main_text: EXERCISES.

title: Tracing Exercise 1
summary: A code tracing exercise asking students to order execution of lines and track the value of char 'c' across multiple function scopes.
main_text: Order It: The numbers below represent lines of code in the program to the right. Order the lines of code from 1-8 [1=first to get executed / 8=last to be executed]. Note: Order them when they START execution not when they finish execution. Blanks for lines: ___ 5, ___ 6, ___ 7, ___ 8, ___ 13, ___ 20, ___ 26, ___ 27. Scope It: Notice that there are many 'char c' declarations and parameters. List the value of the character 'c' (or N/A if no possible value for 'c' exists) just BEFORE the following lines of code get executed: ___ 6, ___ 8, ___ 13, ___ 14, ___ 20, ___ 21, ___ 27. Code: // Assume necessary prototypes have been declared for Q2 and Q3. 1 int main() 2 { 3 double f=1.0, g=2.0, h=3.0; 4 int x=5, y=6, z=7; 5 char c='U'; 6 x = myfunc(); 7 f=doit(x,y,c); 8 } 10 double doit(int cat, int dog, char c) 11 { 12 double x = (double) cat; 13 c = 'S'; 14 x = x / (double) dog; 15 return x; 16 } 18 void yourfunc(char c) 19 { 20 c = 'C'; 21 return; 22 } 24 int myfunc() 25 { 26 yourfunc('!'); 27 return 2; 28 }
notes_text: This exercise tests understanding of execution order across function calls and variable scoping (each function has its own 'c').

title: Exercises List
summary: Lists four practice exercises for students: extract-method1, draw-square, is-lower-vowel, and is-vowel.
main_text: Exercises: extract-method1, draw-square, is-lower-vowel, is-vowel.
notes_text: These are coding exercises students should complete to practice function extraction and argument passing.

title: Breaking Code Into Functions and Calling Them (Section Divider)
summary: Section divider slide introducing more exercises on breaking code into functions and calling them.
main_text: More Exercises. BREAKING CODE INTO FUNCTIONS AND CALLING THEM.

title: Factoring Code / Extracting Functions
summary: Describes the approach for refactoring code into functions: identify blocks that perform one task, name them accordingly, and use generic parameter names.
main_text: At this point, we should be able to go back to any program or exercise and 'refactor' our code into functions (aka 'extracting' functions). Approach: If a block of code performs one main task, you can try to extract that code as a function whose name matches that task description. Argument names in the function DON'T have to match the name used in the calling function (but they can).
notes_text: This slide sets up the methodology for the following extraction examples.

title: Extracting Functions Example
summary: Demonstrates extracting a find() function from a linear search in main, showing before and after code with the extracted function highlighted.
main_text: Before (all in main): int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task cin >> val; bool found = false; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { if(val == data[i]) { cout << i << endl; found = true; break; } } if(!found) { cout << -1 << endl; } return 0; } After (with extracted find function): #include <iostream> using namespace std; int find(int nums[], int len, int target); int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task cin >> val; int loc = find(data, n, val); cout << loc << endl; return 0; } int find(int nums[], int len, int target) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { if(target == nums[i]) { return i; } } return -1; } Here, we extract the code to find an element. Can you see another function that might be worth extracting?
notes_text: The find function is highlighted with a pink box in the after code. The hint at the bottom suggests the array input code could also be extracted.

title: Extracting Another Function
summary: Shows further extraction of a fill_n() function that handles reading array size and elements from input, in addition to the previously extracted find().
main_text: Before (with find already extracted): #include <iostream> using namespace std; int find(int nums[], int len, int target); int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task cin >> val; int loc = find(data, n, val); cout << loc << endl; return 0; } int find(int nums[], int len, int target) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { if(target == nums[i]) { return i; } } return -1; } After (with fill_n also extracted): #include <iostream> using namespace std; int fill_n(int nums[]); int find(int nums[], int len, int target); int main() { // setup array with data int n, val, data[100]; n = fill_n(data); // now perform the given task cin >> val; int loc = find(data, n, val); cout << loc << endl; return 0; } int fill_n(int nums[]) { int n; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> nums[i]; } return n; } int find(int nums[], int len, int target) { . . . } The fill_n function reads n, fills the array, and returns n. Both the array input block and the data variable declaration are highlighted.
