notes_text: fill_n takes the array by reference (so it can fill it), reads n from cin, fills elements, and returns n. This demonstrates extracting a second logical block from the same program.

title: Exercises To Refactor Using Functions
summary: Lists exercises to practice refactoring code into functions, organized by category: array tasks, nested loops, homework, and other examples.
main_text: Array Tasks: Unique, Unique-one, Insert-sorted, Remove-first, Remove-all, Max-To-Last (use to sort?). Nested Loops: etox_range. HW: Grid, Priority. Other examples: Prime Range, Count digits in number.
notes_text: These exercises range from simple array operations to more complex algorithms, all meant to be refactored using functions.

title: Solutions (Section Divider)
summary: Section divider slide introducing the solutions section.
main_text: SOLUTIONS.

title: Tracing Exercise 1 (Solution)
summary: Provides the solution for the tracing exercise, showing execution order and the value of 'c' at each specified line.
main_text: Order It solution: __1__ 5, __2__ 6, __6__ 7, __8__ 8, __7__ 13, __4__ 20, __3__ 26, __5__ 27. Execution order: Line 5 is first (1), line 6 calls myfunc (2), inside myfunc line 26 calls yourfunc (3), inside yourfunc line 20 executes (4), then line 27 in myfunc returns (5), back in main line 7 calls doit (6), inside doit line 13 executes (7), finally line 8 in main is last (8). Scope It solution: List the value of char 'c' just BEFORE the following lines execute: __'U'__ 6 (main's c='U' set on line 5), __'U'__ 8 (main's c unchanged), __'U'__ 13 (doit's c parameter received 'U' from main), __'S'__ 14 (doit's c changed to 'S' on line 13), __'!'__ 20 (yourfunc's c parameter received '!'), __'C'__ 21 (yourfunc's c changed to 'C' on line 20), __N/A__ 27 (myfunc has no char c variable in scope). Code is the same as the exercise slide.
notes_text: Key takeaway: each function has its own copy of 'c'. Changing c in doit or yourfunc does not affect main's c because of pass-by-value. Line 27 has no 'c' in scope at all (myfunc doesn't declare or receive one).

title: Solutions - Unique
summary: Shows a complete solution for checking if all elements in an array are unique, using fill_n, count, and unique_all helper functions.
main_text: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototypes int fill_n(int nums[]); int count(int data[], int len, int target); bool unique_all(int data[], int len); int fill_n(int nums[]) { int n; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> nums[i]; } return n; } int count(int data[], int len, int target) { int cnt = 0; for(int k=0; k < len; k++) { if(data[k] == target) { cnt++; } } return cnt; } bool unique_all(int data[], int len) { for(int j=0; j < len; j++) { int cnt = count(data, len, data[j]); if(cnt > 1) { return false; } } return true; } int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; n = fill_n(data); // now perform the given task bool allUnique = unique_all(data, n); if(allUnique) { cout << "All unique" << endl; } else { cout << "Not all unique" << endl; } return 0; }
notes_text: unique_all checks each element by counting its occurrences. If any element appears more than once, it returns false. This demonstrates function composition: unique_all calls count, and main calls fill_n and unique_all.

title: Solutions - Unique-One
summary: Shows a solution for finding the first element that appears exactly once in an array, using count and unique_one functions.
main_text: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototype int fill_n(int nums[]); int count(int data[], int len, int target); int unique_one(int data[], int len); int fill_n(int nums[]) { int n; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> nums[i]; } return n; } int count(int data[], int len, int target) { int cnt = 0; for(int k=0; k < len; k++) { if(data[k] == target) { cnt++; } } return cnt; } int unique_one(int data[], int len) { for(int j=0; j < len; j++) { int cnt = count(data, len, data[j]); if(cnt == 1) { return data[j]; } } return -1; } int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; n = fill_n(data); // now perform the given task int unique = unique_one(data, n); cout << unique << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: unique_one returns the first element whose count is exactly 1, or -1 if no such element exists. It reuses the same count function from the Unique solution.

title: Solutions - Insert-Sorted
summary: Shows a solution for inserting a value into a sorted array using findFirstLarger, shiftOneRightFrom, and printResults functions.
main_text: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int findFirstLarger(int data[], int len, int val) { for(int k=0; k < len; k++) { if(data[k] > val) { return k; } } return len; } void shiftOneRightFrom(int data[], int len, int fromIndex) { for(int curr = len-1; curr >= fromIndex; curr--) { data[curr+1] = data[curr]; } } void printResults(int data[], int len) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; } int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val; cin >> val; if(n < 100) { int loc = findFirstLarger(data, n, val); shiftOneRightFrom(data, n, loc); data[loc] = val; n++; } else { cout << "No room" << endl; } // Output the results printResults(data, n); return 0; }
notes_text: Three functions work together: findFirstLarger locates where to insert, shiftOneRightFrom makes room by shifting elements right, then the value is placed at the found location. Checks for array capacity before inserting.

title: Solutions - RemoveFirst
summary: Shows a solution for removing the first occurrence of a value from an array using find, shiftOneLeftFrom, and printResults functions.
main_text: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototypes int find(int nums[], int len, int target); void shiftOneLeftFrom(int data[], int len, int fromIndex); void printResults(int data[], int len); int find(int nums[], int len, int target) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { if(target == nums[i]) { return i; } } return -1; } void shiftOneLeftFrom(int data[], int len, int fromIndex) { // shift items up from loc to n // invariant: data[loc] is always safe to overwrite for(int i = fromIndex; i < len-1; i++) { data[i] = data[i+1]; } } void printResults(int data[], int len) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; } int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, loc; cin >> val; // find first occurrence of val loc = find(data, n, val); if(loc != -1) { // shift items up from loc to n // invariant: data[loc] is always safe to overwrite shiftOneLeftFrom(data, n, loc); n--; } // Output the results printResults(data, n); return 0; }
notes_text: The find function locates the first occurrence, shiftOneLeftFrom shifts subsequent elements left to fill the gap, and n is decremented. printResults displays the final array.

title: Solutions - RemoveAll
summary: Shows a solution for removing all occurrences of a value from an array by repeatedly calling find and shiftOneLeftFrom in a while loop.
main_text: #include <iostream> using namespace std; // prototypes int find(int nums[], int len, int target); void shiftOneLeftFrom(int data[], int len, int fromIndex); void printResults(int data[], int len); int find(int nums[], int len, int target) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { if(target == nums[i]) { return i; } } return -1; } void shiftOneLeftFrom(int data[], int len, int fromIndex) { for(int i = fromIndex; i < len-1; i++) { data[i] = data[i+1]; } } void printResults(int data[], int len) { for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; } int main() { // setup array with data int n, data[100]; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } // now perform the given task int val, lead, trail; cin >> val; int loc = find(data, n, val); while(loc != -1) { shiftOneLeftFrom(data, n, loc); n--; loc = find(data, n, val); } // Output the results printResults(data, n); return 0; }
notes_text: RemoveAll extends RemoveFirst by using a while loop: repeatedly find the value and shift left until find returns -1. The same helper functions (find, shiftOneLeftFrom, printResults) are reused, demonstrating function reuse across related problems.

title: Unit 4d - Compiling and Debugging
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 4d on compiling and debugging in CS 102, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 4d - Compiling and Debugging. Mark Redekopp.

title: Editing and Compiling Manually
summary: Section divider slide introducing the topic of manually editing and compiling C++ programs.
main_text: EDITING AND COMPILING MANUALLY
notes_text: This is a section header slide that transitions into coverage of how to manually edit source code files and compile them using command line tools, as opposed to using an IDE's built-in compile button.

title: Review: Print Statements / Narration
summary: Reviews using print statements as a debugging technique to narrate program execution and trace variable values.
main_text: When we first discussed debugging we said an easy way to find an error is to add print statements that will 'narrate' where you are and what the variable values are. Be a detective by narrowing down where the error is. Put a print statement in each 'for', 'while', 'if' or 'else' block... this will make sure you are getting to the expected areas of your code. Then print variable values so you can see what data your program is producing.
notes_text: This is a review of a previously covered debugging technique. Print statement debugging is a foundational skill before learning to use dedicated debugger tools.

images.description: Cartoon detective with magnifying glass, representing the idea of being a detective when debugging code by investigating where errors occur.

title: Editors
summary: Introduces text editors used for writing code, emphasizing the importance of using proper code editors rather than word processors.
main_text: 'Real' developers use editors designed for writing code. No word processors!! You need a text editor to write your code. Eclipse, Sublime, MS Visual Code, Emacs, Atom, and many others. These often have handy functions for commenting, indenting, checking matching braces ({..}) etc.
notes_text: The slide shows logos for Eclipse, Sublime Text, Visual Studio Code, Atom, and Emacs. These are all popular code editors with features specifically designed for software development.

images.description: Logo for Eclipse IDE, a popular open-source integrated development environment.
Logo for Sublime Text editor, shown as a dark icon with an orange 'S' shape.
Logo for Visual Studio Code, shown as a blue crossed-ribbon icon with the label 'Visual Studio Code'.
Logo for Atom text editor, shown as a green atomic orbital icon.
Logo for Emacs text editor, shown as a purple icon with a pen/quill.

title: Compilers
summary: Lists available C++ compilers and introduces the concept of Integrated Development Environments (IDEs).
main_text: Several free and commercial compilers are available: g++, clang++, XCode, MS Visual Studio. Several have 'integrated' editors, debuggers and other tools and thus are called IDE's (Integrated Development Environments).
notes_text: g++ is the GNU C++ compiler commonly used on Linux. clang++ is the LLVM-based compiler. XCode is Apple's IDE. MS Visual Studio is Microsoft's IDE. These tools combine compiling, editing, and debugging into one environment.

title: Using the Command Line
summary: Introduces the command line interface (terminal) as a tool for navigating files, running programs, and compiling code on Linux.
main_text: While GUIs are nice, we often have more control when using the command line interface (i.e. the terminal). Linux (the OS used by Codio and in CS 103, 104, etc.) has a rich set of command line utilities (Mac & Windows do too, though Windows uses different names for the utilities). We can navigate the file system (like you would with Explorer or Finder), start programs (double-clicking an icon), and much more by simply typing commands.
notes_text: The slide shows a terminal icon, a Linux terminal view with the prompt 'student@studentVM:~$', and a Vocareum terminal view showing a g++ compile command.

images.description: Terminal application icon showing a dark rectangle with a command prompt symbol, representing the terminal application.
Screenshot of a Linux terminal window showing the prompt 'student@studentVM:~$' on a dark purple background.
Screenshot of a Vocareum terminal view showing a g++ compile command: 'g++ -g -Wall hw8.cpp -o hw8'.

title: Software Process
summary: Illustrates the three-step software development process: editing code, compiling with g++, and running the executable binary.
main_text: The software process involves three steps: (1) Edit & write code using a text editor like Visual Studio Code (e.g., '$ code test.cpp &'). (2) Compile & fix compiler errors using g++ (e.g., '$ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test' or '$ make test'). (3) Load & run the executable program (e.g., '$ ./test'). The compiler (g++) takes C++ source files (e.g., test.cpp) along with Standard C++ and other libraries, and produces an executable binary image containing machine code (binary numbers like 1110 0010 0101 1001...). This binary is then loaded into memory and executed by the processor. Note: Most documentation and books use '$' as a placeholder for the command line prompt.
notes_text: This is a key diagram showing the complete compilation pipeline. The source code is the input file, and the binary executable is the output file. The g++ compiler translates human-readable C++ into machine code that the CPU can execute.

images.description: Flowchart showing the software compilation pipeline: C++ source file (test.cpp) feeds into the g++ compiler along with Std C++ & Other Libraries. The compiler produces an executable binary image containing binary machine code. This binary is then loaded into memory (RAM) and executed by the processor (Intel Core i7 shown). Below the diagram, three numbered steps show the commands: (1) edit with 'code test.cpp &', (2) compile with 'g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test', (3) run with './test'.

title: Codio Does Both
summary: Explains that Codio's 'Compile and Run' button automates both the compilation and execution steps into one action at the terminal.
main_text: When you click 'Compile and Run', Codio does both steps in one at the terminal/command line. But you could do it manually. The two manual commands are: '$ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test' followed by '$ ./test'. In Codio, the terminal shows the combined command, for example: 'codio@waiternobel-phantomheaven:~/workspace$ g++ -g -o kiosk kiosk.cpp && ./kiosk'.
notes_text: The '&&' operator in the terminal command means the second command (./kiosk) only runs if the first command (g++ compilation) succeeds without errors.

images.description: Screenshot of Codio terminal showing the combined compile-and-run command: 'g++ -g -o kiosk kiosk.cpp && ./kiosk' executed in one step.

title: g++ Options
summary: Describes the most common g++ compiler flags including -o for output name, -g for debug info, and -Wall for warnings.
main_text: Most basic usage: g++ cpp_filenames. Creates an executable a.out. Options: -o => Specifies output executable name (other than default a.out). -g => Include info needed by debuggers like gdb, kdbg, etc. -Wall => show all warnings. Most common usage form: $ g++ -g -Wall kiosk.cpp -o kiosk.
notes_text: The -g flag is essential for debugging because it embeds symbol information (variable names, line numbers) into the executable that debuggers need. Without -g, a debugger cannot map machine code back to source lines.

title: Running the Program
summary: Explains how to compile and then run a C++ executable from the command line using the ./ prefix.
main_text: First ensure the program compiles: $ g++ -g -Wall kiosks.cpp -o kiosks. Then run the program by preceding the executable name with ./: $ ./kiosks. Remember NOT to type the '$'.
notes_text: The './' prefix tells the shell to look in the current directory for the executable, since by default the current directory is not in the system PATH on Linux.

title: Listing Files (Folder Contents)
summary: Shows how to use the 'ls' command in Mac/Linux to view file contents of a directory, comparing GUI and terminal views.
main_text: In Mac/Linux, to view the files in a folder, just type ls (stands for list). The slide shows a side-by-side comparison of a Codio file browser GUI (showing files: .settings, basic1.in, basic2.in, kiosk, kiosk.cpp, README.md, update_settings.sh) and the equivalent terminal output from running 'ls' (showing: basic1.in basic2.in kiosk kiosk.cpp README.md update_settings.sh).
notes_text: The ls command is one of the most fundamental Linux commands. Executable files (like 'kiosk') and scripts (like 'update_settings.sh') are often displayed in different colors in the terminal.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing a Codio GUI file browser panel on the left listing files (HW 7 - Functions copied folder with .settings, basic1.in, basic2.in, kiosk, kiosk.cpp, README.md, update_settings.sh) and a terminal window on the right showing the same files listed by the 'ls' command.

title: Debuggers
summary: Section divider slide introducing the topic of debugger tools for finding and fixing bugs in programs.
main_text: DEBUGGERS
notes_text: This section header transitions from manual compilation topics to debugging tools, covering both GUI-based debuggers (like Codio's built-in debugger) and command-line debuggers (like gdb).

title: Step 4: Using a Debugger
summary: Introduces the core capabilities of a debugger: setting breakpoints, stepping through code, and printing variable values.
main_text: A debugger allows you to: Set a breakpoint (the code will run and then stop when it reaches a certain line of code). Step through your code line by line so you can see where it goes. Print variable values when you are stopped at a certain line of code.
notes_text: These three capabilities (breakpoints, stepping, and inspecting variables) are the fundamental operations of any debugger, whether GUI-based or command-line.

title: Codio Debugger
summary: Shows how to launch the Codio debugger by opening a .cpp file and clicking 'Debug Current File', then waiting for the debug window.
main_text: Open your .cpp file and click 'Debug Current File'. Wait for the debug window on the right to appear. The debug window shows: Program is paused status, Call Stack (e.g., reverse.cpp(42):main()), Local variables (e.g., vals: -136422928, 32767, 0, 0, 1431653488, 21845, 1431652592; num: 1431653565; loc: 21845), Watches (no watch expressions), Breakpoints (e.g., reverse.cpp: 30), and a Console area. The code editor shows the source with line numbers and a breakpoint marker (red dot) at line 48.
notes_text: The local variables show uninitialized values because the program has just started. The debug panel in Codio provides a graphical interface to gdb.

images.description: Screenshot of the Codio debugger interface showing the 'Debug Current File' button at top right, and the debug panel on the right side with sections for Call Stack, Local variables, Watches, Breakpoints, and Console. The code editor on the left shows C++ source code for a reverse array program with a red breakpoint dot at line 48.

title: Codio Debugger - Setting Breakpoints and Running
summary: Explains how to set breakpoints by clicking in the margin, start the program with the play button, and provide input in the debug console.
main_text: Set a breakpoint by clicking in the margin at the line you want to stop at. Start the program running by clicking the play button (green triangle). Provide input in the console area of the debug window, not the regular terminal. The code editor shows the source with a red breakpoint marker at line 48 and the current execution highlighted at line 42 (int main()).
notes_text: It is important to use the debug console for input rather than the regular terminal, as the debugger captures stdin/stdout through its own console.

images.description: Screenshot of Codio debugger showing C++ source code with a red breakpoint dot at line 48 and the current line (42, int main()) highlighted in pink. A green play button is shown for starting execution. The Console area at the bottom shows a GDB warning message.

title: Codio Debugger - Inspecting and Stepping
summary: Describes debugger actions available when paused at a breakpoint: inspecting variables, stepping into/over functions, and continuing execution.
main_text: When the debugger pauses your program due to hitting the breakpoint, you can: Inspect variable values (the Local variables panel shows values like dat: 0x7fffffffea40, len: 10, num: 18, loc_of_num: 0, found: true). Step line by line (if the line calls a function you can step into that function, or step over that function by letting it execute quickly and stop at the next line). Set more breakpoints and continue running. The Call Stack shows: reverse.cpp(30):reverseAndFind() called from reverse.cpp(48):main(). Three control buttons are shown: step into (down arrow), step over (curved arrow), and continue (play arrow).
notes_text: Step into goes inside a function call to debug it line by line. Step over executes the function completely and stops at the next line in the current function. Continue resumes execution until the next breakpoint.

images.description: Debug panel showing the Call Stack with reverseAndFind() called from main(), Local variables panel showing dat, len, num, loc_of_num, and found values, and three debugger control buttons: step into (down arrow), step over (curved arrow), and continue/play (right arrow).

title: Step (Into) / Step (Over / Next)
summary: Explains the difference between step into and step over (next) using a code example with a max() function call.
main_text: Type step to execute one line and then stop (aka single-step). If you get to a line with a function call that you don't want to go into but just have execute fully, type next (aka step-over). A code example illustrates: given a function int max(int a, int b) that returns the larger value, and in main() the line y = max(10,x); - using 'step' would enter the max function and go to 'if(a > b) return a;', while using 'next' would execute max() fully and stop at the next line 'cout << y << endl;'.
notes_text: Step into is useful when you suspect a bug is inside the called function. Step over is useful when you trust the function works correctly and want to stay in the current function's flow.

images.description: Diagram showing a code example with int max(int a, int b) function and int main(). Arrows illustrate that 'step' from the line y = max(10,x) would enter the max function body, while 'next' would skip over max() and stop at cout << y << endl. The step into button (down arrow) and step over button (curved arrow) icons are shown.

title: The Struggle is Real
summary: Humorous meme slide about the challenges of debugging C++ code, showing that fixing bugs often introduces new bugs.
main_text: Two programming humor memes are shown. The first meme shows a frustrated person sitting next to text reading 'C++ CODE NOT WORKING' with the caption 'THE STRUGGLE IS REAL'. The second meme is a four-panel Gru meme showing the progression: 'WE FIND THE BUG' -> 'WE FIX THE BUG' -> 'NOW WE HAVE TWO BUGS' -> 'NOW WE HAVE THREE BUGS', illustrating the common experience of fixing one bug only to introduce additional bugs.
notes_text: This is a lighthearted slide meant to acknowledge the difficulty of debugging and keep students encouraged. It reflects a common reality in software development.

images.description: Meme showing a frustrated person with 'C++ CODE NOT WORKING' and 'THE STRUGGLE IS REAL' text, humorously depicting the difficulty of debugging C++ programs.
Four-panel Gru meme showing the cycle of bug fixing: finding a bug, fixing the bug, now having two bugs, and now having three bugs.

title: GDB and Other Debuggers
summary: Introduces gdb as a text-based debugger for Linux/Unix and lists other development environments with built-in debuggers.
main_text: gdb is a simple text-based debugger that comes with many Linux/Unix based systems. We'll focus on this debugger. Other development environments have built in debuggers: MS Visual Studio, Apple Xcode, Eclipse. Even Codio has a graphical interface for GDB. Online compiler + GUI based GDB tool: https://www.onlinegdb.com/
notes_text: gdb (GNU Debugger) is the standard debugger on Linux systems. While IDE debuggers provide graphical interfaces, they typically use gdb or similar tools under the hood. OnlineGDB provides a web-based alternative for students without local development environments.

title: Running the Debugger
summary: Shows how to compile with the -g flag and then launch gdb with the compiled executable to start debugging.
main_text: Compile your program and include the -g flag: $ g++ -g search.cpp -o search. Then start the debugger giving it the program you want to debug (not the source code): $ gdb ./search.
notes_text: The -g flag is critical here because it tells the compiler to include debugging symbols. Without it, gdb would not be able to show source code lines or variable names. Note that you pass the compiled executable (./search) to gdb, not the source file (search.cpp).

title: Breakpoints
summary: Explains how to set breakpoints at a specific line number in gdb and run the program until it hits the breakpoint.
main_text: Breakpoints stop program execution at a given line number. Set before you start the program in the debugger: (gdb) break 36. Get the program running: (gdb) run. It will run and then stop when it reaches the code on line 36.
notes_text: Breakpoints must be set before running the program (or while paused). The 'break' command can also accept function names, e.g., 'break main' to stop at the start of main().

title: Stepping
summary: Explains gdb's step and next commands for single-stepping through code, with a diagram showing the difference when encountering function calls.
main_text: Type step to execute one line and then stop (aka single-step): (gdb) step. If you get to a line with a function call that you don't want to go into but just have execute fully, type next (aka step-over): (gdb) next. A code example illustrates: given int max(int a, int b) with 'if(a > b) return a;', and in main() the line 'y = max(10,x);' - 'step' enters the max function, while 'next' executes it fully and stops at 'cout << y << endl;'.
notes_text: This mirrors the Codio debugger slide but uses gdb text commands instead of GUI buttons. The concepts are identical: step goes into functions, next/step-over executes them completely.

images.description: Diagram showing the difference between step and next commands in gdb. From the line y = max(10,x), 'step' follows an arrow into the max function body, while 'next' skips over it to the cout line.

title: Printing Values
summary: Demonstrates how to use gdb's print command to inspect variable values and evaluate expressions during debugging.
main_text: At any point in time you can print a variable or an expression. (gdb) print size - Would print the value of the size variable. (gdb) print nums[i] - Would print the value in nums[i]. (gdb) print nums[i] == target - Would print true or false.
notes_text: The print command in gdb is very flexible. It can evaluate any valid C++ expression, including array accesses, pointer dereferences, and comparison operators. This makes it a powerful tool for testing hypotheses about why code is behaving unexpectedly.

title: gdb TUI / GUI
summary: Describes gdb's text-based user interface (TUI) mode for viewing source code alongside the debugger command area, plus keyboard shortcuts.
main_text: Gdb has a text-based user interface (aka 'TUI') that you can enable if desired. To see both the source code and the debugger command area, type: (gdb) layout src (turns on src display). (gdb) tui disable (turns off src display). You can also toggle between the two display modes using the key sequence: Ctrl-X, a. To move your cursor between scrolling in the source window and entering commands in the gdb command terminal, use: Ctrl-X, o to toggle back and forth. A web-based GUI for gdb: https://www.onlinegdb.com/
notes_text: The TUI mode is very helpful for keeping track of where you are in the source code while debugging. It splits the terminal into a source view at the top and a command area at the bottom.

title: Exercises
summary: Lists four gdb practice exercises to complete in Codio: search, sumpairs, count, and primes.
main_text: Practice with gdb in Codio: search, sumpairs, count, primes.
notes_text: These are hands-on exercises for students to practice using gdb commands (break, run, step, next, print) on provided Codio assignments.

title: Codio Exercises 2
summary: Provides an additional debugger practice exercise using the histogram program with a breakpoint at line 8.
main_text: Practice using a debugger: histogram (break at line 8).
notes_text: This exercise gives students a specific breakpoint location (line 8) to practice setting breakpoints and stepping through the histogram program.

title: Unit 4e - Efficiency and Sorting
summary: Title slide introducing the lecture on efficiency and sorting algorithms for CS 102.
main_text: Unit 4e - Efficiency and Sorting. Presented by Mark Redekopp.

title: Sorting
summary: Introduces the concept of sorting, explaining why it is useful and that the course will focus on two simple sorting algorithms.
main_text: Sorting requires us to move data around within an array. Allows users to see and organize data more efficiently. Behind the scenes it allows more effective searching of data. There are MANY sorting algorithms out there, we will focus on two simple ones. An example is shown with an original list [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1] at indices 0-5, which becomes the sorted list [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] at indices 0-5.
notes_text: Sorting is foundational for efficient search algorithms like binary search, covered in later units.

images.description: Two arrays are shown side by side. The original unsorted array contains [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1] and the sorted result contains [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8], both labeled with indices 0 through 5.

title: Bubble Sort
summary: Explains the bubble sort algorithm's main idea of repeatedly comparing and swapping neighbors to move the largest element to the top each pass.
main_text: Main Idea: Keep comparing neighbors, moving larger item up and smaller item down until largest item is at the top. Repeat on list of size n-1. Have one loop to count each pass (a.k.a. i) to identify which index we need to stop at. Have an inner loop start at the lowest index and count up to the stopping location comparing neighboring elements and advancing the larger of the neighbors. Example with list [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: After Pass 1: [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8]. After Pass 2: [3, 6, 5, 1, 7, 8]. After Pass 3: [3, 5, 1, 6, 7, 8]. After Pass 4: [3, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8]. After Pass 5: [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Each pass places the next largest element into its correct sorted position at the end of the unsorted portion. Elements in red are in their final sorted position.
notes_text: Bubble sort requires n-1 passes for a list of size n. After each pass, the largest unsorted element 'bubbles up' to its correct position.

images.description: A series of array states showing the list after each pass of bubble sort. The original list [7,3,8,6,5,1] progressively becomes sorted as the largest elements move to the right end. Elements in their final sorted position are highlighted in red.

title: Bubble Sort Algorithm
summary: Shows the bubble sort pseudocode and step-by-step traces of Pass 1, Pass 2, and Pass n-2, illustrating swap and no-swap decisions at each comparison.
main_text: Pseudocode: void bsort(int mylist[], int size) { int i, j; for(i=... ) { for(j=... ) { if(mylist[j] > mylist[j+1]) { // swap mylist[j] & mylist[j+1] } } } }. Pass 1 trace on [7,3,8,6,5,1]: Compare indices j and j+1 moving left to right. 7>3 swap -> [3,7,8,6,5,1]. 7>8 no swap. 8>6 swap -> [3,7,6,8,5,1]. 8>5 swap -> [3,7,6,5,8,1]. 8>1 swap -> [3,7,6,5,1,8]. Pass 2 trace on [3,7,6,5,1,8]: 3>7 no swap. 7>6 swap -> [3,6,7,5,1,8]. 7>5 swap -> [3,6,5,7,1,8]. 7>1 swap -> [3,6,5,1,7,8]. Pass n-2 trace on [3,1,5,6,7,8]: 3>1 swap -> [1,3,5,6,7,8]. Elements highlighted in red are in their final sorted position after each pass.
notes_text: The ellipsis in the for loop bounds is intentional; students are expected to work out that i runs from 0 to size-2 and j runs from 0 to size-i-2.

images.description: Three detailed pass traces showing each comparison step in bubble sort. Each step shows the array state, pointer positions j and i, and whether a swap or no-swap occurred. Pass 1 performs 5 comparisons, Pass 2 performs 4, and Pass n-2 performs 1 comparison.

title: Bubble Sort Visualization
summary: An animated scatter plot visualization of bubble sort in action, showing how data points move from a random arrangement to sorted order.
main_text: A scatter plot visualization of bubble sort is shown, with Value on the y-axis and List Index on the x-axis. The dots represent data values at various positions in the array. As bubble sort progresses, values gradually move into their correct sorted positions, with larger values bubbling up to higher indices. The visualization is courtesy of wikipedia.org.
notes_text: This is a snapshot from an animated visualization. The scattered points represent the intermediate state during the sorting process.

images.description: A scatter plot showing the state of an array during bubble sort execution. The x-axis represents List Index and the y-axis represents Value. Points are partially scattered but show a trend toward sorted order, illustrating the gradual nature of bubble sort.

title: Selection Sort
summary: Introduces selection sort as an alternative to bubble sort that reduces the number of swaps by finding the min or max value and performing one swap per pass.
main_text: Selection sort does away with the many swaps and just records where the min or max value is and performs one swap at the end. The list/array can again be thought of in two parts: Sorted and Unsorted. The problem starts with the whole array unsorted and slowly the sorted portion grows. We could find the max and put it at the end of the list or we could find the min and put it at the start of the list. Just for variation let's choose the min approach.
notes_text: Selection sort is more efficient than bubble sort in terms of number of swaps (O(n) swaps vs O(n^2) for bubble sort), though both have the same overall time complexity of O(n^2).

title: Selection Sort Algorithm
summary: Presents the selection sort pseudocode and step-by-step traces for Pass 1, Pass 2, and Pass n-2, showing how the minimum element is found and swapped into position.
main_text: Pseudocode: void ssort(int mylist[], int size) { for(i=...){ int min = i; for(j=... ){ if(mylist[j] < mylist[min]) { min = j } } // swap mylist[i] & mylist[min] } }. Pass 1 (min=0): Starting with [7,3,8,6,5,1], scan with j through the array tracking the minimum index. j=1: min stays 0. j=2: min stays 0. j=3: min stays 0. j=5: min=5 (value 1 is smallest). Swap mylist[0] and mylist[5] -> [1,3,8,6,5,7]. Pass 2 (min=1): Starting with [1,3,8,6,5,7], scan from index 1. min stays 1 throughout. Swap mylist[1] and mylist[1] (no change) -> [1,3,8,6,5,7]. Pass n-2 (min=4): Starting with [1,3,5,6,7,8], compare indices 4 and 5. min=4. Swap -> [1,3,5,6,7,8]. Elements in red are in their final sorted position.
notes_text: The outer loop i marks the boundary between sorted (left) and unsorted (right) portions. Each pass finds the minimum in the unsorted portion and swaps it to position i.

images.description: Three pass traces for selection sort. Each pass shows the array with pointers i and j, tracking the minimum index (min) as j scans through the unsorted portion. At the end of each pass, a single swap places the minimum into its correct sorted position.

title: Selection Sort Visualization
summary: An animated scatter plot visualization of selection sort showing the progressive sorting of data points from random to ordered positions.
main_text: A scatter plot visualization of selection sort is shown, with Value on the y-axis and List Index on the x-axis. The dots represent data values at various positions in the array. As selection sort progresses, the leftmost portion becomes sorted while the right portion remains unsorted. The sorted portion shows a clear diagonal line from bottom-left, while the unsorted portion remains scattered. The visualization is courtesy of wikipedia.org.
notes_text: Compared to the bubble sort visualization, selection sort shows a clearer boundary between the sorted and unsorted portions of the array.

images.description: A scatter plot showing the state of an array during selection sort. The left portion shows points forming an ascending diagonal line (sorted), while the right portion shows scattered points (unsorted). The x-axis is List Index and y-axis is Value.

title: Operations on a Sorted Array
summary: Section divider slide introducing the topic of operations that can be performed on a sorted array.
main_text: OPERATIONS ON A SORTED ARRAY
notes_text: This section transitions from sorting algorithms to discussing how to maintain a sorted array through insertion and removal operations.

title: Insertion to a Sorted Array
summary: Explains how to insert new data into a sorted array by finding the correct position and shifting elements to make room.
main_text: Another option rather than sorting an unordered array is to always insert new data into the correct location of the array. To insert, we must: Iterate until we find the appropriate location to place the new value. Make room for the new value by shifting the remaining items back a spot. Example sequence: insert(7) -> [7]. insert(3) -> [3, 7]. insert(8) -> [3, 7, 8]. insert(6) -> [3, 6, 7, 8]. For insert(6), the process is shown in detail: starting with [3, 7, 8] at indices 0-2, first copy 7 and 8 to the right by one position to get [3, 7, 7, 8], then place 6 at index 1 to get [3, 6, 7, 8].
notes_text: This approach maintains sorted order at all times, which is useful when data arrives incrementally rather than all at once.

images.description: Two columns of diagrams. The left column shows a sequence of insertions building a sorted array: insert(7)->[7], insert(3)->[3,7], insert(8)->[3,7,8], insert(6)->[3,6,7,8]. The right column shows the detailed process of insert(6): starting with [3,7,8], shifting 7 and 8 right to make room, then placing 6 at index 1.

title: Removing from a Sorted Array
summary: Explains how removing an element from a sorted array requires shifting all subsequent elements forward to fill the gap.
main_text: Erasing / removing item at any location other than the very last item requires us to copy all items behind the removed item to the previous slot. Example: To delete/remove the item at location 2 requires us to move everyone else up. Array [30, 51, 52, 53, 54, 60] at indices 0-5. Removing index 2 (value 52): shift elements at indices 3, 4, 5 forward by one position. Result: [30, 51, 53, 54, 60] with the last slot now empty.
notes_text: Both insertion and removal from a sorted array require O(n) time due to the shifting of elements, which is a key limitation of array-based sorted data structures.

images.description: A diagram showing the removal of element at index 2 from a sorted array. The original array [30, 51, 52, 53, 54, 60] has index 2 crossed out, with arrows showing elements at indices 3-5 shifting left by one position to produce [30, 51, 53, 54, 60] with a dashed empty cell at the end.
labels: To delete/remove the item at location 2 requires us to move everyone else up

title: Complexity and Runtime
summary: Section divider slide introducing the topic of algorithm complexity and runtime analysis.
main_text: COMPLEXITY & RUNTIME
notes_text: This section transitions to analyzing how efficient sorting algorithms are in terms of time complexity.

title: Time Complexity
summary: Introduces the concept of time complexity as a way to judge how good an algorithm is by counting steps of work in terms of input size n.
main_text: Coming up with AN algorithm to solve a problem is often not TOO hard. Coming up with a GOOD algorithm to solve a problem can be a bit harder. We need a way to judge how "GOOD" an algorithm is. For us "GOOD" will mean how long the algorithm takes to solve the problem. We will count steps of work and come up with an answer in terms of n, where n is the size of the input/problem.
notes_text: Time complexity provides a hardware-independent way to compare algorithms. It focuses on growth rate rather than absolute time.

title: Bubble Sorting Complexity Analysis
summary: Analyzes the number of steps per pass in bubble sort, showing how the work decreases each pass and asking students to fill in the step counts.
main_text: Recall the bubble sort. How much work do our nested loops require us to do. Think of each step/iteration as 1 unit of time/work. Original List is length N (N=6 for this example). Starting with list [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Pass 1 (____ steps): result [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8]. Pass 2 (____ steps): result [3, 6, 5, 1, 7, 8]. Pass 3 (____ steps): result [3, 5, 1, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 4 (____ steps): result [3, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 5 (____ steps): result [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 6 (____ steps): result [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Students are expected to fill in the number of comparisons per pass: Pass 1 has n-1 steps, Pass 2 has n-2 steps, and so on.
notes_text: The total work is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n*(n-1)/2, which is proportional to n^2. The blanks are meant for students to fill in during class.

images.description: Two columns: the left shows the original list [7,3,8,6,5,1] labeled as length N=6. The right shows the array state after each of 6 passes with blank step counts for students to fill in. Sorted elements are highlighted in red.

title: Complexity of Sort Algorithms
summary: Compares the time complexity of bubble sort and selection sort (both O(n^2)) with more advanced algorithms that achieve O(n*log2(n)), illustrated with a growth rate chart.
main_text: Bubble Sort & Selection Sort: 2 Nested Loops. Execute outer loop n times. For each outer loop iteration, inner loop runs i times. Time complexity is proportional to n^2. Other sort algorithms can run in time proportional to: n * log_2(n). A chart shows three growth curves for N, N^2, and N*log2(N) plotted against N (x-axis from 0 to 20) and Run-time (y-axis from 0 to 400). The N^2 curve grows much faster than N*log2(N), which grows much faster than N. At N=20, N^2=400 while N*log2(N) is approximately 86.
notes_text: Examples of O(n*log n) sorting algorithms include merge sort, quicksort, and heapsort. These are covered in more advanced courses.

images.description: A line chart comparing three growth functions: N (linear, green), N^2 (quadratic, red), and N*log2(N) (linearithmic, blue). The x-axis represents N from 0 to 20, the y-axis represents Run-time from 0 to 400. The N^2 curve dominates, reaching 400 at N=20, while N*log2(N) reaches about 86 and N reaches 20.

title: Importance of Time Complexity
summary: Demonstrates why time complexity matters by showing a table of different complexity classes and how their runtimes grow dramatically with input size.
main_text: It makes the difference between effective and impossible. Many important problems currently can only be solved with exponential run-time algorithms (e.g. O(2^n) time). Usually, algorithms are only practical if they run in polynomial time (e.g. O(n) or O(n^2) etc.). A comparison table shows runtimes for different complexity classes at various input sizes: For N=2: O(1)=1, O(log2 n)=1, O(n)=2, O(n*log2 n)=2, O(n^2)=4, O(2^n)=4. For N=20: O(1)=1, O(log2 n)=4.3, O(n)=20, O(n*log2 n)=86.4, O(n^2)=400, O(2^n)=1,048,576. For N=200: O(1)=1, O(log2 n)=7.6, O(n)=200, O(n*log2 n)=1,528.8, O(n^2)=40,000, O(2^n)=1.60694E+60. For N=2000: O(1)=1, O(log2 n)=11.0, O(n)=2000, O(n*log2 n)=21,931.6, O(n^2)=4,000,000, O(2^n)=#NUM! (overflow).
notes_text: The #NUM! entry for O(2^n) at N=2000 illustrates that exponential algorithms become computationally infeasible even for moderate input sizes. This connects to the P vs NP problem in computer science.

images.description: A comparison table with rows for N=2, 20, 200, and 2000, and columns for O(1), O(log2 n), O(n), O(n*log2 n), O(n^2), and O(2^n). The table dramatically shows how exponential complexity becomes infeasible: at N=2000, O(2^n) overflows while O(n^2) is 4 million.

title: Unit 5 - K-Means Capstone
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 5 on the K-Means Capstone project for CS 102, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5 - K-Means Capstone. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. This unit covers the K-Means clustering algorithm as a capstone project for the course.

title: K-Means Algorithm
summary: Introduces the K-Means algorithm goal of classifying n points into k clusters based on distance, with two example scatter plots showing data that could be clustered.
main_text: K-Means Algorithm. Goal: classify n points into k clusters (groups) based on distance. Limitation: Must choose k in advance. Two scatter plot examples are shown. The left plot shows approximately 10 data points on a small scale (x: 0-7, y: 2-10) that appear to form natural groupings. The right plot shows a larger dataset of approximately 30 points on a larger scale (x: 20-70, y: 10-80) where clusters are less immediately obvious, demonstrating a more realistic use case for K-Means.
notes_text: The two scatter plots illustrate that K-Means can be applied to datasets of varying sizes and scales. The left plot has more visually obvious clusters while the right plot shows a scenario where algorithmic clustering is more valuable.

images.description: Small scatter plot showing approximately 10 data points with x-axis 0-7 and y-axis 2-10, illustrating a simple dataset with visually apparent clusters.
Larger scatter plot showing approximately 30 data points with x-axis 20-70 and y-axis 10-80, illustrating a more complex dataset where manual clustering is harder.

title: K-Means Algorithm Steps (Iteration 1)
summary: Explains the iterative K-Means process: start with random centers, update centers to cluster means, reassign points to nearest center, and repeat until convergence.
main_text: K-Means. Start with k random center points and even assign the n points to the k centers randomly (or to the nearest random k). Do: Step 1: Update the center point to be the mean (average) of the points assigned to that cluster. Step 2: Then reassign each point to the nearest cluster center point. Repeat until none of the n points change which cluster they are closest to. The scatter plot shows the initial state with data points colored by their current cluster assignment (blue, green, orange) and triangle markers representing the cluster center points (centroids). Three clusters are visible with centers shown as dark triangles.
notes_text: This slide shows the first iteration of the algorithm. The triangles represent centroids. Points are colored to indicate their current cluster assignment. The algorithm alternates between updating centers (Step 1) and reassigning points (Step 2).

images.description: Scatter plot showing K-Means iteration 1 with data points in three colors (blue, green, orange) representing cluster assignments and dark triangle markers showing the current centroid positions for each cluster.

title: K-Means Iteration 2
summary: Shows the second iteration of K-Means where centroids have moved after recalculating means and points have been reassigned to their nearest updated center.
main_text: K-Means. Iteration 2: Step 1: Update the center point to be the mean (average) of the points assigned to that cluster. Step 2: Then reassign each point to the nearest cluster center point. Repeat until none of the n points change which cluster they are closest to. The scatter plot shows the state after iteration 2. The centroids (triangles) have shifted position compared to iteration 1 as they were recalculated as the mean of their assigned points. Some data points may have changed cluster assignments. The three clusters (blue, green, orange) are becoming more distinct as the algorithm converges.
notes_text: Compared to slide 3 (iteration 1), the centroids have moved closer to the natural centers of the data groupings. Points near cluster boundaries may switch assignments between iterations.

images.description: Scatter plot showing K-Means iteration 2 with updated centroid positions (triangles) and reassigned data points in three colors (blue, green, orange). Centroids have shifted compared to the previous iteration.

title: K-Means Iteration 3
summary: Shows the third iteration of K-Means with centroids continuing to converge toward stable positions and clearer cluster separation.
main_text: K-Means. Iteration 3: Step 1: Update the center point to be the mean (average) of the points assigned to that cluster. Step 2: Then reassign each point to the nearest cluster center point. Repeat until none of the n points change which cluster they are closest to. The scatter plot shows the state after iteration 3. The clusters are becoming more stable with the blue cluster grouping in the lower-left area, the green cluster in the upper region, and the orange cluster in the lower-right. The centroid triangles continue to adjust toward their final positions.
notes_text: By iteration 3, the algorithm is close to convergence. The cluster assignments are becoming stable with fewer points changing clusters between iterations.

images.description: Scatter plot showing K-Means iteration 3 with three clusters (blue, green, orange) becoming more clearly separated and centroids (triangles) nearing their final stable positions.

title: K-Means Final Result
summary: Shows the final converged state of K-Means where no points change clusters, demonstrating the algorithm's termination condition.
main_text: K-Means. Final: Step 1: Update the center point to be the mean (average) of the points assigned to that cluster. Step 2: Then reassign each point to the nearest cluster center point. Repeat until none of the n points change which cluster they are closest to. The scatter plot shows the final converged state. The blue cluster contains points in the left-center area around coordinates (1-3, 4-9). The green cluster contains the upper points around coordinates (3-6, 8-9). The orange cluster contains lower-right points around coordinates (4-7, 2-3). The centroid triangles are now at stable positions where no further point reassignments occur.
notes_text: This is the termination state where Step 2 produces no changes. The algorithm has converged. The final cluster assignments and centroid positions represent the algorithm's output.

images.description: Scatter plot showing the final converged K-Means result with three stable clusters (blue, green, orange) and their final centroid positions (triangles). No further reassignments will occur.

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Divider slide indicating that the following slides contain solutions that should not be viewed until after the in-class activity.
main_text: SOLUTIONS - DO NOT VIEW UNTIL AFTER IN-CLASS ACTIVITY. This is a section divider indicating that the remaining slides contain solution code for the K-Means implementation exercise.
notes_text: Students should attempt the K-Means implementation on their own before viewing the solution code on the following slides.

title: Assigning Points to a Cluster (Code)
summary: Provides C++ solution code for the assign_clusters function that assigns each point to its nearest cluster center using squared Euclidean distance.
main_text: Assigning Points to a Cluster. The function assign_clusters takes arrays of point coordinates (ptsX, ptsY), cluster assignments (ptsCluster), number of points N, center coordinates (centersX, centersY), and number of clusters K. It returns 1 if any assignment changed, 0 otherwise. For each point i from 0 to N-1, it initializes best distance to 1e30 and bestc to -1. For each cluster c from 0 to K-1, it computes dx = ptsX[i] - centersX[c] and dy = ptsY[i] - centersY[c], then computes squared distance d = dx*dx + dy*dy. If d < best, it updates best = d and bestc = c. After checking all clusters, if ptsCluster[i] != bestc, it updates ptsCluster[i] = bestc, sets changed = 1, and prints which point changed to which cluster. The function returns the changed flag.
notes_text: This implements Step 2 of K-Means. Note that squared Euclidean distance is used (no square root needed) since we only need relative comparisons. The function signature uses C-style arrays with separate X and Y coordinate arrays.

title: Updating Cluster Mean (Center) Code
summary: Provides C++ solution code for the update_centers function that recalculates each cluster centroid as the mean of its assigned points.
main_text: Updating Cluster Mean (Center). The function update_centers takes arrays of point coordinates (ptsX, ptsY), cluster assignments (ptsCluster), number of points N, center coordinates (centersX, centersY), and number of clusters K. It returns void. For each cluster c from 0 to K-1, it initializes sumx = 0, sumy = 0, and ccnt = 0. For each point i from 0 to N-1, if ptsCluster[i] equals c, it accumulates sumx += ptsX[i], sumy += ptsY[i], and increments ccnt. After iterating through all points, if ccnt > 0, it sets centersX[c] = sumx / ccnt and centersY[c] = sumy / ccnt. This computes the arithmetic mean of all points assigned to each cluster to update the centroid position.
notes_text: This implements Step 1 of K-Means. The guard if(ccnt > 0) prevents division by zero in case a cluster has no assigned points. The function uses a nested loop structure: outer loop over clusters, inner loop over all points to find members of each cluster.

title: Unit 5 - Review Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing the Unit 5 Review for CS 102, authored by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5 - Review. Mark Redekopp.
notes_text: This is the title slide for the Unit 5 cumulative review covering all major topics from the course.

title: Units Overview
summary: Summarizes the four main units of CS 102, from scalar processing through divide and conquer, with visual diagrams for each unit.
main_text: Unit 1: Scalar processing. Unit 2: Linear (1D) Processing. Unit 3: Multidimensional Processing. Unit 4: Divide & Conquer (Functional Decomposition). Each unit builds on the previous, progressing from processing single values to processing arrays, then multidimensional data, and finally breaking problems into smaller functions.

title: Questions 1 - Pass-by-Value vs Pass-by-Reference and Conditionals
summary: Review questions covering array passing conventions, scalar variable passing, function argument naming rules, and simplifying conditional expressions.
main_text: Arrays are passed-by-____________. What does that mean? int, double, char, and bool variables are passed-by-____________. What does that mean? True/False: The name of an argument in a function signature must match the variable passed to the function. Assuming x is an 'int', write an equivalent if statement to replace if(x < 40 || x > 40). Example code shown: void f1(int x) { ... } int main() { int x = 5; f1(x); }. The code demonstrates that the parameter name in the function definition does not need to match the variable name used when calling the function. The blank for arrays should be filled with 'reference' and for scalar types with 'value'.
notes_text: Arrays are passed by reference, meaning changes inside the function affect the original array. Scalar types (int, double, char, bool) are passed by value, meaning a copy is made. The equivalent if statement for if(x < 40 || x > 40) is if(x != 40). The True/False about argument names is False.

images.description: Code snippet showing a void function f1 that takes an int parameter x, and a main function that declares int x = 5 and calls f1(x), illustrating that parameter names are independent of caller variable names.

title: Questions 2 - Conditionals, Boolean Logic, and Strings
summary: Review questions on if/else rules, evaluating compound boolean expressions, null-terminated character arrays, and the difference between character literals and string literals.
main_text: True/False: It is possible to have an 'else' statement without a corresponding 'if'. True/False: It is possible to have an 'else if' statement without a following 'else'. True/False: If x = 100 and y = -100 then the following 'if' statement will evaluate to true: if ( x != 100 || y > 0 || y != 100) { }. Character array strings (written in double quotes ("...")) end with what special character? True/False: There is no difference between 'a' and "a".
notes_text: An 'else' without an 'if' is not possible (False). An 'else if' without a following 'else' is valid (True). For the boolean expression with x=100, y=-100: x != 100 is false, y > 0 is false, y != 100 is true (since y is -100, not 100), so the overall OR expression is true (True). Character arrays end with the null terminator '\0'. There IS a difference between 'a' (a char) and "a" (a string containing 'a' and '\0'), so the statement is False.

title: Questions 3 - Character Arrays, C++ Strings, and Pass-by-Value
summary: Review questions on character array concatenation limitations, C++ string size tracking, and tracing function calls with pass-by-value semantics.
main_text: True/False: You can append a character to a character array using the '+' operator. For example: char str[10] = "Hi"; str = str + "t"; would yield "Hit". How could you make the char array have the word "hit"? True/False: C++ strings track their size. What will the code to the right print? Code shown: int f1(int x) { x = x-1; return x; } int main() { int x = 5; f1(x); cout << x; }. The question tests understanding that since x is passed by value to f1, the modification inside f1 does not affect x in main.
notes_text: You cannot use '+' to concatenate C-style character arrays (False). You would need to use strcat() or manually assign characters. C++ string objects do track their size (True). The code prints 5 because x is passed by value to f1, so the decrement inside f1 only affects the local copy. The return value of f1 is not captured, so x in main remains 5.

images.description: Code snippet showing function f1 that takes int x by value, decrements it, and returns it. Main declares int x = 5, calls f1(x) without capturing the return value, and prints x. This demonstrates pass-by-value behavior where x in main remains 5.

title: Trace the Program Output - Array Reversal
summary: A code tracing exercise where students must determine the output of a program that reads an array, attempts to reverse it using a swap loop, and prints the result.
notes_text: This is a common tracing pitfall. The swap loop runs from i=0 to i<n instead of i<n/2, so every swap is undone. At i=0 it swaps data[0] and data[3], at i=1 it swaps data[1] and data[2], at i=2 it swaps data[2] and data[1] (undoing the previous swap), and at i=3 it swaps data[3] and data[0] (undoing the first swap). The output is the original array: 3 17 8 1.

images.description: Full C++ program in a yellow code box that reads an integer n, reads n integers into an array, runs a swap-based loop over all n elements attempting to reverse, then prints the array contents separated by spaces.

title: Trace the Program Output - Multiple Functions with Arrays
summary: A complex code tracing exercise involving three functions (f1, f2, f3) operating on an array, testing understanding of pass-by-reference arrays, modular arithmetic, and function calls.
notes_text: This is the problem slide without solution annotations. Students must trace through f3(dat[7], dat[1], 3) = f3(12, 5, 3) first. Since 12 % 5 != 0 and 12 % 3 == 0, it returns c=3. Then f1(dat, 8, 3) sets d[i] = 9 for i=0 to i<=8/3=2, modifying dat[0], dat[1], dat[2] to 9. Then f2(dat, 1, 6) sums even elements from index 1 to 5: dat[1]=9(odd), dat[2]=9(odd), dat[3]=8(even), dat[4]=2(even), dat[5]=4(even) = 14. Output is 14 on the first line, then 9 9 9 8 2 4 2 12 on the second line.

The right box shows f3 (conditional return based on modular arithmetic) and main (initializes array, calls functions, prints results).

title: Trace the Program Output - Solution
summary: Provides the annotated solution for the multi-function tracing exercise from slide 8, showing step-by-step how f3 returns 3, f1 updates the array, and f2 returns 14.
main_text: This slide shows the same code as slide 8 with solution annotations. Step-by-step trace: f3(dat[7], dat[1], 3) = f3(12, 5, 3). Since 12 % 5 != 0, check else if: 12 % 3 == 0, so b -= 1 (b becomes 4) and return c, which is 3. f3(...) returns 3. f1(dat, 8, 3) is called. Loop runs for i=0 to i <= 8/3 = 2. Sets d[0] = 9, d[1] = 9, d[2] = 9. f1(...) updates d[0] = 9, d[1] = 9, d[2] = 9. Array is now {9, 9, 9, 8, 2, 4, 2, 12}. f2(dat, 1, 6) sums even elements from index 1 to 5: dat[1]=9 (odd, skip), dat[2]=9 (odd, skip), dat[3]=8 (even, sum=8), dat[4]=2 (even, sum=10), dat[5]=4 (even, sum=14). f2(...) returns 14. Output line 1: 14. Output line 2: 9 9 9 8 2 4 2 12.
notes_text: Key takeaways: Arrays are passed by reference so f1 modifies the original dat array. Integer division 8/3 = 2 (truncated). The modular arithmetic in f3 determines which branch executes. Note that c += 2 in the first branch and b -= 1 in the second branch are local modifications that do not affect the caller since a, b, c are passed by value.
